- - BABY IN THE LOOKING-GLASS. What a naughty face is this, Frowning 'neath each sunny curl! Who can this be? Barely not Father's own dear little girl. Father's pet has gentle eyes, And a month that on me smiled; But within the glass I see Nothing bat a naughty child. Let me look again. Ah ! now, What sweet face ía this I see? Why, it's father's own dear lass Dimpling o'er with sunny glee.
•—ro-Peep for September.
THE FALLOW FIELD.

Ths days were bright, and the year was young, As the warm sun climbed the sky; And a thousand flowers their censers swung, And the larks were singing high; For an angel swept on silent wing To the grave where the dead earth lay ; And the Easter dawned as the angel Spring Rolled the rugged stone away. Then the fields grew green with springing corn, And some with flowers were bright; And each day came with an earlier dawn, And a fuller, sweeter light. So the year grew older noon by noon, Till the reapers came one day, And in the light of a harvest-moon They bore the sheaves away. But one field lay from the rest apart, All silent, lone, and dead; And the rude share ribbed its quivering heart Till all its life had fled. And never a blade, and never a flower Oa its silent ridges stirred ; The eunshine celled, and the passing shower— It answered never a word. It seemed as if some curse of ill Were brooding in the air, Yet the fallow tield did the Masieel will Though never a blade it bare; For it turned its farrowed face to heaven Catching the light and rain: It was keeping its riabbath—one in seven— That it might grow rich again. And the fallow field had its harvest. moon, Reaping a golden spoil ; And it learned in its ever-brightening noon That rest for God was toil. —Good Words. EIENRY BURTON.

When about to break up for the holidays, Mr. Spurgeon dismissed his young men with a caution. "Don't get court- ing. That is not good for students. Come back, as some one puts it, with you hearts and manners uncracked. Walk in the fields like Isaac, by all means, and meditate, but don't lift up your eyes for Re;ma. She will come soon enough." WEAR. Sarms.—Which will you do—smile and make others happy, or be crabbed and make everybody around you miserable? You can live as it were, among beautiful flowers and singing birds, or in the mire, surrounded by fogs and frogs The amount of hanoiness you can produce te incalculable if you show a smiling face, a kind heart, and Speak pleasant words. There are ten things for which no one has ever yet been sorry :—For doing good to all, for speaking evil of no one, for hearing before judging, for thinking before speaking, for holding an angry tongue, for being kind to the dis- tressed, for asking pardon for all wrongs, for being patient towards everybody, for stopping the ears of a talebearer, and for dieJelieving evil reports. "THAT'S How."—After a great snowstorm a little fellow bsgan to shovel a path through a large snow-bank before his grandmother's door. Be had nothing but a small shovel to work with. "Bow do you expect to get through that drift?" asked a man passing along. "By keeping at it, sir," said the boy, cheerfully; "that's how." That is the secret , of mastering almost every difficulty under the sun. If a hard task is before you, stick to it. Do not keep thinking , how large or how hard it is, but go at it, and little by little it will grow smaller and smaller until it is done. How TO MIKE AN AQUATUCTM FOR CHILDIIEN.—A cor- respondent writes :—I beg to recommend the following method of stocking a small aquarium for children; and it need be, I shall be glad to communicate with applicant by letter, telling him where some of the things may be obtained. First, as to selection ofitceptacle. I prefer the bell-shaped glass to the square or oblong aquarium with wood or other frames. The former looks very pretty, and is no trouble on account of leakages. Then, as to choice and treatment of plants. The first and foremost, no doubt, is valisneria ; a dozen roots would be eufficient—cost about ninepence, and may be hod of any naturalists. After trying many methods recommended in books, I find these to thrive beat, as fol- lows :—Take a little good soil, rather clayey, and press a small portion round each root separately, then arrange the roots according to taste in a layer of the soil, at the bottom of the aquarium. Other plants, such as frog-bit, anacharie, or chars valgarie, might be added in the same manner, but the valisneria alone, which is said to be the only fresh- water evergreen, looks very pretty, and grows luxuriantly if treated as above. Over this earth sprinkle some fine river sand, well washed and scalded with boiling water. A few shells and pebbles nicely placed add to the beauty of the aquarium. Then fill with clear water. Avoid tsp.water, if other can be obtained, as it does not contain support enough for the live stock. If the mud from the bottom rises and does not clear, empty the water out a time or two; refill, and let it stand for seven or ten days before adding the live stock. After this yon may safely put in, say, a dozen fishes, such as minnow, dace, roach, or golden carp. A few trumpet snails, and common snails are also useful as scavengers. With these you may have a very pretty aquarium, and if the animal and vegetable life be nicely balanced, the water need rarely be changed. But the glass will occasionally require cleaning. A kind of green scum accumulating on the glass is a sure sign that you have too many plants in the aquarium. You may vary the stock, however, by adding newts or water-beetles, of which letter there are many varieties, two Interesting specimens being the "boatman. beetle " and the little "whirligig beetle," There is also another amusing inhabitant of ponds which might be introduced, and that, for want of the correct name, I cal a fresh-water shrimp. It is exceedingly like an ordin- ary shrimp, but not more than half an inch in length. The newts are, however, addicted to taking nocturnal walks abroad unless the aquarium is provided with a perforated zinc cover. A little virgin cork floating on the surface of the water and covered with 11109S1 forms a convenient island for the newts to climb on to. The shrimps will also hide on it, and the snails breed there. The fishes are apt to be troeblesome to the beetles, &C., and will in time destroy 'Orem. SEASONABLE HINTS.

It is often found at this season of the year that chickens are troubled with diarthcet, chiefly resulting from the green food eaten by them, though sometimes a too rich diet is the cause. As a preventive there is nothing better than bone meal, which we have often recommended before, and of which a little should be put in the soft food every day. It has a most beneficial effect upon the stomach, and at th same time provides material for building up the frame o the bird, supplying just those qualities which are often wanting, and which in a state of nature the fowls would be able to obtain for themselves quite easily. Should diar• rhosa declare itself, a little more bone meal may be mixed in the soft food, and if that does not stop it, a drop of chlorodyne should be given in water twice a day. This we have found a most valuable remedy in attacks of diarrhce both with human subjects and fowls.

The Marquis of Londonderry conducted the consecration ceremony or a new masonic lodge launched on temperanc, principles, at Sunderland, on ttuclay, The lodge is named the Londonderry, number 2039. The drill-instructor of an old English regiment—one of the old stamp of martinet sergeants—who was the terror of every recruit, and the remorseless tyrant of the awkward squad, was putting a firing party through the funeral exercise. Raving open the ranks, so as to admit the passage of the supposed cortege between them, the instructor ordered the men to "rest on their arms reversed" Then by way of practical illustration, be walked slowly down the lane formed by the two ranks, saving, as he moved, "Now, lam the corpse! Pay attention." Raving reached the end of the party, be turned round, regarded them steadily with a scrutinising eye for a moment or two, and then remarked in a solemn tone of voice, " Your 'ands is right, and your 'eads is right; but you 'aven't got that look of regret you ought to 'ave."
TYPHO:D OR DRAIN FEVER, AND HOW TO PREVENT IT.

This fever has been called drain fevtr, from its frequent association with bad and imperfect drainage in houses. At °Fie time it was confounded with typhus fever; hence i s name typhoid, but it is now known to be quite a distinct disease. It is also often spoken of as low fever, from the great exhaustion and weakness waich attends it. It is a highly contagious fever. The means by which this disease may largely be preven• ted from spreading are very simple, and depend upon the fact that the poison by which it sureads is to a great extent contained in the discharges from the bowels. Dr. W. Budd gives the following excellent directions for preventing the spread of this disease. Ile says the discharges from the bowels infect- 1. The air of the sick-room.
2. The bed and body linen of the patient. 3. The privy and the ce3spool, or the drains proceeding from them.

From the privy or the drain, the poison often soaks into the well, and infects the drinking water. This last, when it happens, is of all forms of fever-poisoning the most deadly. In these various ways, the infection proceeding from the bowel-discharges often spreads the fever far and wide. The one great thing to aim at, therefore, is to disinfect these dis- charges on their very escape from the body, and before they are carried from the sick-room. This may be perfectly done by the use of disinfectants. One of the best is made of green copperas. This substance, which,is used by all shoemakers, is very cheap, and may be had everywhere, A. pound and a half of green copperas to a gallon of water is the proper strength. A teacupful of this liquid, put into the nightpan every time before it is used by the patient, renders the bowel. discharge perfectly harmless. To disinfect the bed and body linen, and bedding generally, Calvert's Carbolic Powder, or the Universal Disinfecting Powder (non-poisonous), is more convenient. These powders should be sprinkled, by means of a common dredger, on soiled spots of the linen, and about the room, to purify-the air. All articles of bed and body linen should be plunged, immediately on their removal from the bed, into a bucket of water containing a teaspoonful of chloride of lime or half a teacup- ful of Condy's Fluid, and should be boiled before being washed. The privy, or closet, and all drains communicating with it, should be flashed twice daily with the green copperas liquid or carbolic acid, diluted with water. In towns and villages where the fever is already prevalent, the last rule should be put in force in all houses, whether there be fever in them or not, and for all public drains. In the event of death, the body should be placed as soon as pos ible, in a coffin surrounded with charcoal, sprinkled with disinfectants. Early burial is, on all accounts, desirable. As the hands of those attending the sick often becomo unavoidably soiled by the discharges from the bowels' they should be freqnently washed. The sick room should be kept well ventilated, day and night. The greatest poseible care should be taken with regard to drinking water. Where there is the slightest ri,k of.its having become tainted with fever-poison, water should be got from a pure source, or should at least be boiled before being drunk. Immediately after the illness is over, whether ending in death or recovery, the dresses worn by the nurses should be washed or destroyed, and the bedroom occupied b‘ the sick should be thoroughly disinfected. These are golden rules. Where they are neglected, the fever may become a deadly scourge. Where they are strictly carried oat, It.sel- dom spreads beyond the person first attacked. A yard of thin wide-width gutta percha placed under the blanket, under the breech of the patient, by effectually preventing the discharges from soaking into the bed, is a great additional safeguard. ,

TEE FOUNDING OF COVENT GARDEN Mani:W.—Who would imagine that Covent Garden, with its shady, many- scented arcade, with its Babel of aoices and crush of bas- kets, its flowers "a-growing and a-blowing," its carious mixed atmosphere of town and country—who would now imagine that this had once been an " Enclosure or Pasture," "browsed by deep-ndder'd kine," and where, maybe, the nightingale, "in April suddenly, Brake from a cripples gemm'd with green and red"? Yet so it was. Covent Garden or "Convent Garden,"lying between Long Acre and the Strand, originally formed part of the grounds of the ancient Abbey of Westminster. There is still extant a document," written in very choice Italian" (if so one may term law Latin), in which it is described as •• le Covent Garden . . . wiper pertinens Monasterio Sancti Petri Westmonasteriensis.' Under Edward the Sixth it was granted by that King to his uncle, the Duke Of Somerset. At Somerset's attainder it reverted to the Crown, and then' "with seven acres called Long Acre" was re- granted by patent to John Earl of Bedford. This was in May, 1552. Upon part of the " terre et pasture" so ac- quired, the Earl built the old semi-wooden structure known as Bedford House, which looked into the Strand, and the long wall of whose garden at the hack corresponded to what is now the south side of the market. Under Francis Duke of Bedford, circa 1631, the square was laid out, and the arcades or piazzas erected.—The English Illustrated Maga- zine for September. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The usual monthly meeting of the shove body was held on Tuesday evening, at the CRIOCii Chamber at the Town Hall, under the presidency of the Mayor (Alderman Harri- son), there being also present Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Kean Piclimere, rhewlie, Davies; Councillors Dixon, Fran- comb,, Brown, Burgess, Wallington, Taylor, Crosfield. Whittle, Mackie, Ashton, Bolton, Caldwell, and John Pier- point. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.—THE WOOD PAVING.— A SERIOUS NUISANCE. Alderman ICEeN moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee. They had, he said, resolved that the borough surveyor should report upon the wood paving in Sankey-street. He had expected they would have had that report before them, but the surveyor had not had time to go into the matter. At the next Council meet- ing they would have full particulars. Councillor MACKIE asked if the borough surveyor, with ' all his knowledge, cleverness, and experience, could give them a report that could in any sense be trustworthy? He could not see any great wisdom in asking the surveyor, especially if he was busy, to give that report. Would it not be as well to let the matter rest for twelve months? To him it smacked of a wish of some that the paving should not last and be a success. At the end of twelve months the committee would be able to give a very good report. Alderman BURGESS, referring to the minute that the com- mittee considered the question of the damage done to the sewer in Folly-lane, caused by the drainage of the railway embankment of the Cheshire Lines Committee into it, and resolved that the borough surveyor be instructed to request Mr Scott, the engineer of the com- pany, to send a competent person to inquire into the matter, eaid that there was something of much more serious consequence to Warring- ton than the damage done to the sewer by the drainage. He meant the stench that was in consequence emitted from the sewer, and he hoped that the committee in dealing with I this matter would take good care that the railway cone- pane', who were the originators of the stench, which had be- come intolerable, should be given to understand that nothing less than the removal of the CillS3 of the nuisance would ! satisfy the inhabitants. A great advantage had been taken by someone, but the railway company was answerable for it. With reference to an application from the Post Office De- partment, requesting permission to take up the footpath, and cross the roads from Dellam-lane, along Tanner's-lane, Bewsey-street, Edgeworth-street, Legh-street, and Sankey- street to the Post Office, for the purpose of laying a pipe for : ander greund wires, and a recommendation that permission be granted subject to the Corporation relaying and making good the roads at the cost of the Post Office, be said that he should like to know if that was all that was required from the committee. He presumed that if a private company made a similar application the committee would secure the right of removing at any time the under ground wires. He did not know whether the Post Office had special power in the matter, but if not he thought there was a weakness about the recommendation, and that the Post Office should be re- quired to pay a small annual fine or acknowledgment that they were trespassing. Regarding the wood paving in Sankey-street, he differed from Councillor Mecaie, as he thought an opinion might be formed then as well as twelve months hence. Councillor Mackie seemed. to have got the idea that he was there simply to protect and improve Sankey- street—(laughter)—and he (Mr. Burgess) did not care how much he did .hat, if it was not at the cost of the borough generally. The MAYOR mentioned that there was wood paving in some thoroughfares in London, where the traffic was enormous. Alderman BURGESS: I may say London is the last place in the world I should ask for information. Alderman KvAN: But he has frequently gone there. Laughter.) The minutes were then confirmed. THE INSURANCE OF PICTURES. Councillor BURGESS, in moving the adoption of the mine utes of the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee, which were passed,, remarked that at the last meeting of the Coun- cil, something was said in reference to the cost of insuring the pictures received as loans, and mentioned that the policy already held by the committee was sufficient, so that no further cost would be incurred. TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman PICKMERE seconded the adoption of the minutes of this c tritnittee. Alderman THEWLIS was glad to see that from tire to time the dead trees had been removed from the park. There were yet some left, and the sooner they were removed the better, as it would add to the appearance of the park. Alderman BURGESS said that no harm would be done if a little attention was paid to the planting of young trees to take the place of those removed. There did not seem to be a sufficient amount of attention paid to that particular. Alderman ICEAN said that proper attention should be paid to trees planted in the streets. They were informed by com- petent people that they would flourish as well as those in the park if they were properly attended to. Councillor MACKIE remedied that it was due to the com- mittee to say that the question had frequeutly been dis- cussed. He was afraid that the committee had come to the conclus'on that between the Warrington climate and the Warrington boys there was no chance for the cultivation of trees in the streets. If any of them could give information on the subject he was sure the committee would carefully inquire into it. Alderman PICKMERE said that they had gene to consider- able expense in renewing trees in the streets, and although they had been watered and fresh soil put down they did not flomish.

A discussion followed as to the condition of the trees in various ports of the town, after which the minutes of the committee were adopted. SANITARY COMMITTEE —TTIE DANGERS OF SANITARY NEGLIGENCE. Alderman BURGESS, in moving the confirmation of the re- port of the Sanitary Committee, referred to a report of the Medical Officer on Precautions against diarrhea and cholera." There was no desire, he said, that anything like' excitement should attain in consequence of the issuing of that report, but the recommendations it contained to house- holders and others, were good, and should bc attended to at any and all times. There was nothing to be lost, but a good deal to be gained, by carrying out the recommendations. People did not always know the dangers that arose in their own houses. It had come to his knowledge that in one in- stance there was a cistern that supplied several houses with water that bad only been clesns2d once within the last 15 years. When it was emptied about ten days ago, about a ton and a half of black solid material was taken from it. That was by no means an isolated case, and people could not be to) careful in regard to such matters. Occupiers of houses should pay strict attention to such matters, and where they required assistance should communicate with the Sanitary Committee, who would ren- der all possible help. Councillor CROSFIELD seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor DIXON was a little cli<appointed that they had no report on the new machines at Longford depot. He thought they should have some report as to what progress hat been made, and whether the machines were likely to answer the purpose. Alderman BURGESS said they had no report of a formal character to present, but it might be satisfactory to Mr Dixon to keow that the result of the experiment at Long• ford had so far exceeded their exoectetions. In a short time the committee would be prepared to submit a report and ask the Cornell for privilege to extend the system so as to deal with the whole of their property. The report was confirmed. FIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE. Alderman PICKMERE, in proposing the adoption of the minutes of this committee, said that on making ir quiries he found that there had been a very good attendance on the part of the members of the brigade; the committee were perfectly satisfied with the attendance. Councillor Dix ee said that the insurance companies were presaine for a higher insurance in this district in consequence of the Fire Brigade not being in as efficient a state as in other districts. Alderman PICKMERE said that he had never heard any complaint of the brigade, eor bed he heard of the insurance companies asking a higher rate, and Councillor MACKIE re- marked that it was only just to state that one of the insu- rance companies had been insisting on a higher rate of insu- rance for some years.—Alderman PICKMERE thought that the reason was the scarcity of water. The minutes were adopt,d. THE LETTING OF CORPORATE PROPERTY. Councillor BURGESS moved "That the following resolu- tion passel by the Council on the sth August, 1834, be re- scinded, viz. :—That Messrs W El Pritchard and E Williams of White•street, be allowed the use of the upper room of the building in John-strset, on Sundays, for the next six months et a rent to be arranged afterwards." He said that it might be objected that it was not desirable to move the rescindment of a resolution so soon after it had been passed by the Council, but that in question was, he thought, an ex- ceptional one. It involved a very important principle and less than half the Council were present when it was pissed. There was a strong feeling on the part of many members of the Council that it would be a m;stake to allow the resolu- tion to stand, for if so it would form a doubtful precedent. (Hear, bear.) Under these circumstances he did not hesi- tate to take upon himself the responsibility of asking that the matter should be reconsidered that night. They had been asked to let the building in question to two young men who would use if for the performance of divine worship on Sundays. He believed that they were very respectable men and he did not care to what denomination they be- longed, but he thought that it would be a mistake to allow them to use a corporation building for religious purposes, when there was accommodation elsewhere. Even if there were no other accommod ition he doribted whether they would be justified in taking that action. He did not doubt that the young men were anxious to hold religious services, end it was creditable to them, but he considered that their request for the use of A room that was a portion of corporate property was ill-advised. He should like to know whether the Council had sufficiently considered whether they were eoing to provide a public building for the parpore of nur- sing religions bodies. These people, no doubt, wished to do good, but there was plenty of room in Warrington both for them and their religious teaching, and he did not think that the Council would be inflicting any harm upon them, or in any way hinder their work, by adopting the course that he proposed. Alderman HOLMTS seconded the proposition. NIZEIGN NEWS. 'EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. TRE GORDON RELIEF EXPEDITION. CAIRO, SATURDAY.—A telegram from Wady Haifa, dated Friday, 9 p.m., announces that the steamers Mahalla and Saidieh have arrived there with Sir Evelyn Wood, Colonel Duncan, and Major Sandwith, and staff, together with two companies of the 4th Egyptian Battalion and two more companies of the Royal Sussex Regiment. CAIRO, SIINDAY.—A telegram from Wady Haifa, dated one o'clock, announces that the steamer Nile has arrived with two more companies of the Royal Sussex Regiment, making a total of 600 men at that place. One company will start for Saross to-morrow. CAIRO, MONDAY.—A despatch from Wady Haifa of Yesterday's date states that Major Kitchener telegraphs that five letters have been received from General Gordon, the latest of which is dated June 15th, and announces that Khartoum cau hold oat for four months. The despatch adds that the Massifhera has arrived at Wady Haifa with the cables and gear for the second cataract, and will be towed up to-morrow. The Mudir of Dongola is sending snore boats to the cataracts for the transport service. Sir Evelyn Wood has called a meeting of the doubtful Bishareen Sheikhs, SIJAKIM, FRIDAY.—The Jaffariyeh overtook, not far to the south of Suakim, the three dhows recently captured by, the rebels. The latter, on being overtaken, ran the boats aground, and escaped inland. The crew of the Jaffariyeh subsequently burned the dhows.—Monday: The rebels made their usual attack on the forts last night. On Saturday afternoon her Majesty visited Osborne Bay and inspected one of the boats built by Mr J. White, of Cowes for the Nile expedition. Orders have been tele- graphed to Ireland for 120 men of the let Battalion of the King's Royal Rides to embark early in the forthcoming week at Queenstown in the Poonah to strengthen the 3rd Battalion of th a same corps already in Egypt. It is ex- pected that another large force of Royal Marines will be despatched to take part in the expedition, and the com• mending officers of the various divisions have been instruc- ted to hold strong drafts in readiness for immediate em- barkation. Great activity prevails in the Ordnance De- partment at Chatham in preparing the stores which will be taken out by the 8:h and 11th Companies Royal Engineers, which embark for the Nile expedition. At the Royal Albert Docks the equipment and telegraph stores for the Royal Engineers are being shipped on the steamer Rewa. The 400 men of this cc rps, who go to Egypt in the Rewa, com• prise men of every trade. Lord Northbrook and Lord Wolseley paid a visit to Os- borne on Saturday, and took leave of her Majesty prior to their departure for Egypt. Lorel Northbrook left Victoria Station at 10 a.m. on Sunday for Canterbury, proceeding thence over the Deal and Dover Railway to Weimer Castle. Earl Granvillere state carriage was in waiting at the station, and conveyed his lordship to the Castle. Lord Wolseley left London on Sunday evening for Dover, en route for Egypt. From Cdais Lord Wolseley. with ford Northbrook, Proceeded direct to Vienna, in a through`carriage reserved for their use. _ _ _

A force will be despatched to the frontier of Egypt (Wady Haifa) with a view to being sent on to Dongola should the course of events render it necessary. Although the move- ment of mounted infantry and of some battalions of in- fantry up the Nile has already commenced, the strength and composition of the force will not b 3 settled till Lord Wolseley has arrived in Egypt and consulted with Sir F Stephenson. Four hundred boats for the transport of the force will arrive in Alexandria between September 21st and 30th, and a further supply of 400 boats will follow, at an early date. Five hundred Canadians will arrive at Alexan- dria at the beginning of October, and 300 Kroomen from Africa about the 10th of the same month to assist in navi- gating the bolts. Etcti °oil will contain 100 days' supplies. The first consi4nment of 400 boats will be at once forwarded to Wady Haifa. The ration for the boat service is special, based on the assumption that the troops may be for a con• eiderable perio I entirely dependent on these supplies. It is believed th it the force will be in a condition to advance 'from Wady Lialfa, should circumstances render it necessary, by November Ist. A Woolwich telngram says 1,000 tarpaulins for boats used in Khartoum have been contracted for, as also 30,000 yards of rope for towing purposes. A second order for half a million pounds of beef has been cent to Chicago. The hired transport Poonah arrived at Queenstown on Tuesday from Plymouth, and embarked additional troops 'for Egypt. SDAKIM, TIIESDIY.—Another mine, laid by the British outside the town, was removed by the rebels. It was after- "wards seen to explode in the Enemy's clog, at Handvoh.

CAIRO, TIIESDAY.—M ijor Kitchener telegraphs that the route from Dmgola to Berber is practically open, the hostile tribls having dispersed, and the flying column of four or five thousand British troops could easily march across.
CAIRO, TUESDAY—The Khedive has placed the Kasr-el- lioussah Palace, in Cairn, at the disposal of Lord Wolseley, Who has accepted the off n. of his hirchness. PROPOSED NEW CONFERENCE ON EGYPT.

VIENNA, WEDNESDAY —The Earl of Northbrook and Lord Wolselev arrived here to-day. They will resume their journey to Trieste tomorrow morning. PARIS, WEDNFSDAY.—The 'Republique Francaise of this morning believes that the report is correct that Austria and Germany intend proposing a fresh Conference of the Powers. The journal adds, however, that the Conference would only be occupied with the discussion of two points, namely, the settlement of the Alex andriaindetnnities and the sanitary uolice measure for the Suez Canil. There would be-no question of the adoption of measures against the Anse- CiliStS. BERLIN. WEDNESDAY.—The rumours of the proposal for a second Conference on Egyptian affairs are regarded in semi-official circles Isere as indicating a desire on the part of the French Government for the se'tlement of the Egyp- tian question throu_eh the intervention of diplomacy. CArao, WEDNESDIY.—A. telegram from Wady Haifa, dated six o'clock yesterday evening, announces that the steamer Ghizeh has arrived, and will endeavour to pass the second cataract to-d ty. The steamers when going up the cataracts will be slung in cables passed under their keels and attached to steel hawsers passed round their hulls, by Which they will be hauled. The Mudir of Dongola asks that the first steamer which gets up may be sent to him at Merawi, his own steamer being out of order. THE ATTACKS ON &TAMIL
SUAIKIM, TII-U7R-S—DAY.—For -t-he. last three nights the at- tacks of the rebels have been feeble. Spies from Osman

Digma's camp teport that 15 deaths occurred from the ex- ! plosion of the mire. They state that the rebels intend to I make an attack in force shortly. A mail which has arrived here from Maspowa reports that the Abyssinian frontier is undiqurbed. The town of Kassala is surrounded by a large body of rebels, and no communication from that place is at present possible.—DaU y News, THI3 WAR BETWEEN FRANCE AND CHINA.

--- SUANGIIAI, SATITRDAY.—AII French subjects have now left Canton. 'I he French quadron, under Admiral Courbet, has left the Min river, after completely destroying the forts. Its destination is said to be Canton, though nothing positive is known on the subject. The Chinese military commanders have received an Imperial order from Pekin instructing them to attack all French war ships and merchant vessels entering or having the treaty ports, and ordering all French merchant vessels already in those ports to leave without de- lay. Telegrams ire not accepted by the Chinese Govern- ment lines unless written in the English language. PARIS, SATURDAY.—GeneraI Minot, French Commander in Tonquin, has asked to be relieved of his post on grounds of ill-health. The Government has sanctioned his return to France. General Briere de Lisle _will succeed him in the _ _

Chief -command. The Minister of Marine has received from Admiral Courbat a telegram, dated Fic Aign, six o'clock es eiday evening :—All the b ttteries on the river Min are destroyed, and wo have exploded with gun-cotton the • greater part of the.guns. All the ships of the squadron left the river Min to-d g, and several have reached the Matson anchorage. I shall arrive there to-morrow. We have ten killed, including one officer ; 1 seriously wounded, includ- ing one officer; and 28 wounded, including one superior officer and three subalterns-51 in all. FOOCHOW, SATURDAY.—AdmiraI Dowell was fired upon recently. The English Consul narrowly escaped from the Viceroy's,ratnen in Chinese costme. The French believe and hope that their programme of bombarding and then leaving will involve the Chinese with the Neutral Powers. HONG KONG, SUNDAY.—The French ships had, on the day . previous to the attack, saluted the Chinese flag on the occa- sion of the Emperor's birthday: The foreigners resident in the treaty ports severely censure the French action in enter- lug the Min under the b inner of friendship, the forte being arranged so as to fire outwards towards the s-a. pAnis, T"srAy,—. V telegram freua Shanghai dated this .morning says —According to letters from Tientsin, Li Hung Chang has been degraded, and deprived of his titles of Chief Minister and Vicroy. This news, however, requires con- firmation. The Kreach here are expecting that an order will be issued expelling them from Shanghai. The Chinese authorities are in a most excited state. PAZ'S, TCTESlUY.—Presithnt Grev7 has received a letter signed by members of the Extreme Left, demanding the convocation of tbe Chsobers, in view of the war with China and the expenditure of credits not authorised by the As.sernbly. ADMIRAL C,W.RBE PS MOVEMENTS. _

PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—Tbe Paris denies the report that ,General Millet has asked for reinforcements. The Temp states that the present movements of Admiral Courbet's ,cquadron remain a secret, but that it is very probable that the Admiral has gone to (3=o point where he will be able to meet two steamers and a transport which are on their way from Tonquin with troops destined to co-operate with the feet in some fresh operations. A telegram frcm Hongkong dated midnight, announces that the Frencl ironclad L Galissonike had just ar- rived there for the protectior..Of the French merchant marine. FARIS, Tnunsni,..x.—A despatoh, dated 12-35 this after- noon, has been receival here from liong Kong stating that the Chinese have cut a military road through the French cemetery at Canton, destroying a rnatiffoientn in the course t)f their operations. It FoLadded that they also rifled several tombs. The Frmch Consul at Hong Kong yesterday received from the Chinese authorities the sum of 27,000 dollars, the indemnity agreed upon for the loss suffered by French subj,cts in the riot at Canton, in September, 1883.

SPREAD OF THE CHOLERA. PARIS, MOND'IY.---91:1 Sa'urdiy, at Marseilles, 15 deaths from cholera wern eported, yesterday 5, and to-day 9. At Toulon there wire no deaths on Saturday; and only two on Sunday. In the departments 79 %TM reverted on Situdab Rin4 23 yesterday.

ROME, MONDAY.—The cholera is rapidly increasing. The following is one day's bulletin :—Provinces of Aguila, one case of cholera, followed by death ; Bergamo, 15 cases, 6 deaths; Bologna, 3 fresh cases, 3 deaths; Campabassa. 9 cases, 4 deaths; Cremonr, 1 care; Cuueo, 35 cases, 21 deaths, 8 of the latter occur, Mg at Busca ; town of Cuneo, 20 deaths; Provinces of Genoa, 27 deaths, of which 24 oc- curred at Spezia; Massa Carrara, 14 cases, 6 deaths; Parma, cases, 2of which proved fatal ; and Turin, 5 cases. No ft...A cases or deaths are reported from the city of Naples. One death has occurred at Sant Anastasia. MADRID. TUESDAY. —.There now appears little doubt that the disease which has broken out in the province of Alicante is cholera. It is believed to have been imported by a family which recently arrived at Alicante from Cotte by way of Algiers, to avoid undergoing quarantine on the Spanish frontier. The vessel in which they arrived from Algiers underwent seven days' qu trantine. Another case of sickness occurred yesterday at Alicante. The patient was immediately isolated. Sixteen persons have been at- tacked in all, and five have died, NAPLES, TllMDAY.—Forty,iige cases of cholera, of which twenty-one proved fatal, are announced as having occurred here. The increased number of cases is attributed to intem- perate living on Sunday, which was a fête day. ROME, TOESDAY.—The official bulletin to-day reporta the following deaths from cholera :—Province of Aguila, 1 ; Province of Bergamo, 9 ; Province of Campobasso, 1 ; Province of Cuneo. including Buoca, 11; Province of Genoa, including Speiza, 15; Province of Massa Carrara, 1; Pro- vince of Modena, 1; Province of Parma, 3; Province of Tuna, 3. NAPLES, WEDNESDAY.—Between sunset-on Monday and sunrise yesterday morning there have been 120 cases of cholera in this city. The epidemic is spreading in the neigh- bouring districts. MADRID, WEDNESDAY.—The mortality from cholera since the outbreak of the epidemic in Spain is stated in offi- cial quarters to be as follows :--Province of Alicante—Town of Etche, six cases, two deaths ; towd of Novelda, 42 deaths since August 28, 20 cases at present under treatment; town of Alicante, five deaths, three cases ander treatment. Pro- vince de Albacete—One Case in the town of Candete.

VIENNA., MONDAY—Four persons arrived here to-dry from Pesth, who are believed to be anarchists of the most danzereus character. At the house of one of them, an iron- worker named 'neer, various discoveries were made, includ- ing machinery for the manufacture of bombs and a number of bombs unmounted. The pcdica als) found a model for a dynamite box, which could not fail to explode on being opened.

BEREIN, SATURDAY.—lntelligence rec2ivecl here from St Petersburg states that during the recent anti-Jewish riots in the village of Dubrovitz t, neer Kovno twenty houses and twelve shops were pillaged by the mob. Many Jews were wounded, and one women was killed. The attempt made by Maria Kaljushnia to assesinate Got. Katanskv, at Odessa, was an act of revenge for the sentence of penal servitude passed upon her brother, a member of the Revolu- tionary party. RELEASE OF AN ENGLISII SUBJEC IN TURKEY.

CONSTANTINOPLE, SUNDAY.—Judge Fawcett has ordered the release of an English subject named Fischer, who has been detained for the !tat three months in a lunatic asylum at Ferkery, a suburb of this city. The grounds of this deci- sion are that Mr. Fischer is not insane, and was illegally sent from Smyrna to the asylum by some rela:ives without notice being given to the authorities. Mr. Fischer is now at the British Consulate pending further inquiry into his case.

div.head: UINTITEb STA.TES.—FATAL RIOTS.
div.p: UINTITEb STA.TES.—FATAL RIOTS.

NEW Yon, Mr:mom—On Saturday night some miners on strike in the Hocking Valley, Ohio, attacked the guards placed over the mines, killing one and wounding several of them. Since then the riot has assumed serious proportions. The coal hoppers have been burned and the telegraph lines cut. The last report states that the mob is beyond control. The miners are now encamped near the mines to prevent non-unionists from working. Troops have been despatched to the scene, and the Sheriff will real the Riot Act to-day. --4 p nt.—The riots have now subsided, and it is believed the worst is over.
