The funeral of the late Lord Ampthill took place on Wed- nesday at Chenies, Hertfordshire. The Duchess of Albany is unable to leave Claremont at present, in consequence of the precarious condition of her infant son.

A boy natned Avery, sentenced to a month's imprison- ment for etaling cigars, banged himself on Thursday morn- ing in hie cell in Durham Gaol. ASIATIC CHOLERA IN ENGLAND—What is described by the local medical officer of health as an unmistakable case of Asiatic cholera has occurred near Cardiff. The Italian steamer Abyssinia arrived in Penarth Roads on Friday from Marseilles. Three of the crew, rep)rted sick, were removed to the hospital prepared for cholera cases, and one of them died on Wednesday morning. The body has been taken out to aea and buried.

WIGAN CORPORATION FRAIIDS.-I:IOLT'S CONFESSION.— On Tuesday, at the Wigan Police Court, Willian Holt, late borough treasurer, and John Caldwell, stock and sharebroker, and late professional auditor to the Corporatiun, were again charged with stealing moneys belonging to the Corporation. They were further charged with a joint falsification of the annual accounts of the Corporation, and there was also a charge of conspiracy. The only evidence of interest on Tuesday was Holt's written confession. Holt traced all his troubles to the auditor (Caldwell) being a sharebroker. Reynolds, assistant to Caldwell, knowing prisoner's joint affairs, had sent him (Holt) scores of threatening letters' and he had had to keep him in idleness. Twice he had been sent to America, but had returned to extort more money. Holt had also been guarantee for Mawson for £5OO, and had lost money in a quarry at Withell, as well as on the Stock Exchange, by the advice of Reynolds.—At the Wigan Police Court, on Wednesday, Wm. Holt, late borough treasurer, and John Caldwell, stockbroker and professional auditor, were again brought up charged with jointly steal- ing several sums of money belonging to the Corporation, and with falsifying the annual accounts of the borough. The burgess auditors were examined and explained the character of the discrepancies and irregularities in the offi- cial books, after which a further remand was granted till next day. RECOLLECTIONS OF NELSON.—There is still living at Merton, in possession of all his faculties, a hale and hearty man, named Hudson, over 90 years old, who well remembers Lard Nelson as a visitor here, and who stood by the door of the postchaise in which, early on the morning of September L3th, 1805, the gallant admiral—so soon after orards doomed to fall at Trafalgar—drove off from Sr William Hamilton's gates. He states that, as a boy, he used often to see Nelson fishing in the Wandle, near the Abbey Mill, and sauntering with Sir William and Lady Hamilton about their pretty grounds, which extended on both sides of the high road. The admiral would often stop and speak kially to the bays who were at play in the street, and who regarded his weather. beaten form and features possibly with all the more rover. once becanse of the fruit and the pence which he would bestow on the youngsters. Two cottages at the bottom of the Abbey•lane, he says, were built by Lord Nelson for his coachman and gardener—BO entirely had a community of goods been carried out by this affectionatetrio •, in one of these he and hia wife, a daughter of Cribb, Nelson's gar- dener, have lived for upwards of half a century. This cot- tage is marked by a mulberry tree, which Nelson desired to be planted there. Over the mantelpiece of his little dwell- ing is a mirror in a gilt frame, which once formed part of the ornaments of Nelson's room in Sir William Hamilton'e house, and this he and his wife treasure as their only relic l'of the adnaird...-Cassell's Greater London.

Mr GLADSTONE, who was magnificently received, alluding to his speeches in Midlothian four and a half years ago, said their opponents bad stated that the declarations of the Mid- lothian campaign had been forgotten; but he would easily undertake, and perhaps before this visit concluded he might be able to show that they are still fresh in his recollection, and that he receded from none of them. (Loud cheers.) Having regretted that Scotch business had suffered, along with English and Irish, from the recent unhappy action of One branch of the Legislature, he referred, in passing, to the CIS3 of the Highland crofters, and said it was the deep con- viction of the Government that when they c mid find the Opportunity it would be their duty to give serious and sym- pathetic attentima to this question. Ile proceeded to dwell on the special purpose for which he had come to speak—to ; prom ee by every means in his power the speedy passing of the Franchise Bill. (Loud cheers ) If the word "re- jected "was civilled at by the Lords, he should say "Very well; we will only call it effectual stoppage of the bill," for there was no doubt that was a moderate, literal, and war- rantable description. But the rejection of that bill, and re- jection was the simplest and best phrase, had already drawn into its train other questions of the gravest kind, and had suggested to the minds of a vast portion of this people the inquiry whether the time has come when it will be necessary to study the means of introducing an organic change into the constitution of the House of Lords. (Loud cheers.) He looked with reluctance to entering upon question of or- ganic change in the Constitution until the moment catne , when he could no longer deny them. He believed the ' House of Lords had not yet placed itself in a position of ir- retrievable error, and it was possible it might come back I with dignity anti honour. (Laughter and cheers.) He de- tailed the position of the Government and the Opposition ' on the franchise question, showing the unanimity with which the bill finally passed the Commons. Be disposed of the Tory contention that a Redistribution Bill should be ! joined to the Franchise Bill by saying that the Conserva- tives knew as well as the Government did that had the , latter been such idiots and such dolts to join the two bills in one measure a disgraceful failure would have been the result. Re denied that tne Franchise Bill amounted to a revision of the Constitution, for it altered none of the powers of either Hausa of Parliament. The " service franchise," giving a vote to gamekeepers, sub-agents, and others not householders, was intended to disarm the Opposition. The ame with the ancient rights franchise, such as freemen en- soyed, both of which tended towards Toryism. They, how- ever, took the opportunity to stop the monstrous abuse of manufacturing faggot votes. (Loud cheers.) The Radical party, properly so called, viewed with very great jealousy those property franchises. They held the one man one vote principle. Several colleagues of his leaned a good deal to that principle. (A Voice : "Chamberlain.") Yes, and some whom perhaps they would not suspect. He was con- sidering that the Government returned in the lump the property franchises, grateful to the Radical party for their generous support. They did not look at the specialities of ' their own opinions. They looked at a great measure of enfranchisement ; they hailed it with enthusiasm, and they had adhered to it with fidelity. Every section ;of the party had worked as one man in carrying , I forward a great cause to a great consummation. (Cheers.) I Lord Cowper had proposed that they should lay a Redistri- bution Bill on the table of the House of Commons, but un- fortunately Lord Cowper had not been able to tell them whether tho Tories were ready to enter into such a bargain. ; (Laughter.) In quitting the franchise question, and revert- ing to the House of Lords, the right hon. gentleman spoke of its past history, and said its influence had been much re- duced since the Reform Act of 1832. They had had twelve , Parliaments since that Act—he was proud to have sat in ' every one of them—and the national opimion had been ex- hibited thus :—Ten of those twelve Parliaments had been Liberal. The eleventh Parliament sat from 1841 to 1817, , and was elected as a Tory Partiament, but in 1846 it put out the Conservative Government of Sir Robert Peel and' sup- ported till its dissolution the Liberal Government of Lord John Russell. The twelfth Parliament they knew a great deal about. They talked largely of its merits or demerits before the last election. With that one Parliament, which was Tory from beginning to end, the Lords were in sym- pathy. The House of Lords ought to be content with the power it possesses ; ought to be content with the impunity with which that power has been exercised, and not to 'challenge the nation upon a qttestion like the extension of the franchise; and ought not to push its opinions to ex- tremes. (Cheers.) Ho traced the obstructive action of the I House of Lords and the waste of time caused by it in the Commons during recent and former years. In the case of the Ballot Bill, on which the House of Commons spent 25 nights in 1871, the whole work had to be dune over again in 1872. The House of Commons must necessarily be the stronger house. It had spoken on this franchise question by a decisive majority, and would he asked to speak again. (Prolonged cheers ) The doctrine that it was the function of the House of Lords to point out the time of aiesolution wed determine when the country was to be reftered to, was a doctrine which had no place whatever in our history or our constitution. (Renewed cheers.) Redistribution had been joined with a franchise bill in 1832 because it was necessary, though difficult and dangerous, and caused the Commons 35 days discussion in Committee. In 18C7 the redistribution joined with the franchise was nominal, though enlaeged and helped to the uttermost by the Liberal Opposition. In 1836 Lord John Russell was defeated by that very means of joining redistribution with the fran- chise, and the present Government, recollecting that, were not likely to fall once more into the earns trap, for in die- cuesions on complex legislation the minority was in the present state of business master in the House of Coin- ' mons. Out of the 65 nights of last session at the disposal lof the Government, Supply took ;il4. The Op- position knew as well as the Government the im- possibility of passing a combined Redistribution and Fraechise Bill. Some of them had coafessed it. After a franchise bill, one for redistribution would follow. Let one carriage go first, and do not attempt to force two along a narrow lane at once. In conclusion, he said : I have ; shown that it is unwise and dangerous for the hereditary Chamber upon a great constitutional issue to court a direct 'conflict with the representative House which proceeded from the people which returns to the people, and which, if the people are dissatisfied with its action, is punished by the peo- ple, as the Parliament of 1874 was punished in 1880 (chee.rs)—by the indignant anion of the country. In those circumstances it is that Parliament, while it lasts, and until the Crown dissolves it, or until its legal term is reached, re- presents the people of the country. The hereditary Chamber lis unwise if it seeks a conflict with such a body. The con- sideration of its own interests, and the larger and more I generous view which its minority have taken, and which its majority, I trust, will be induced to take, ought to show them that they may trust those classes in the country which , they have trusted in the towns, that the nation is attached to its laws and to its institutions, that the ace sion to the number of the constituency will be an accession to the strength of the Empire, that the Throne will stand more I firmly—yet more firmly—upon a broader foundation, and that every consideration alike of principle and of policy, and even of narrow and selfish interest—if that must be appealed to—dictates that they should no longer tamper with the question, but seize the first opportunity of giving a ready as- sent to the Francuise Bill.
The right hon. gentleman, having spoken an hour and 33 minutes, sat down amid a perfect storm of cheering, and the audience rose as one man in order to give full tongue to their enthusiasm.
SECOND ADDRESS-FINANCE AND FOREIGN POLIO Y.

On Monday evening, Mr Gladstone addressed the second section of his constituents in the same hill. He was again surrounded by a host of distinguished supporters, and the Earl of Stair presided. Mr. limansToNE, who, if possible, had an even more en- thusiastic reception than on Saturday, entered into a defence of the Government policy, and replied to Lord Salisbury's criticisms. Lord Salisbury said Mr. Gladstone is reported to have uttered these words in a recent speech :—" In ISSO they gave promise after promise. They held out before you a splendid picture of taxes reduced, of peace all over the world, of Ireland pacified, of trade revivified." Now, it would be impertinence in me to suppose that Lord Salisbury had me principally, or wholly, in his mind when he deli- vered that sentence; but yet, considering how fond the Tories have been throughout these years of making vague references, and therefore perfectly worthless references, to the speeches made in Midlothian, I presume that Lord Salisbury had them partially in his view—(laughter and "Hear, hear")—and what r wish respectfully to says this—that so far as he had them in his view, so far as they had reference to anything said by me and heat(' by you, the sentence tbat I he read is a pare and perfect work of the imagination. (Laughter and cheers.) Gentlemen, I made you no brilliant promise, I drew no splendid picture; I drew, on the contrary, a dismal exhibition—(" hear, hear," and a laugh)—of all the mischiefs that we have bad before us. I could have addressed the Government of Lord Beaconsfield —espnially in its latest years while Lord Salisbury was its Foreign Minister—l could freely have addressed it in the words of Tennyson, viz., 1 The children born of thee are fire and sword,

lied ruin and the breaking up of. laws. "The evil that men do lives after thein,"—(cheers)—an I, unfortunately, in no department of human existence is that proposition more profoundly and more disastrously true than it is in this wide world of politics, where the deeds of individual statesmen tell with a fatal power upon the weal the woe of millions of their fellow-countrymen. Mr. _iladstone went on to say that he had charged the late lovernment with having broken through every rule of +ound finance. If they desired honest and safe finance they nust pay their way. The four last b lance sheets of the 'ate Government presented the aggregate deficiency of £7430,000. The four years of the present Government, Jespite heavy charges and lack of high fiscal prosperity, had

net presented a single deficit, and on the whole there was a surplus of £1,580,000. (Loud cheers.) In the four last Years of the Beaconsfield Administration they paid off .£lO 984,000 of national debt. In the four years of the pre- sent Administration, the only four entire years, £25,015,000 ' had been paid off. (Laughter and cheers.) So that upon that chapter there, was an improvement at any rate of £14,000,000 (Renewed cheers.) It was hoped that on March 31st, at the close of the present financial year, the repayment of debt during this Government will have reached £33,000 000.—(loud cheers)—end the payment, the liquidation, of £33,00),000 of debt means the total abolition of £1,000,000 of permanent burdee necessary to raise the standard income of the country. The bill for the following conversion of 3 per cent, stock would resalt in a further considerable alleviation of public burdens. As to reductions of taxation, the Government in DM repealed the malt tax, regerdlog which the Tories had broken every pledge they , made. The present Government had further dealt with the gross anomalies existing in the shape of the death duties, so that wherever the property was under £3OO the executors had no need to go to a legal adviser at all. About 500 people each week were reaping advantage from this. He reverted to the heavy annual expenditure at present as a reason why the Chancellor of the Exchequer had not much to give. The education vote grew rapidly, and who among those he was addressing would check its growth? (Cheers.) They in Scotland knew well the value of education. A pain- ful charge which came upon them when they took office was the greatly increased cost of t'ne civil government of Ireland. The main cause which had kept toe expenditure of the country so high bad been the military charge, which was due mainly, if not entirely due, to the policy of the fore- going Government and the engagements with which they had saddled those who succeeded them. In the four last years of the late Government the gross expenditure of the country was 329 millions. In the four last years of the present Government the expenditure of the country had been 342 millions. That was apparently, on comparing the two .Governments, that the Liberal account was 13,000,000 to the bad. But deducting the cost of c Alec' ion connected with the post office, telegraphs, and so forth, whichto charge as taxation would be absurd, he found these during the last four years of the late Government were 2971 millions, and during the last four years of the present Government 3031 millions. Then as to the remaining 91 millions the Govern- ment had paid off 25 millions of debt, as against 11 millions by the late Government, which made the Liberal balance to the good 4k millions. (Cheers.) Besides that they had paid q millions to India on account of the Afghan war, and thus came out 91 millions better on the finance of four years. In South Africa and Egypt war expenses of 21 millions and 4,1 millions had been entailed. so that they claimed to stand 161 millions better than the Government which went before. (Leila cheers.) In reviewing the state of Ireland from the time of Lord Beaconsfield's letter to the Duke of Marlborough, Mr Gladstone said the conspiracy which they had had to confront was at this moment broken up. (Great cheering.) From 4.439 agrarian crimes in 1831, the Humber sank to 870 in 1883, and for the beet seven months there was no sign of an increase. The qaality as well as the quantity of the crimes showed a change for the better. By means of the Irish Land Act, he felt that almost every case of over-rent in Ireland had been settled. It was true that £540,000 had been taken off upon the aggregate from the rent of the landlord, but that was in the main a debt of justice, and after all not more than one- fourth of the Irish landlords had had to make a sacrifice. He did not assert that the Irish question was altogether settled. The organisation called the Nationalist party would for some little time disturb the action of our Parliamentary system, time would be wasted, measures obstructed, and there would be a trial of temper, and a Ministry now and then might be overturned, but never could it happen that Ireland would be dissevered from Great Britain. (Prolonged Cheers.) Dealing next with foreign affairs, he said there wee in the first 20 years of his political life no broad differ- ence of principle between the Liberal and Conservative par- ties with regard to foreign politics. lii those 20 years the Conservative party were the peace party. Judge, then, the enormous space that the Tories of to-day had travelled in deputing from the wisdom of their forefathers. His idea of foreign policy was to take the simple rule of behaving to each and all as they would have them behave to us. (Loud cheers.) He deprecated the anxiety with which German colonisation was said to be regarded by English and Scotch people. Germany could cot rob us if she wi3hed. He now asked the audience to turn to their discussions in 1879 and 1880, and consider the state of foreign politics at that time. The Treaty of Berlin left the Montenegrin and the Greek question stagnant, and it was ene of the Liberal Government's first duties to remedy that state of things. A still sadder case wee Afghanistan. If anything could have made the ambition of Russia really formidable, it was un- doubtedly to throw the people of Afghanistan, by our hos- tile measures, into the arms of the Emperor of Russia. Such was the condition of affairs under the late Govern- ment. but thauks to Lords Ripon, Hertington, and Kimber- ley, Afghanistan was again united, and kindly relations were again being built up between its ruler and people, while instea I of 6.5,000 foreign soldiers being detailed for the defence of the north-western frontier or for the occupa- tion of Afghanistan, 25,000 men are now sufficient for that work, leaving 40,000 available for other purposes. (Cheers.) The Liberal Government had redeemed their pledge to re- store freedom to the native press of India, which the strange and guilty infatuation of the late Government, without the knowledge of Parliament, took away. Touching South Africa, the Government on taking offize were told that the people of the Transvaal were perfectly content to be an- nexed by the British Empire, but before long they showed their feeling unmistakably, and obtained several successes over the email body of British troops then in South Africa. A force sufficient to defeat the Boers was sent. The Boers (continued Mr. Gladstone) asked us for an accommodation. What was called the Jingo party in this country were Ire- mendemsly scandalised because we listened to that applica- tion. We had force there to overpower them. We might have shed their blood. We mieh• have I aid prostrate upon the field hundreds, possibly thetas ands, of that small community, and then should have vindicated the reputation of this country according to the creed of that particular party. (Laughter and cheers.) But, gentlemen, having undoubted power in our hands, we thought. and I believe you think, that the time to be anPrciful is when you are strong. (Cheers.) We were strong. We could off )rd to be merciful. We entered in- to arrangements with the Transvaal, and the Transvaal as at this moment—not at every point, but in the main and for praeical purposes—recovered its independence. (Cheers ) Passing to Egypt, he answered the questiou, " What took you to Egypt?" by saying " Honour took me to Egypt.; slighted faith took me to Egypt." (Vociferous cheering.) Ha traced our interference in Egypt from 1876, when the opinion was more or less hazarded that England ought to take some control of Egyptian finance. When he heard that doctrine uttered, he lest not a moment in protesting against it, and in saving that if they once began to touch Egyptian finance, probably the time would cot be long be- fore they would find themselves confronting the question whether they were to assume the dominion over Egypt. (Loud cheers.) That was in 1876. Lord Derby, now Sec- retary for the Colonies, was then Foreign Minister—(cheers) —and nothing of thie kind was done as long as Lord Derby continued Foreign Minister; but when Lord Salisbury came into his place, the meddlesome indivesition—(loud cheers and laughter)—began to undergo a portentous develop- ment. He believed these proceedings of Lord Salisbury's were well meant, though he condemned them in judgment and discretion, and he related the unfortunate steps which led to the present Egyptian difficulty. Ha lamented the failure of the recent Conference, and said the present Go- vernment were endeavouring to regulate Egypt's finance upon the principle of a fair distribution of effort and nerd. flee among all parties, and in considering the best means to fulfil their pledge to General Gordon. Should the mission of General Gordon fail the whole Tory party would then discover that they disapproved of,,it from the first—(l augh- ter)—but that they were too patriotic to say so. On the other hand, should the mission of General Gordon succeed ' in effecting a peaceful evacuation of the Soudan and war- ding off the flood of war from Egypt, then it was not un- likely that the Tory party will say, "Oh, we always ap- proved of this mission, and we saw that it was a grand stroke of policy, but we were too modest to claim any share of the credit." (Hear, hear.) He ridiculed the pretensions of Mr Gibson, that the whole country were against the Govern- ment on the Egyptian question, and afterwards showed the I growth of business in Parliament and the obstruction. Sup- posing all the 650 members of the House of Commons spoke as long as two Tories whom he might call babies in long clothes, the session would require to be of 13,975 hours in length, or one year, seven months, and seven days (laughter and cheers) sitting twenty-four 1 hours every day, and Sundays included. (Laugh- ter and cheers.) He believed very large changes in the organisation of the House would have to be made if they required business to be done, and he instanced the fact that the Franchise Bill, which contained only three simple Pro- positions, consumed 25 n'ghts. They had heard much of late about an organic reform in the House of Lords. (A Voice: "Aye, and we'll hear more.") That was a question he did not propose to discuss, hut there was no organic re- form that the wit of man could devise in the House of Lords which would be half so inanertant for the progress a liberty, for the maintenance of the credit of Parliament, and for the general welfare of the country—viewed even from the ultra' Liberal point of view—there is no such reform that would . be nearly so important as a sound, judicious, and sufficient change in the rules of the House of Commons so as to enable it to do its business----(cheers)—it is the unbinding of the arms of the House, it is the strengthening of its feeble knees, and giving nimbleness of movement to its feet. It is a fundamental and essential change not in its composition, but in its capacity to perform work; and there was nothing that he had more at heart than to bring those convictions to the mind and intelligence of everyone whom he addressed. (Cheers.) It was one of the greatest misfortunes of the House of Lords that it is led at this moment by a mass of brilliant power, Lord Salisbury—a man of whom justice and convic- tion led him to soy that he believed he served what he be- lieved to be the interests of the country, and was certainly not guided by motives of personal ambition. (A Voice: " On.' ) But his opinions were of a much higher Tory colour than the average opinions of the Chamber %bleb he !ed. (Hear, bear.) He recited the warnings received in 1831, when, under the influence of a star yet more malig- nant, the House of Lords endeavoured to stop the Reform Bill of that day. What happened ? Riots, conflagrations in the county—the bill again presented in the course of a few months, and a surrender which cannot be termed less than ignominious. (Hear, hear.) In closing, Mr Gladstone 'aid: How many warnings are necessary before the voice of prudence can be heard 2 (Hear, hear.) Gentlemen. there was a saying of the old Bourbon family that it was well known of them that they learned nothing and forgot nothing; but there is a predicament one degree more pitiable

The noble. CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said they were assembled there to welcome a statesman whose aim and work has been to lighten the burdens of the work- ing classes and to secure to them the fruits of their toil, who had raised the financial credit of England to a point which was unknown in the history of this or any other country. and who had never taken a leap in the dark. (Loud cheers.) Mr. Thom (president of the Edinburgh Trades Council) presented an address from that body to the Right Hon. Win. E. Gladstoce, M.P. The address stated that in the present crisis the declared and attested sympathies of the Trades Council were decidedly with Mr. Gladstone. The delay of the Franchise Bill and other measures had been brought about mainly by the tactics of snscrupulous men. Mr. GLADSTONE, who was received with loud and long continued cheers, said : In this crisis what we, the Minis- ters of the Crown, desire is to hear the voice of the nation. ketteers.) I thank you for enabling me to meet this vast assemblage, which is perfectly spontaneous ; it is not under the command of any organisation. (Cries of " No.r) It is not by the use of the long puree of a wealthy party— cheers) ; it is not by providing gratuitous tickets be rail- ways for bringing together the population of many coun- ties, or at least that fraction of the population which can be induced to go. (Laughter and cheers.) These are not the means by which you have been brought together. It has been by your own personal and conscientious impulse, ; and the request made to me to receive your address has been prompted from youselves. (Cheers.) I felt, gentlemen, that although you had offered that I should receive this address in silence, it was impossible for ma to waive the op- , i portunity of returning to you my grateful thanks for so re- ' ' markable and extraordinary a manifestation. You are not less deeply interested than myself in the great question which is now before us, and to the speedy settlement of which I trust that you will materially contribute. (Loud cheers.) I cauld not undertake, for physical strength would not suffice for it, to set ferth before you, as I have endeavoured to set forth before other audiences less vast, points of interest and importance that crowd upon the mind , in connection with the present juncture, but one or two ' things I will say to you briefly, and endeavour to leave an impression on your minds. We have approached the con- flict in which we are engaged in the spirit, I trust, of firm- ness, but ia the spirit of conciliation. We have made our bill less perfect than, we ceuld have desired in order that it might be simple, that it might be intelligible, that it I might afford no fair pretext to those who were disposed to encumber its progress and to prevent its arrival at the goal by reason of the infinite number of questions that are connected with the representation of the people. Our bill is a bill for the enfranchisement of two millions of men, and it is a bill for little else. (Cheers.) But we think that that brief description has made it worthy of your acceptance, and has secured for it a place that cm- not be shaken in your hearts and in your consciences. (Loud cheers.) Gentlemen, I have mentioned it as an act of con- ciliation on our p trt—one among many—that, together with the extension of the hou ehold franchise to the coun- ties, we have introduced what is termed the service (ran- i chise—(cheers)—and I have said—inasmuch as the classes concerned in the service franchise are of all others, perhaps, in the closest relations with the property andc what and rank of the cmntry—that is a sign of conciliation. But I know well, and I know particularly in Scotland, that those who will be enfranchised by means ef that enectment will give just and loyal, but at the same time perfectly independent votes. (Cheers.) The only return our efforts at concilia- tion have met has been the adoption of indirect and evasive modes of opposition, and the proposal of a condition for passing the Franchise Bill, which condition we know and which condition our opponents know to be impracticable. (Laughter.) Well, now, there is one point on which they have dwelt, which I will briefly notice to you because the declaration which they make has A gOund of pletteibility about it. They say "This Parliament is too old. (Criee of "No, no," and laughter.) It does not come fresh enough from the mind of the people." (Laughter.) They say, "We wish it to go back to its constituents, and then We will attend to what it says." Gentlemen, it is a truly edify- ing spectacle to hear from the highest Tories in the land an arguMent for short Parliaments. (Laughter.) Now there is a great deal to be said for short Parliaments, but this I will add, if you are to have short Parliaments you will have them by the law of the land—(loud cheers)—and not by the dictation of the majority of the House of Lords. (Re- newed cheers ) The Parliament was not four years old when we introduced the Franchise Bill, and it is, indeed, a squeamish and scrupulous conscience which has led these Tories to doubt whether a Parliament four years old is to be trusted. (Laughter and cheers.) But if they say it is too long a time since we were in contact with the people, I want to know how long it is since they were in contact. ( Laughter and loud cheers.) Now, gentlemen' your chair- man has said that there is a cry about the Constitution being in danger. Well, I am not sure but that there is a state of facts on which, if our opponents were strong enough for the purpose, the Constitution would be in some danger; for, gentlemen, what is our Constitution with respect to this grave subject of the dissolution of Par- liament? You know it as well as I do The Parliament must by law terminate within a certain number of years; bat, beside that, there is a Power given to the Crown, although upon the advice of the Executive Government, to dissolve the Parliament if occasion arise. A dissolution, gentletnen, moans a great deal. It means a heavy burden upon the country ; it mans a great loss of Parliamentary time and interruption of legislation ; a great amount of change and a great amount of labour to be undertaken, both by candidates and constituencies; and it is no trifle that there should exist a power of imposing this burden upon the people, a burden necessary to enable them to exercise their choice. Well, how has7the Constitution regu- lated this matter ? It has regulated it by placing the power of dissolation in the hands of those who, if if they wrongly advise the Crown to dissolve the Parliament will be punished for that advice by the people, and when the new Parliament is elected will be sent about their business. (Laughter and cheers.) There is somethiug rational in a system like that. A vast power, and even possibly a dangerous power, is committed to Ministers, but when they exercise it they know that they will be called to a strict and immediate account. (Cheers.) The doctrine now set up is this—that besides the discretion of Ministers to advise the Crown, and besides the power of the Crown to dissolve Parliament, the House of Lords shall be entitled to bring legislation to a dead lock—(cries of "No" and "Never,")—and then to proclaim that the Parliament mast be dissolved. (Renewed cries of " Ne.") Well, that is at first sight to say that the House of Lords shall have the power of doing that which, as you know, the Ministers of the Crown

• can do, viz.,'advise a dissolution, and, with the assent of the • I Sovereign, mikes a dissolution. But what is the case of the House of Lords? The Ministers of the Crown, if they wrongly advise a dissolution, are punished by dismissal. If the House of Lords wrongly advise a dissolvion, is it to be punished by dismissal ? (Cries of " Yes.") No, the pro- posal is that the House of Lords should have the power of virtually advising and compelling a dissolution, and that if they are wrong they shall remain exactly as they were be- fore, to play the same prank over again as often as they pleased. (Cries of "Get away with them.') Well, gentle- men, that is the Constitution of this country. (Laughter and cheers.) It is said that we ought to join Redistribution with the Franchise. Now, I wish to join issue very plainly with our opponents on this matter. (Cheers.) What they mein is, that conferring the franchise is not conferring a public advantage; but that it is bringing into existence an inconvenient power which can only be rendered tolerable by distributing, cutting, anti carving it in a certain way. (Hear, hear.) In opposition to that doctrine, I wish to proclaim on my own part and on the pert of my colleagues, that in our view the franchise is a good conferred upon the people with redistribution or without it. (Cheers.) NJ doubt it is a greater good if we can follow it up with redistribution, and make a more just and equitable division of political power; but we must insist upon this—that the franchise of itself, that the introduction of two millions of intelligent fellow subjects to the exercise of political powers, is a great good Conferred upon the nation—(cheers)—and when our oppo- nents call out for redistribution, what they really mean is this, that in their view the franchise is not a good, but is in the nature of an inconvenience which can only be rendered tolerable and rendered manageable by joining it with parti- cular methods of arrangement, According to a simile which I once ventured to use about it—and I think it is a true one—they seem to proceed as if it was a question of the arrival of a great lot of wild beasts at a place where they were to be expected, and the people who were to have the charge of them when the caravans containing them arrived very naturally say that they will not be safe with these wild beasts until they are all and each of them lodged in their separate cages. (Loud cheers and laughter.) And, there- fore, gentlemen, when these two million voters arrive, as they are now knocking at the door—(cheers)—the Tories ref ass to let them in until they have got all the cages ready in which they consider that these large number of voters , may be safely deposited. (Load laughter and cheers.) Gentlemen, you see how wide is the difference between our opponents and ourselves. (Hear. hear.) But let me tell you that this question does not rest with us. It rests with the nation. It is the voice of the nation that will prevail. We, the Ministers of the Crown, have scrupled to assume a great activity in stirring up the people, because we conslder that the expressions of opinion which we desire and invite should be their act and not ours—(cheers)—and conse- quently, though I have come here to address my friends and constituents in Midlothian, neither I nor the Ministers in general have gone scampering about the country— (laughter)—to this place and then to that, as , others have, to make a show of opposition to the Govern- ment. No, gentlemen, we look to you for your support, for the free, natural expression of opinion and conviction. We invite it with a good conscience, and we accept it with 1 a sanguine expectation—(cries of "You will get it," and cheers)—because never were you engaged in a more ' honour- able never in a more politic, never in a more constitutional I I undertaking than now, when you are endeavouring to pro- cure that large extension of the Parliamentary constituency I which will give to the illustrious throne of her Majesty a , yet broader basis, and to the laws and constitution of the I country a yet firmer foundation, to meet the vicissitudes of I ages to come, with a more and more complete and affection- ate regard rendered to them from the heart and from the in- I , telligence of the people. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, I thank , you, for your admirable address, and for the patience with which this vast assembly has been pleased to listen to me. (Prolonged cheers.) A vote of thanks to Mr Gladstone having been moved and seconded by working men, who were constantly interrupted by cries of "Rosebery," Lord Rosebery, who was greeted with vociferous cheering, said he was proud to have been the medium of communica- ting their wish to Mr Gla lstone that he should meet them I in this hall. The present meeting was the answer of the men of Edinburgh to the invitation of Lord Salisbury. I (Laughter,and hear, hear.) But why then did they ask one who knew their feelings like the member for Midlothian to be present on this occasion? (A Voice: "It's because we like him," and loud cheers.) They should perhaps have done just the reverse. He (Lord Rosebery) saw that Sir Stafford Northcote was about to commence that most wearisome and most unremunerative part of his annual toil—( leugh)—which was called his political visit to Scotland. (Laughter, and a voice, "Its no use.") Sir Stafford would not get fat on what he got here—(laughter) —but if they wanted to do him good why not ask him to a meeting like this. (Laughter.) And now this Midlothian I visit was nearly over—(A voice: "Mores the pity," cheere and laughter)—they could sum up its result, and they knew that the task of the Prime Minister had been not to stimulate but to stay, not to excite but to soothe the ardour ; and the passion of a justly indignant people. (Cheers.) They heard the body which had undertaken so much with so I idadequate means, they heard that body called the House of Lords. (Laughter.) But he would have them remember I , that it was not all the House of Lords—(cheers)--and he called them to witness, and bethought they knew, that there; were in that House not one, not two, not a score, but many I who would be prepared to march with the people—(loud cheers)—abreast with the people certainly, but if necessary, ' in front of the people—(vociferous cheering)—in this just, this necessary, in the highest sense this truly conservative { campaign for the maintenance of the rights of the nation and of the true balance of the constitution of this country. (Tremendous cheering). On the motion of Mr H Broadhurst, MP, seconded by Mr Monro Ferguson, M P for Ross-shire, a vote oi thanks was tendered to Lord Reay. Mr Gladstone and the party accompanying him then left the market amidst great enthu- siasm.
GENERAL NEWS.
On Tuesday, at Aberdeen, five men were sent —for trial charged with the murderof George Stewart, on Sarurday week.

Edward Player, clerk fo Messrs. Vivian, was sentenced at Swansea, on Tuesday, to six months' bard labour for fraud. Three boys were run over and killed on the railway near Glasgow on Wednesday night by an express train, the ap- proach of which they had not noticed. The wagon works of the Midland Railway Company. Sheffield, were on Wednesday night destroyed by fire. The damage is estimated at £B,OOO to £lO,OOO. On Wednesday evening a ball wag given in Cork by the Mayor and citizens in honour of the visit of the Duke of Edinburgh and the Channel Squadron to Cork Harbour. The Duke of Edinburgh retarned to Qaeenstowu on Thurs. day after his visit to the Earl of Shannon at Castlemartyr. His Royal Highness WRS cordially received on his return. An athlete named" Ohmy "during a gyrnrastie perform- ance at the Blackpool Winter Gardens on Tuesday night fell from a considerable height upon the stage, but sustained no worse injury than a number of bruises and a nervous shock.

Thomas Moss, clerk of the Hinckley (Leicestershire) Local Board, was arrested there on Wednesday night charged with embezzling moneys of the Board. The defal- cations upon which Moss has been surcharged by the public auditor amount to over £6OO. The Irish National League on Wednesday passed a reso- lution denouncing the Lord Lieutenant's refusal to reopen the Myles Joyce case. Mr Healy, M P., made a violent speech, in which he threaten( d the overthrow of the Go- vernment in the coming session. SEVERE THUNDERSTORM—A severe thunderstorm passed over Argyllshire on Wednesday night, accompanied by a heavy rainfall. Three cows and a nunaber of sheep were killed at Loch Gilphead, and serious damage was done to property. The rivers are all in good. DEATH OF A VENERABLE MINISTER.—The death is announced of the Rev. John Morrie, at his residence, Sunderland, at the advanced age of 92 years The deceased gentleman was the oldest minister of the English Presby- terian Church. He relinquished his ministerial labcras in 1878.

On Wednesday, at Ashtod, the six Irishmen charged with rioting and attacking the National League flail at Mossley were again before the magistrates. The defendants, who were said to be members of a rival organisation, were boncd over to keep the peace, with the exception of one old man, who was discharged. At Sutton, near London, on Wednesday, a coronet's jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against a man named Nickilson, a widower, who is alleged to have systematically starved and otherwise ill-used his three children, the eldest of whom,.a.girl two years and nine months old, was shown

I AIR, GLADSTONE IN AHDLONIAN.
FIRST ADDRESS-THE FRANCHISE BILL.

Tie Premier on Saturday evening begin a third series of speectres which will be memorable not only in the history of Midlothian but also in the history of the present ago. After receiving an address of welcome from the Lord Provost and Corporation of Edinburgh at the Council Hall, Mr Glad- stone reptired to the Cora Exchange, which WAS crowded with his constituents and a proportion of non-electors. Ac- companying the Premier, or with him on the platform, were Mrs Gladstone, Miss H Gladstone, Mr Henry Gladstone, Lord and Lady Rosebery, Lady F Ma joribanks, the Earl ot Aberdeen, the Earl of Dalhousie, the Earl of Elgin, Lord Hew, Lord Napier and Ettrick, Lord Belhaven, Viscount Dalrymple, a number of Scotch and English members of Parliament, Edinburgh University professors, the Lord Prom( pf Edinburgh, and other reproentative gectletriai. The chair was fatten by Mr 3 Cowan, chairman or the Mid- lothian Liberal Association. _

than that, and that is to learn nothing and forget every- thing. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) Let us hope that, with- out fear, without compulsion, without strain on the consti- tution, the innovations of the past may suffice, and that great ass3mbly, calling hick to life the glorious traditions of its remoter past, may take the course which will best tend to place it in clossr harmony with the convictions of the nation, and to prolong its o..vn existence for an honourable share through ages yet to come in the direction of fortunes of this mighty empire. The right hon. gentleman then resumad his seat, amidst loud cheering, after having spoken upwards of two hours. PRESENTATIONS, AND SPEECH TO WORKING

div.head: MEN.
div.p: MEN.

Previous to Tuesday evening's demonstration, held in the Waverley Market Hall, the Prime Minister received a depu- tation from the Leith Corporation, and a body of artisans from the Forth Bridge Works. In the afternoon the right hon. gentleman, aczompanied by the Earl of Rosebery, hid walked out in the grounds of Dalmeny House, and pro- ceede las far as the New England plantation. On returning to the house he received the Leith Town Council, who drove out to Dalmeny. Their address was presented by Provost Pringle and the Town Clerk (Mr Laing). Mr Gladstone said the reception of such addresses was of great support to him in his work. Mr Gladstone next received the deputa- tion of Forth Bridge workmen, who presented an axe for Mr Gladstone and an inkstand for Mrs Gladstone. These were given as mementoes of their visit to the works on August 28th. The axe, which was of polished steel, was made out of one of the bed plates of the bridge, a represen- tation of the bridge as it will stand when completed being artistically engraved upon it. It likewise bore the following inscription:—" Presented to the Right lion. W E Gladstone by the ernployos of the Forth Bridge Works, as a token of their respect and high appreciation of his life-long services to the country. 28th August, 1884." The inkstand bore a suitable inscription. The Prime Minister and Mrs Glad- stone expressed their delight at the gifts, and the former, as he handled the axe several times, exclaimed, "This is most interesting." One of the members of the party explained to the Premier that the ash handle of the axe was made from a tree felled by the right hon. gentleman when staying at Dalmeny House during his famous Midlothian campaign. "Ah," instantly rejoined Mr Gladstone ; "I recollect felling the tree very well." He thee proceeded to ask the party as to the progress of the works. This bridge, be said, is a sub- ject that interests me very much. If you had any such obstruction in your business as we have in Parliament you would very soon discover the means of getting rid of it. There is not a vestry or Corporation in the country which, if it were in the condition of the House of Commons, would not get rid of that obstruction, and it must be done.—Here the Prime Minister again took up the axe, and expressed his admiration of it, whereupon Mr Moir observed that it was symbolical of the right hon. gentleman clearing away all obstruction. Mr and Mrs Gladstone next cordially shook hands with the members of the deputation, and the party withdrew.

The great meeting of working-men in Edinburgh on Tuesday evening formed a striking climax to the series of popular demonstrations which have signalised the Premier's visit to Midlothian. It was held in the Waverley Market Hall, which was used for a like purpose in 1879. The scene now presented was scarcely lees picturesque than en that occasion, and although in the remoter corners of the vast area the crowding was less denee, there mast have been present on Tuesday evening an assemblage of nearly 15,000 persons. One advantage of the present meeting was that it had been somewhat better organised, and, profiting by the lessons of experience, the committee had the floor of the hall intersected with barricades, so as to check the pres- sure. The surrounding gallery was reserved exclusively for ladies, of whom there were about 1,000 present. After having driven from Dalmeny, along roads crowded for miles. Mr. Gladstone arrived in the hall at 7-15, and was received with prolonged cheering by the upstanding audience whilst the band played "Auld Lang Lyne." Lord Reay occupied the chair, and amongst those p-eseat were Mrs and the Misses Gladstone, the Earl and Countess of Rosebery, Mr Henry Gladstone. the Earl of Dalhousie, Lord Carrington, Mr H Broadhurst, M.P., Mr W Summers, M.P., Mr J Dick Peddle, M.P., Mr Buchanan, M.P., Mr Marjori- banks, M.P., Sze. .

div.head: JOURNEY TO ABERDEEN.
div.p: JOURNEY TO ABERDEEN.

Mr Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs and Miss Gladstone, left Dalmeny House, oa Wednesday, on a visit to Colonel Farquharson, at Invercauld, Aberdeen. All along the route there were great manifestations of enthusiasm. At Manuel, the rust important stoppage, an address was presented from the Ba'ness Liberal Association, and, in replying, the Pre- miar remarked upon the gravity of the present constitutional crisis. The opinion of the nation, he said, was now wanted. Whet Ministers wished to be able to say was that there was nothing but fallacy and delusion in the statement that the people were with the Lords in their extraordinary proceeding. Such a statement deserved only to be treated with laughter. He believed the people would do their duty. At Stirling an address was presented from the Cor- poration, and, in reply, Mr Gladstone said the expressions of sympathy he had received were a testi- mony that he was communicating with the whole people of Scotland. At Perth and Aberdeen there was much en- thusiasm displayed. At the latter place some thousands of people congregated.—The Premier, in the course of a few remarks, said that if every one did his duty many intelligent men in Aberdeenshire and elsewhere would before we were much older be voters. After inquiring as to when Her Majesty passed through Ballater, and receiving the infor- mation it was on the previous day, Mr. Gladstone entered the carriage which was awaiting him, and followed by the cheers of those assembled, he and those with him drove away to Invercauld, a distance of about 14 miles. THE PREMIER AT THE BRAEMAR FESTIVAL. Mr Gladstone spent Thursday morning quietly at foyer- cauld House, and is in the enjoyment of excellent health. A Braemar correspondent telegraphs that Mr Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs Gladstone and daughter, on arriving on the ground on which the gathering takes place, was loudly cheered by those assembled. Sir William and Lady Harcourt were also with the party. Shortly afterwards, the Prince and Princess of Wales, with their sons and daughters and the Duchess of Edinburgh, arrived, and were greeted with enthusiasm. Earl Fife, Colonel Farquharson, and Sir Henry James were present. The Premier looked re- markably well,

Cnorarts' DEMONSTRATION.—A demonstration of crofters took place on Wednesday at Dingwall, about 400 of them marching in procession from the rail way station to the place of meeting, followed by a procession of some 1,500 sympathisers. Professor Blacaie presided, and was sup- ported by Mr. Macfarlane, M.P., Mr. Macintosh, M.P., and Sir George Campbell, M.P. The proceedings were most enthusiastic.

A CRAFTY lAMOSTER.—At the Rochl ale Police Court, on Wednesday, William Whitehead, a returned convict, was brought up on remand, charged with having obtained money and goods from a number of persons by false pretences. Ac• cording to the evidence, the prisoner had obtained money from persons in various towns by pretendinT that he had brought preasnts for them from their relatives- in America, that the presents were lying at his house, which he usually represented as being in a North-east Lancashire town, and that he would forward the same on payment to him of the cost of carriage. He obtained sundry goods by preten- ding that certain relatives in America had requested him to take back dresses, &c, frem their relatives in this country. The prisoner was committed for trial at the quarter ses- sions. A STRANGE Soy.—The story of the disappearance of a Mrs. Sheehan and her daughter and one of her sons, whose bodies have been found in a well near Fermoy, is a remark- able one. A former servant of•the family had made h statement to the effect that she saw her mistress and the daughter on the night of their disappearance seven years ago, and on her asking about their whereabouts a short time afterwards she was told by one of Mrs. Sheehan's sons that his mother had decided to leave for America. Tbis explana- lion satisfied the neighbours. The son just mentioned re- mained at the farm for a few years, and then went to Australia. The neighbours say that there were disputes in the family respecting the farm. A coroner's jury has re- turned a verdict of wilful murder against some person un- known. -

ALLEGED EXTENSIVE STOCKBROKING FRAUDS AT LEEDS. —Charles Foster, a well-known stock and sh trebroker, car- rying on an extensive business at Leeds, has been arrested on a warrant charging hint with having fraudulently con- verted several valuable securities to his own use. He was brought before the borough justices on Friday, when it was stated that the sun:o, which it was alleged the prisoner had misappropriated, amounted to £lO,OOO, the frauds having extended over a period of several years. The specinc charge now brought against him was that he had misappropriated two sums of £2,000 and £l,OOO respectively, the securities of which had been entrusted to him by a widow named Mrs Sampson to be deposited in the bank.— prisoner was remanded fo: a week, the magistrates declining to accept bail.

, to have died from want of food. PARTRIDGE SHOOTlNG.—Favourable accounts are given of partridge shooting on Monday from all parts of Great Britain. The weather was fine but dull in the morning, but In the afternoon heavy showers of rain fell in some districts. Birds are plentiful, healthy, and wild on the wing. Some good bags were made. Tun RIBBLE IMPROYEMENTS.--A special meetinr, of the Preston Town Council, on Wednesday, decided by 31 votes to 14 to sanction the proposal that the tender of Mr. Walker, of London, be accepted for the construction of a forty-acre dock and the improvement of a portion of the River Ribble. The costa the former is pat down at £439,359, and the lat- ter at £17,000. STRIKE AT THE NESTOR COLLIERIES.—The whole of the men employed at the Neston (Cheshire) Colliery have struck work for higher wages. So impossible do the col- liery proprietors find it to meet these demands that it has been determined to discontibue the working of the colliery for a time. The colliers are leaving the district for Wigan and the Lancashire coalfields. SCUTTLING CASE.—The Liverpool Stipendiary Magistrate on Wednesday resumed the hearing of the charge preferred against Williams of attempting to scuttle the Welsh brigan- tine Catherine and Alice, of which. the accused was master and owner, off St. Alban's Head, on the 13th of May last. Some further evidence haying bun gives, the accused was committed for trial, bail being allowed. LIBERAL CLUB FOR NANTWICH.—k new Liberal club WAS on Wednesday afternoon opened in N rntwich by Mr James Tomkinson, one of the Liberal candidates for West Cheshire. In the evening a public meeting was held, at which addresses were delivered by Mr Tomkinson. Mr D Duncan (the second Liberal candidate for the division), Mr G W Latham, and others, and resolutions were plssed in support of the Government and in condemnation of the House of Lords. Six MEN DROWNED.—A terrible disaster occurred on Monday night four miles from Galley Head, off Cork Har- bour, whereby six persons in a host belonging to Queens- town perished. The men were in the beat, but so high were the seas that they were several times washed out. Five were drowned, and of the remaining two, one died from the effects of exposure. The boat, with a sole survi- vor, was picked up yesterday mornia; by a passing hookor. THE LEICESTER ANTINACCINATIONISTS.—The opposition to the Vaccination Acts at Leicester has become so strong that the law cannot be carried out, and about 3,000 people are waiting to be summoned. The Local Govern- ment Board have been solicited for advice under the cir- cumstances. Meantime smallpox has been introduced from London, and it is asserted that all the persons suffering have , been vaccinated. The authorities hope by isolation to , stamp out the disease. - - -

• A BISHOP ON WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE—The Bishop of Car- lisle has declared himself in favour of women's suffrage. He 1 asks what there is in the mere accident of sex, if a woman be a householder, to make it tight te say that she shall have no political influence. He does not desire that married women should vote; but when an unmarried woman satis- fies every condition but that of sex, then it seems to him to be impossible in reason, and he believes it will soon ba im- possible in fact, to deprive her of a vote. THE GRAVESEND COLLISION.—The Board of Trade in- • quiry into the collision between the steamships Dione and Camden, off Gravesend, concluded on Friday. The court found that the cause of the collision was the excessive rate of speed of the Diane, and suspended-the certificate of her master for six months, allowing him, however, a chief mate's certificate. The master and second officer of the Camden were not to blame, and Mr Rothery did not think ' the pilot could have avoided the collision.

WHALLEY WILL CASE.—Charles Thomas, Thomas Nash, and Edward Dannell were charged at Bow-street, oh Tues- day, with uttering a "forged will with intent to defraud. Mr Danckwearts, who appeared for the public prosecutor, intimated that Nash cud Thomas would be charged with actual forging of the will, while Gunnell would only be charged with uttering and conspiracy. The testator's signa- ture had pencil marks under the ink, and he would call Rees to show that money had been promised him to swear hard. —Remanded.

DOCK PURCIIASES BY BRISTOL CORPOR4TION.—OR Mon- day the city of Bristol entered into possession of the Avon- mouth and Portishead Dock, undertakings which have been purchased for £BOO,OOO. and they will be amalgamated with the Bristol Docks, already the property of the citizens. The purchasl-money is to be paid in Corporation bonds, bearing intercst at 31 pa. coat. There was no public ceremony, the fact being simply indicated by the hoisting of a flag bearing the City arms at the Avonmouth and Portishead Dock.

Tag ARM:11315000P OF YORK ON TEMPERANCE.—In a letter addressed to the working classes of Sheffield with regard to the Church of England Temperanca Mis.ion which is about to be opened in that town, the Archbishop of York says that almost all thinking men in the country are agreed that that which most hinders the moral and spiritual welfare of the people is the .prevalrnce of drinking habits. The clergy knew very well that it was impossible to hope that the truth of God would have free course among the people, and would prevail over sorrow and sin, so long as drink stood in the

Way. CLEATOR MOOR RIOT.—SUPPOSED 01:MUG& —Thera is good reason to beheve that an attempt was made on Satur- day night to blow up the residence of Mr Thomas Moffat, manager for Mr John Stirling, colliery proprietor, Ceator Moor, Cumberland, Mr Moffat lately discharged some men who had been concerned in the recent Orange riot. On Saturday night, alter the family had retired to rest, a loud explosion was heard. It shook the building and wrecked the kitchen frontage and furniture; but nobody was injured. Presumably the explosion was caused by dynamite, which was placed on the window-sill, and tired by a fuse. No ar- rests have yet been made. THE DROWNING OF i WIFE. Mr Hugh Shortland, whose arrest in connection with the drowning of his wife in the neighbourhood of Plymouth c-eated so much sensation a few months ago, sailed for New Zealand on Saturday, hav- ing, as he states, been offered an appointment in one of the Government departments by his father, an eminent states- man in the colony. Before he left Mr Shin nand comnawni- cated tiwthe Western Daily Mercury a letter containing eigh,y reasons why the Lord-Lieutenant of Devon should set the Home Office in motion with a view Of discovering his wife's murderer, and giving physiological and other reasons why she could not have met her end by suicide or accident.

TRE PAYMENT OF IRISH MEMBERS.—The first practical step in the movement for paying salaries to Irish members of Parliament has been taken by the electors in Queen's County, who from the Payment of Members' Fund have presented to the two county members, Mr Richard Lalor and Mr Arthur O'Connor, £256 each. Mr Lalor, in ac- knowlekng the receipt of this, says his state of health will prevent him from discharging his 'parliamentary duties in future, and he asks the electors to fill his place as soon as possible. Mr O'Connor, in thanking his constituents, says he is convinced that a system of paying Irish members must be generally adopted if the Irish fight i in Westminster s to, be carried out with full effect. Mr O'Connor adds that the monetary assistance thus received will enable him to con- tinue at his post in Parliament. RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.—A. wheel of a tender atticbed to a passenger engine on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Railway broke on Thursday morning when the train 3 was running between Barnsley and Sheffield. The line was damaged, but the train did not leave the metals, and a tem- porary !amok of traffic was the worst result of the accident. —On Thursday morning a serious collision occurred on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway near Accrington. A' goods train was being shunted at Rishton, part of the train being across the main line, when a heavy-laden goods train came up sod the driver, expecting the line to ha cleared be. fore he reached the train, passed the signal; the engine dashed into the rear of the shunting train, smashing three waggons to matchwood and scattering the contents. Gangs of men were obtained from Accrington and Blackburn and the line was cleared in three hours, only the goods traffic haying been interfered with.

div.head: TILE EXAMINER.
div.p: TILE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 6, 1884.

THE PRIME MINISTER struck the key-note of his Midlothian speeches at Warrington on Wednesday week when, referring to the Franchise Bill, he said it was a matter which ' now lay in the hands of the people. The Government have done what they can up to a certain point; let the people now do their part; and it is cheering to see that Scotia's sons are in this respect in no wise lacking. They are still foremost in their devotion to the chief whom they hailed in a dark hour, and who has since led his forces from victory to victory. There were some Tories who were mean enough to suggest, when Mr. GLADSTONE was unable through illness to give a promised address to his constituents, ' that he was afraid to face them. What an answer to their assertions as to his waning popularity is the stir we have had during the past week in "the Heart of Midlothian ! " His influence on the wane? It is greater , than ever. He has roused the people from the stupifying and demoralising nightmare of BEACoNSFIELDISM, and, arising in their strength, they mean to continue in the straight path of that righteousness which ex- alteth a nation. There has never been a doubt amongst true men of "light and lead- ing," that the House of Lords would be beaten in its latest conflict with the people, and the conviction grows stronger in view of the tremendous enthusiasm in Scotland which Mr. GLADSTONE's presence has evoked And yet he has not held aloft "the fiery cross," as was predicted of him; he found that there was no need for it—that there was an eagerness for the fray which required rather to be kept under control, and he has therefore, with characteristic magnanimity, held out the olive branch to the House of Lords. It remains to be seen whether they will accept it; if not, then upon their own heads be the burden of their sins—they will be crushed with the avalanche which will assuredly fall upon them. The people are patient, but there is a limit to their endur- ance, and, although they may hold back for a time, the blow, if they are compelled to strike, will finally come with all the greater force. Lord SALISBURY ought to know by this that he is utterly unable to cope with the power that is arrayed against him; and, fur- ther, that there is not the least likelihood of the acceptance of the revolutionary doctrine he has propounded as to the enforcement of a dissolution of ?arliament at the pleasure of the Peers. Perhaps the finest passage of Mr. GLADSTONE'S magnificent speech on Saturday was in the vigorous protest he made against this unconstitutional proposal. "To tamper." he said, "with that doctrine, to give it the smallest countenance, to admit one jot or tittle of it would, in my opinion, be treason to British liberty—(loud cheers) and I tell you fairly, gentlemen I would far rather abandon my share in the Franchise Bill, and that which would go with it, my share in political life, than for one moment cease to raise the loudest protest in my power against the introduction of this gross innova- tion, which, neither in a reformed Parlia- ment, nor in an unreformed Parliament, was ever heard of on the part of a majority of the House of Lords. (Cheers.)" What will their lordships think of this? Some of th we imagine, will rub their eyes, and suspect, for the first time, that they have been sleep- ing in a• fool's paradise. They will wonder wha: Lord SALISBURY has been about, and perhaps conclude, as Shakespere has it, that thty have been "led by the nose as asses are."

With regard to the question of redistribu- tion, Mr. GLADSTONE by a few simple statistics demonstrated the impossibility of passing a Franchise Bill and a Redistribution Bill in one Session. This, it may be said, is what has been done before, but he did more; he proved by quotatiops from speeches of members of the Opposition that they were of

/ the same opinion, thus exposing the hollow- ness, and dishonesty of the demand for a complete Reform Bill in a single Session. What the nation fully realises, as the Pitruil MINISTER pointed out in his speech to working-men on Tuesday night, is that the franchise is a good thing in itself—" a good conferred upon the people with or without redistribution." The main point to Dick, and Tom, and Harry living in county con- stituencies is to get the vote; it is of moment, but of less moment, that there should he a redistribution of seats, for with the franchise in their hands they could and would make short work of any Government that refused to go forward and give something like equal value to each vote. As to the present Government, however, there is no fear that they will not introduce a Redistribution Bi.ll next year, if the Franchise Bill be passed this year. Lord SALISBURY has admitted that he could accept the promise of the Government on that head. But he fears, so he would have us believe, the Government might fail to carry it through, if they devoted a whole Ses- sion to it; and yet in the same breath he de- rides the Government for not attempting to deal both with Redistribution and the Fran- chise in one Session. This is a specimen of Tory consistency! ' On Tuesday evening the great speech of the great orator was devoted to a review of home and foreign policy. There was a time when the leaders of the Conser- vative party kept " pegging away at the bad state of affairs in Ireland. They didn't try to mend matters; they preferred to act on the assumption that the worse things i were n Ireland the better they were for them; but, as Mr. GLADSTONE was able to show, Ireland has improved despite their sneers and jeers, so that it can now be said that a wide-spreading conspiracy in the Sister Isle no longer exists. At the present moment the Tories have their eyes on Egypt' but somehow matters will not go sufficiently, wrong even there to "give them a chance; while what there is of trouble is a chick from a Conservative egg. Scotchmen might well cheer the quotation—" the evil that men do lives after them "—as the PRIME MINISTER, step by step, revealed the bad results of the meddlesome and aggressive Imperialism Of the BEACONSFIELD Government. It cost this country at the time an enormous sum, and the legacy of the debt which ensued is to. this day a burden upon the Exchequer. It ls hard that a Liberal Government in coming into office should always have to pay the war debts of its predecessors, but it is harder still to have to listen to reproaches as to heavy expenditure from those who have made .it unnecessa,ily heavy. Bul. truth alvays prevails in the end ; and, although th 3 Tories have had a pretty good run with their absurd crY of extravagance, Mr. GLADSTONE has made it all the worse for them by coming down sledge-hammer like, and pounding their facts and figures to pieces. Taking the balance sheets of the last four years the Conservatives were in office, he shows that there were deficits amounting in the aggregate to £7,330,000, while for the four years the Liberals have been in office, notwithstanding war charges, there is a surplus of £1,580,000. But it will be said that the Liberals on the whole have spent more. As to this, Mr' GLADSTONE takes the total expenditure for each four years and puts it beyond question. by taking the 24_ millions of national debt paid off by the present Administration as against ii millions by the BEACONSFIELD Government, that the Liberals stand oi millions to the good as compared with the Conservatives. There is over zi millions to the credit of the present Government for each year it has held the purse strings—a fact which should loosen the tongues of Liberals whenever Conservatives in the future venture to speak of finance. And they will speak; they will stand up again as soon as they have recovered from these knock-down blows, and, parrot like, tell the same old tale. Happily it will be of no avail—we are not a nation of parrots.

THERE was a big discussion at the monthly J meeting of the Warrington Town Council, on J Tuesday evening, on what, on the face of it. I was a little subject. It was a question a rescinding or confirming a resolution to let a room, in property in John-street belonging to the Corporation, to two young men for re- ligious services to be conducted in the Welsh j language At the previous meeting of the Town j Council it was decided to let the room iv question for six months, but Councillor BUR- GESS now moved that the resolution be ! rescinded, on the ground that it would be "a precedent of doubtful wisdom" for the Cor- poration to allow "the use of the building for religious services." Councillor MACKIE, on the J other hand, justly contended that as there ! was "nothing against these men or their - religion," and, as the Corporation let the Fair Ground for Punch and Judy and other exhi- bitions, there ought to be no difficulty thrown ;in the way of a good work by refusing the use of the room. If he had stopped there, there would have been a broad but simple issue, but he complicated, and, as it seems to us, damaged the case by doing that which he 1 I advised others not to do—" beating the drum ecclesiastic." He should have followed the 1 principle for which he contended to its logical issue; but he stopped short. He made it a. matter of " isms " and sects by drawing the line at Mormonism and Atheism. Mor- monism, he said, was against the law; but as a matter of fact, it is as lawful to preach Mormonism as to preach Metho- dism. So with Atheism—the law does not I prohibit its advocacy, and if a ratepayer? Iroom could be let for a Theist, why not for an Atheist ? It was, we believe, a perception of the incongruous , position taken up by Councillor MACKIE which caused some members of the Council who are undoubted friends of civil and religious liberty to take the stand that, so far as the Corporaion is concerned in letting its rooms, it would be best to steer clear alike of religion and poli- tics. The issue was thus reduced to one or expediency, and on this Plead his WorshiP the MA.YOR pertinently remarked thit he "failed to see why the Corpora:ion, or anY Corporation, should be restricted from lettinf, its property in any way that pleased them. As a matter of fact, there is no restriction except that which prudence imposes, and, seeing the heat generated by this par- ticular discussion, it is perhaps wise of the Corporation—we have our doubts on the. point—to turn its back upon itself by undoing at one meeting what has been done at another. The resolution was rescinded, and the Corporation now stands in the position of being pledged to a policy which, if convenient for the moment' ' may prove inconvenient hereafter. What): sauce for the goose must be used as sauce 10 the gander, and if Churchmen should reqinr.e. the use of the Town Hall in the future, a's. ' they have done in the past, they will be inel" point-blank by a resolution which Churchree"
