TRIPS Fetoet WIDNES.—On Monday morning 'a special train was run from the Widnes Central Station re Man- chester (Belle Vue) on the occasion of the brass band con- test. About two hundred passengers were booked. A train was also run on the London and North-Western line, but few passengers booked by it from Widnes. NEW TEMPERANCE HALL, WIDNES.—Mr J 11 Hudeon inaugurated the New Temperance Hall which he has formed under one of the arches of the Cheshire Lines Railway at Widnes by a concert on Wednesday. The room provides accommodation for between two and three hundred persons, and presents a comfortable aspect. The vocalists who took Part in the concert were Miss Hudson, Miss Hetton, Mrs Jones, Miss rye, and Messrs rye, Jessop, and Joaes. Miss Rattan was at the piano. There was a good audience, and the proceedings passed off very successfully, Mr T Rallason Presiding. PRIMITIVE METHODIST MEETING.-1 public tea and meeting, in connection with the Warrington and Widnes circuit of Primitive Methodists, were held in the school- room and chapel, Legh-street, Warrington, on Saturday 'afternoon. The objects of the meeting were the extinction of the station debt and the securing of a more united action on the part of the different societies forming the circuit for aggressive operations. A large number of officials and mem- bers from Widnes were present, and the tea meeting was largely attended. In the evening the Rev J CelVert pre- sided, and addresses were delivered by Messrs T Marshall, Shuttleworth, Tayler' and rillinger. Anthems were also sang by the choir, the music being provided by the bend, the choir being conducted by Mr 11. Thornton, and the band by Mr J Podmore. "Musa IVEsmAer CHAPEL, WIDNES. Daring the Present weak the Her D Angel Richards concluded his pas- torate at the Welsh Wesleyan Chapel, Widnes, having been appointed to the Wesleyan Chapel at Rhos Brymbo, near Wrexham. Whilst in Widnes Mr Richards has worked earnestly for the canse of which be has been the guiding Spirit, and he has especially identified himself with the movement for erecting a new chapel. Through his exer- tions the funds for that purposehave been largely increased. On Sunday evening he preached his valedictory sermon to a good congregation at the Cromwell-street Chapel, Widnes ; and subsequently a special sacramental service was heal, and the members assembled to wish Mr Richards farewell. Mr Roberts (deacon) made an appropriate eptech. On Mon- day evening Mr Richards was present at a tea meeting at the Mount Zion Chapel, Liverpool. when he was the re- cipient of a testimon'al in the shape of a purse of gold. The Rev J P Jones, late of Birmingham, now takes charge of the pastorate. DEATH OF MRS. MACI3Ot7GALL AT RIINCORN.--Widespread sorrow has been c msed in Runcorn by the death of Mrs MacDou3all on Saturday evening, the anniversary of her first wedaing day. Her infant child, born on the previous Thursday, died a few hours earlier. Great sympathy was expressed on all hands for Dr McDougall. The body of the deceased lady and of the intent were conveyed by train to Leighton Buzzard on Monday mornine, and at the railway Station had gathered several personal friends who expreeeect to the bereaved husband the sympathy and regret they felt. The interment took place on Wednesday at the church where twelve months ago the lady was made a happy bride. At the meeting of Ranc=an Board of Guardians on Tuesday the Rev Canon Barclay (chairman) moved "that the Guar- dians tender to Dr MacDougall. the medical officer for the Runcorn district, a vote of sympathy and condolence with him under the deep affliction which has so suddenly fallen upon him in the death of his wife and infant child."—Mr Handley seconded the motion, both gentlemen being greatly affected —The resolution was passed unanimously. THE LATE MR. THOMAS ANDREW 3, OF RUNCORN—At Bethesda Congregational Chapel, on Sunday, the Rev J D Thomas preached a sermon having special reference to the death of Mr Thomas Andrews, of Waterloo-road. The rev gentlemen based his discourse on 1 Corinthians, xv., 20 : " The last enemy shall be destroyed in death," and com- menced bv saying never bad he known so many in the seine congregation to have been touched within such a short space of time by the shadow of death. Within a fortnight nine or ten families, more or less closely connected with Bethesda Chapel, had suffered the loss either of a child, or wife, or husband, or mother, or father. The late Thomas Andrews was a man of unimpeachable integrity. Strictly just and honest in !all his dealings he woa the confilence of his employers and employes. Although he resided in the town for over 20 years, yet not once during that period was:his reputation in any wise tarnished. To all the institutions of their church he was a liberal contributor, and although his deeds of kindness were not noised abroad, still he thought there would be not a few who would miss his private bene- factions. After a reference to Mr Andrews' connection with Bethesda Chapel, the preacher said he died as he had lived. He had set his house in order, and leaving done so he awaited calmly and patiently the hour of dissolution. Under the conductorship of Mr F Fairhurst the choir sang hymns specially selected for the se•Yice, and at the close the " Dead March" in "Saul" was played on the organ by Mr R evens-

Crof I. SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT HALE BANIL—On Tnesday morning an accident of a shocking description occurred on the London and North-Western Railway at Hale Bank. The unfortunate victim was Patrick Murphy, 48 years of age, who resided at 7 Court, Quarry-street, Woolton. Murphy was a brick setter in the employ of Mr Fish, of Spring Brook, Preston, contractor for the erection of the new station at flalebank, and about twenty minutes past six he was crossing the main line carrying a hod full of bricks, when the milk train from Liverpool came along at a speed of 17 miles an hour, and he was struck by the buffer and sent a distance of 30 yards. The wheels of the engine passed over one of his legs, and his bead was crushed in a frightful manner, his brains being scattered about the line. The inquest on the body was held at the Millfield Inn. Litton, on Wednesday morning by:Mr W T Husband, deputy coroner. Mr Ferrand, from trio solicitors' department, Lime-street station, was present to watch the proceedings on behalf of the company. —Johanna Murphy, the wife of the deceased, identified the body.—James Corrigan, contractor's labourer, deposed that he worked with the deceased. He warned Mfurphy not to cross the line as the train was coming, but he replied "I Will manage it." He was, however, killed as described. Another man who was crossing at the earns time with a hod of bricks just contrived to get across and avoid the train.— William Thompson, of Christ Church Villa, Preston, the driver of the train, deposed that when he was about 150 yards from the platform he saw two men crossing the line, and he opened the engine whistle. One of the men suc- ceeded in getting across, but the deceased seemed to hesit- tate, and then made a dart for the platform,,but he was caught ho the buffer and killed.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was recsrded. HOLY TRINITY DAY SCHOOLS, RIINCORN.—D will pro- bably be within the recollection of our readers and the pub- lic generally, that when the children attending these schools gave their last annual concert, the promise of a summer ex- cursion was made to all who attended school regularly, and to this purpose any surplus arising from the concert was to be devoted. By many, apparently, the announcement was taken as meaningless, although it was often brought before the children's notice by the teachers, and when at last some parentaawoke to the reality they discovered that their past negligence debarred their offspring from participation. The highly successful and enjoyable outing took place on Fri- day, when about 200 day school children and parents, under the control of the entire teaching stiff, and accompanied by the Rev W Preston M.A.., and Messrs Churchwarden Fisher, Hankinson, and Rogerson (managers), had a full day in the ancient city of Chester. The only condition fora free pass was that 90 per cent. of the possible attendances for twelve months had been made. Judging from the ex- pression of anxiety upon the countenances of those who had originated the picnic, the owl rug showers and thick banks of ominous looking clouds c tused great perturbation. Before reaching Chester the elements became propitious, and a brighter day for the outing could scarcely have been Wished for. Upon reaching the city a procession was formed. and a perambulation of the walls made. Every object with which a scrap of his' ory is connected was duly pointed out, and proved especially interesting to the elder children. Possibly, however, the growth of some very fine apples within the walls proved more interesting than aught else. About two hours were spent upon the Boodee in amuse- 'Cents and games, and then the Nag's Head coffee rooms in Foregate-street were made for. Here a good tea was given to each child, and at the conclusion the steps of all were directed to the Cathedral. The vergers and officials in attendance at this ancient sanctuary were exceedingly kind, and took great trouble to see all seated comfortably within the beautiful choir. At the conclusion of the service great astonishment was expressed as to where the clergy were seated and the organ situated ; the stall carvings and sue- pliced choir having entirely baffled the msjority of the children. A procession along the Rowe and amusements upon the river terrace concluded the day's programme. The hilarity of the children upon their return, and the spon- taneous cheers given by them for their teachers, were a true indicaticn that the day had been thoroughly enjoyed.

f THE IMPROVED COMMUNICATION TO SOU /lIPORT.----Abollt 50 persons have been booked from Widnes to Smetlepert during the past week by the new line opened by the Che- shire Lines Committee on Monday. A CHILD DROWNED AT WESTON Poteer.-A boy, aged four years, son of Mr Joseph Whitley, listrnan, Weston Point, was drowned in the canal at that place on Thursday afternoon. The child was missed during the afternoon, and as he had been seen playingon the canal side a search was- made. The body was found in the water near the bridge leadinglfrom the village to the docks about six o'clock. ORDINATION OF PRIESTS AT DITTON COLLECIE.---Tbe Rt. Rev. Dr. O'Reilly, Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool, held an ordination service at Ditton Hall College on Sun- day morning. The deacons admitted to ordination were the Rev. John Joehring, Rev. Emil Reichmuth, Rev. Joseph Schwarz, Rev. James Rebmann, and Rey. Otto Pfaelf, of various dioceses in Switzerland. THE LIVERPOOL ART GALLERY.-At a meeting of the Liverpool City Council on Wednesday a letter was read from Sir Andrew R. Walker, the donor of the Liverpool Art Gal- lery, asking to ba allowed to defray the entire cost (about £12,000) oe the recent additions to the building, which have been carried out by the Corporation. On the motion of the Mayor, seconded by Mr. A. B. Forwood, the offer was accep- ted amidst loud applause. PROPERTY IN THE MARICET.-On Wednesday afternoon Messrs Hayhurst and Taylor offered fer sale by auction, at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, "all those compact and well- situated paper-making and manufacturing works, with the land and appurtenances thereto belonging, containing in the whole 15 352 superficial square yards or thereabouts, situate at Earlestown, and commonly known by the name of the Sankey Mill." The machinery aud plant was also offered There was not a large attendance, and the property was not disposed of. MUNICIPAL ELECTION IN LIVERPOOL.-The first munie cipal election under the new Act extending the boars of polling to eight o'clock in the evening took place on Tues- day in Liverpool in Great George Ward, The contest was exclusively of a political character. The ward contained over 1,100 voters, of whom 872 went to the poll, a large number recording their votes in the evening. The proceed- ings were free from any disturbance, and in the result the Liberal candidate, who is a Catholic and moderate Horne Ruler, was returned by a mejority of 78. SALFORD AND THE SHIP CANAL-At the monthly meet- ing of the Salford 'I own Council on Wednesday, a letter was read from Mr Daniel Adamson asking the Corporation to become joint promoters in the Manchester Ship Canal Scheme, and to contribute towards the cost of obtaining the bill. A discuseion•ensued, Solis members thinking that a declaration of what support the Corporation would give should be made at once, and others arguing that it would be premature to take such action before the nature of the new scheme was determined upon and made known. Eventually the matter was referred to the River Irwell Con- servancy Committee, with instructions to report to the General Purposes Committee. Bombay Staff Corps-To be lieutenant: Lieu- tenant Charles Herbert Brackenbury, from the Lancashire Fusiliena. MARRIAGE or Ma. W. E. Ramos, 51. P.-The marriage of Mr W E Briggs, M.P. for Blackburn, with Miss Anna Mary Stewart, eldest daughter of Mr T J Holland, of Broom House, Didebury, took place on Wednesday morning at the ancient parish church of Dideburv. The bride, who was given sway by her father, was attired in a dress of white Irish poplin, trimmed with rich Saxony lace, and wore a handsome tulle veil interspersed with pearls. Her brides- maids, four in number, were Miss Jesse and Miss Siddo Rolland, Miss Tysoe, and Miss Christian Carter, and they each wore dresses of white Llama. The bridegroom's best man was Mr .1 Rutherford, of Blackburn, and, the officiating clergymen were the Rev Dr Rogers, rector of St. Thomas's, Heaton Norris, assisted by the Roy T F Clarke, Knutsford, and the Rev j Denton Thompeon, curate of St. James's, Didsbury. The wedding breakfast. was served at Broom House, where, in the afternoon, a garden party was held, and subsequmtly Mr and Mrs Briggs proceeded on a tour in Scotland. The marriage was witnessed by a large number of persons. Among those present at the party were Mr W Ooddington, the Conservative member for Blackburn, and Mr John Slagg, M.P. There was a large number of pre- sents, including a handsome tea and coffee service from the executive of the Liberal Association at Blackburn. LANCASHIRE MEMBERS AND THEIR VOTES IN PARMA. NEW BOOKS, Sze —Messrs. Cassell and Company ore now issuing in monthly parts, ptice sevenpence, the fine-art edition of Longfellow 's poems, hitherto published only in half-crown parts. The first part, which is before us, has for its frontispiece a splendid portrait of Longfellow, and the text is amply illustrated with a large number of charming high-class engravings. The work will be compete in 21 parts, and will thus come within general reach at a corn- paratively small cost. The edition is alike worthy of the firm and of the poet. Part 8 of Cassell's Etacyclopaslic Dictionary (illustrated) is, like its predecessors, all that the reader can desire, and so far as it goes,gives a complete history of every we'd. This month's sections of The Book of Health" and "Popular Gardening" by the same firm are especially interesting. The former deals with the distinctive features of life, and the influence of stimulants and narcotics; and the latter includes articles, amongst others, OR ferns, common garden flowers, the vine and its fruit, and the rose and its culture. "Familiar Garden Flowers " for this month contains two beautifully coloured plates of the svringa and the menreon. In the September number of The Quiver Mr. C. M. Sawell, the City District Secretary, tells the story of the London City Mission—and well may ' he call it a romance. Other papers in this magazine are "The Lord's Jewels," by the Rev. Prebendary Moore; "Christ Revealed in St. Paul," by the Rev. Dr. Stoughton; an exposition of the story of Philip the Deacon,by the Rev. Dr. Hugh Macmillan; and a piper for oung people by the Rev. Gordon Calthrop. "Opening the Earth Records of Palestine" describes the work of the Palestine Exploration Fund in and around Tyre; the two serial stories are by C. Despard and the author of "Witness my Hand," and there are also three shorter stories in the number. When cholera is raging in France, and is even threatening our own land, the first article in the September number of Caszell's Magazine," A Word about Disinfectants," by An Analytical Chemist, should be of interest. "Our Sailors and Ship's" gives facts and figures relatinz to our much-discussed mnr- chant shipping; a paper on Portraiture explains the most popular branch of amateur photography; and the Hon. P. Carteret Hill, formerly Premier of Nova Scotia, gives " More Impressions of England." "Some Vanquishing Rural Types,' shows that the rustic is not yet quite ex- tinct. Fiction is represented by two serial and two complete stories and music in a new song by E. Burritt Lane. Little Folks ,Magazine for September, which opens with a season- able frontispiece in colour called "In the Orchard "—con- tains a specially-written paper, with four original illustra- tions, entitled ;' A Day on Board H M S. ' Britannia,'" by the Rev. J. Clement P. Adams, Chief Instructor and Chap- lain to Naval Cadets. The number also contains numerous stories, papers, poems, and anecdotes.—" The English Illustrated Magazine" (Macmillan and Co.) is adorned with a delightful frontispiece illustrating a couplet from the poet Keats. "The Tour of Covent Garden," by Mr. Austin Dobson, is interesting alike in text and illustra- tions; and there is a suggestive paper, with illustrations from H. Rylands' drawings, on "The Women of Chaucer." A paper on Cricket, also illustrated, gives quite a history of the favourite game.—" Pieuresque Wales," by Mr. Godfrey Turner, is an official hand-book of the scenery ' accessible from the Cambrian Railway. It is well written, and full of the right sort of information. The illustrations are numerous and excellent; they alone arc worth double the sum (61) at which the hand-book is published.—The current issues of "La Moniteur de la Mode,"" Myra's Jour- nal," and Myra's Threepenny Journal," with their wonderful variety of fashion plates—"ever charming and ever new," are also to hand.

A RUNCORN RUFFIAN —Before Mr la Reynolds and Mr James Handley, at Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday, Thomas Jannion, a well-known rough character, was brought up under a warrant charged with assaulting his sister, Fanny Jannione—The proseoutrix said she WAS a single wornan, and lived at 33, Cooper-street. On the 30th July 'the prisoner came into the house in a state of drunk- enness early in the evening. His wife got into a row with her, and then the prisoner knocked her to the ground and abused her in an awful manner. He struck and kicked her about all parts of the body, and made her arms very black. —lnspector Atherton deposed that he saw the woman on the day of the assault, and she was very badly bruised.— The prisoner was then charged with having on the previous evening unlawfully assaulted P.C. Smith whilst in the ex- excution of his duty, and also damaged his uniform to the extent of 53—P.C. Smith stated that a little after eight o'clock on the previous evening he hod a warrant for the I arrest of the prisoner in his possession, and in company with P.C. Bason he went in search of him. The constable ore- finding prisoner said he must go at once, whereupon the pri- soner swore that he would have his supper first. Smith seized hold of prisoner by the arm and got him into the street, where he acted very violently. He struck Smith a blow on the left side of the jaw that sent the officer flying to the ground. When he got up he saw P.C. Bane strug- gling With the prisoner against the wall. He therefore seiz id on the prisoner, and closing with him got him on the ground and placed the handcuffs upon his wrists. The pri- soner lay on the floor a considerable time cursing and kick- ing his legs about.—P.C. Bason corroborated.—Superinten- dent Leah said this was not the first time the prisoner had treated the police in this way. Ile had been three times be- fore the court three times.—The Bench fined the prisoner 103 and casts 183, or 14 days, for assaulting- his sister, sentenced him to a month's imprisonment for ass suiting the police, and to 14 days for damaging the uniform. ;quite a new kind of people- are to be seerrin tke-Parin-o;: though perhaps the simple explanation is that though they are always there they are from May to the third week ht July obscured by the light, and life, and colour of the but- terfly throng now scattered far and wide in country houses and holiday haunts.

Clearly the protession, of luggage-laden cabs tower& the stations has begun to be exchanged for a procession heading the other way. Paterfamilias from the country with mater and the children are coming back, the pleasures of memory now taking the place of the pleasures of hope indulged in a short month ago. Nevertheless, all the watering places, with the possible exception of Folkestone, are fulkand land- lords and lodging-house keepers are reaping a harvest as exceptionally bountiful as that which blesses the farmer. Curiously enough Boulogne shares the sad latifot.Folke- stene, which silly persons avoid under the impression that people flying from the Mediterranean will leave the cholera there. Why they should keep it specially for Folkestone or Boulogne is not made clear. But the scare undoubtedlres- ists, greatly to the detriment of the interest of these two towns. The Isle of Wight, which is in tempting proximity to all the towns at which passengers from • the Continent wauld land, is crowded. A friend of mine bound thither- wards with his family could not find rest on the island for the soles of their feet. After vainly trying .sit'srarions !Places, he re-crossed the Solent. Then the happathought , occurred to him that there was Bayling Island, a place no one was likely to think -of. So he posted off there to find' every private room engaged, and only so-so accommodation •at 'ruinous prices to be had at the hotel. I have.ir most melancholy letter froralim, in which he announces his ins-- mediate return to town:. Another holiday making_ friend, writing trom Hamburg, says "I am taking hese-what is singularly enough called the cure. If I can keep it up it will probably make sae a confirmed invalid. Bat- I an in great hopes I may break down before my coarse is-complete. If I sere-ire I hope to :Aimee in a fortnight, and, shall pro- bably try Folkestone air as a restorative." On the whole begirt to doubt whether holiday making is not a. mistake.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess.

The only case will be found in Monday's hat. MoNnlv.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alderman Davies, aud Mr J Fairslough. DRUNKENNES3.—For drunkenNess the following persons were dealt with as follows :—James Stol:es, in Hill-street, on Saturday, 203 and costs ; Henry Jordan, in Bridge-street, on Saturday, 53 and costs; Sarah Moon, in St Alban's- avenue, on Sunday, 5s and costs ; Martin Burke, on the 10th October, 1883, in Cockhedge-lane, 103 and costs. UNFORTIINATES.—Rebecca Dolt and Eliztbeth Ann Har- rison, two young women, one lholonging to Manchester and the other to Bury, and, described as factory hands, were charged with having been found sleeping in a shed with two soldiers.—On promiting to leave the town they were discharged. ALLEGED THEFT OF A SrawL.—Levi Ainsworth and William Ainsworth, who were said to be blacksmiths be- longing to Eccles, were charged with having stolen a shawl and brooch, t e property of Thomas Jones.—The prisoners, it appeared, came into Warrington on Saturday night, and went to lodge at J Imes Kimbling's lodging-house, 17, Dial- street. About 10 o'clock one of the prisoners was seen to pick up the shawl belonging to the complainant's wife, who was also a lodger, and both prisoaars afterwards left the house. Information was given to the police, and prisoners were arrested, and on being tahen to the police office one of them was seen to slip the shawl under a form.—The priso- ners were discharged. VIOLENT FEMALES —Elizabeth Bate and Margaret Bald- win, two young women, were each bound over to keep the peace for having caused a disturbance in Tanner's-lane, on the 25th ult. Funtors DRIVING—John Farre:l, a young man, was fined Is for driving furious'y in Bridge-street, on the 25th ultimo.

STRAYING PONlES.—George Brooks and Joseph Wilkin- son were each charged with having allowed a pony to stray in Battersby-lane, on the 22nd ultimo, and were each fined 2s 6d including costs. TUESDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- men Davies and Holmes, Councillor Broadbent, and Mr John Fairclough. DRUNKENNESS.—Patrick Mannion was fined 5s including costs for being drunk and disorderly in Parker-street, on the previous day.—Robert Halstead, for being drunk in Sankey-street and begging on the previous day, was fined 5s and costs, or 7 days —Ellen Connor was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street, on the 9th instant, and with committing a breach of the peace by fighting. She was dismissed on promising to mend her ways. MISCHIEVOUS &M.—Four boys, named Wm. Isherwood, John Clare, Thomas Green (sen ), and Thomas Green (jun.), were charged with stealing tins of salmon from the shop window of John Broadhurst, provision dealer, Church- street.—lt appeared that a pane of glass in the shop win- dow had been accidentally broken, and that the boys had been unable to resist the temptation of taking out the salmon.—They were each 'ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod.

WEDNESDAY—Before Aldermen Chandley and Burgess. BEGGING —James Sheridan was charged with begging in Mill-street on the previous evening—He was discharged on promising to leave the town. A DESERTER.—Martin Garratty, who pleaded guilty to being a deserter, was remanded to Walton to await an es- cort. .
TITURSDIY.—Egore Captain Litton. DRUNKENNESS —Margaret Burns was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street on the previous day. She was dismissed. _

FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Captain Reynolds. NEGLECT OF FamiLY.—Alfred Mortimer was charged with neglecting to maintain his two children.—The case had been adjourned twice in the hope of his getting work, but he had not done no. Pi saner now said that he bad work to go to, and he was discharged on promising to- make provision for his family. BEGGING —Thomas Armstrong was charged with begging in Manchester-road the same morning, ant was dismissed on promising to leave the town. . CARELESS FCSTIAN CUTTERS.—CharIotIe Higham was ordered to pay 12i, at Is GI per week, on a claim made by Messrs James Platt and Son, as compensation for damage occasioned by neglecting her work.—Thomas Duckworth, on the complaint of Stephen Moss, was ordered to return to work.

ALLEGED ILLEGAL ItFaIOVAL OF GOODS --IIMeS Slater was charged with fraudulently removing goods from a house occupied by him wh ii under distress for rent, the arrears being .£2 145 101.—The defendant said that he had given notice, it was not accepted, and he therefore left the house. —The case was dismissed.

Assarim.—Benjimin Tomlinson, labourer, Lythgoes- lane, was charged with assiulting his wife.—Mr A Browne appeared for the complainant, and described the alleged as- 9ault.—Ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, or go to prison for a month in default.—Joseph Sirncock, joiner, Wellington-street, was charged with assault- ing Ann llincroft.—Mr r Davies defended —Fined 20s and costs, or 14 days. THREATENING LANGIIAGE.—L2Ihe Ellis, 12, Bucklev•st, was charged with using threatening language towards Mar- garet Davy: D missed on payment of the cost of the summons,
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETIT SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY—Before Mr Marson.

--- DRUNKENNESS.—The folio's/lag cases of drunkenness were disposed of, v'z :—William Ruse, drunk and disorderly at Sankey on the 31st alt, fined 53 and costs; Martin Con- cannon, drunk at Ris'on, fined 53 and costs; Joseph Ashton and Thomas Heath, drunk and disorderly at Penketh, fined 5s and costs each; Thomas Kenwright, drunk and disor- derly at Penketb, fined 103 and costs; James Morgan, fined 103 and coats; Thomas Jennings, drunk at Woolston, fined 5s and costs; Catherine Hands, drunk at Orford, fined 23 64 and coats; Bridget Daley, drunk at Orford, fined 5s and costs.
A CARELESS BICYCLIST.—WiIIiam Murray, for riding a bicycle without having his lamp lighted, was ordered to pay the costs.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr W Bankes and Mr II Reynolds. MISCELLANEOES —Williarn Boyle and William Seddon, were each tined 103 and costs for drunkenness and disorder- ly cnnduct.--J thn Henry Turner was fined 103 and nests for having on the 22nd ult used obscene and profane lan- guage in Queen-street. TEMPORARY AIITHORITY.—Mrs Elizabeth Chadwick ap- plied for permission to sell at the Greenway Vaults, Green- way, Runcorn, under the license held by her late husband. THEFT OF TURNIP3.—James Sergerson, an elderly man, living in Shaw-street, was charged with stealing two turnips belonging to John Morris, grocer and farmer, Greenwav-rd. The prosecutor said he had had a great deal of damage done to his crops of potatces and turnips during the past few months. Several lots of potatoes bad been stolen during the past fortnight.—P S Lormdes. Paid about twenty minutes past midnight on Saturday, be saw the prisoner come out of the prosecutor's turnip field. He had two turnips in his possession, and some turnip tops in his pocket. He said" 0 Lord let me go, le will ruin me if you take me."—The Bench fined the prisoner 103, and costs 63 4d. Poox RITES W Sutton, assistant overseer, had issued summonses against 68 persons for non-payment of poor rates. Twenty-dye cases were heard, and the usual orders were made. The other cases were settled.

ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT. FRIDAY.—Be fore Mr J C Gamble and Dr Gaskell. P.I2Oi:ANE LA Noo. John Devlin, of Parr, was sum- moned for 113',',1 profane language, and for being drank and disorderly on to previous Monday. As he did not appear be was fined 10a and c ,sts for bin g drunk and disorderly, and 63 6d and costs for the profane languase. PITC3I AND Toss.—Jan Dyer of Windle, was summoned for playing at pitch and toss, and as he had. been frequently convicted for similar off mcks he was fined he and costs.-- Michael Galigan, fhomas Buckley, John Brannan, and Pat- rick Reid, all of Eccleston were summoned for playing at pitch and toss on canal bank, wes', on the previous Sunday. They were each fined 2s 6d and COIL MONDAY.—Before Messrs H S Hall, J C Gamble, and Alderman Harrison. CHIMNEY ON FIRE. John Thorpe, a resident of Parr, was summoned for having the chimney of his dwelling- hones on fire on the 27th ult, and was fined 7s, including costs.
ALLEGED ASSACLT —Jarnes Logan, a young man, was summoned for assaulting Michael Kierman, on the 15th ult, by striking him on the head with a stick, but the Bench dismissed the case.

DAMAGING TURNIPS. Joseph Ellison, John Ellison, Richard Highcock, and Thomas Mason were summoned for trespassing in a field of growing turnips at Sutton, belong- log to John Noonan, on the 24, h August, and each defen- dant was fined 7s 61 and ordered to pay the damage.

WARRINGTON V. S. HELENS (2ND ELEVENS). This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and resulted in a draw much in favour of Warrington. Score :—Warriogton, 146; St. Helens, 57. WARRINGTON WESLEYAN let' V. PENNINGTON PARK IST. —This match was played on Saturday on the ground of the former, and resulted in a victory for the home team. Score : —Pennington Park 41, Warrington Wesleyan 58. BIRKENHEAD PARK V. HCYTON.—The match between the above clubs was played on the ground of the former at Bir- kenhead Park, on Saturday, in showery weather, Huytan winning by twenty-one runs and two wickets. Score : Bir- kenhead Park, 88 ; Huyton, 109. ST. HELENS RECREATION V. BIRKENHEAD VICTORIA.— This m Itch was played at Boundary-road, St. Helens, on Saturday. and resulted in a victory for the home team, for whom Parr bowled excelleetly, taking seven wickets for 11 runs. Score :—R creation, 08: Victoria, 30. LATCHFORD (2ND) V. THE GARRISON, WARRINGTON.— This match was played at Latchford, on Saturday, and re- sulted in a very easy win for the home team owing to the splendid bowling of W Green and J Thornton. Score : Latchford, 41; The Garrison, 16. The Garrison went in a second time, and were doing much better when time pre- vented further play. WINWICK V. GOLDORNE (2ND )—Played at Winwick on Saturday last, in showery weather. The home team win- ning the toss, knocked up 190. Thompson of the Warrington Grammar School, playing a faultless innings of 42. Got- borne could do nothing with the young Winwick left-hand bowler Harrison, who took his eight wickets for six runs. Scores :—Winwick 190, Gollerne 18. THE EMPLOYES OF MR. THOMAS FLETCHER, GAS AP- PARATUS WORKS, V. THE EMPLOYES OF ATLANTIC WORKS, BROADHEATII —A very enjoyable game at cricket was played on Saturday afternoon last, between the above clubs, and resulaed in a victory for Mr. Fletcher's Employes. Messrs. Roachan I Darwin bowled well, and Messrs Knowles, Gray, and Birchall batted well for the winning side. Score : —Mr. Fletcher's Employes 39, Atlantic Works, Broadheath, 20.

Sr. HELENS AND GROUND. —This match was played on Arpley Ground on Saturday afternoon, and resulted in a draw, in favour of the home team. Several showers fell during the afternoon, and once drove the players to shelter. Warrington won the toss, but a late start was made. Fa irclough and Wallington began batting to the bowling of Hammill and Bray. Several short runs were got, and the fielding was smarter. Wallington made a good start by bitting Bray for two fours and a single in one over. Fairclongh served Hammitt similarly, and Fidler went on for Hammill. A grand off-drive by Faircloug,h was taken, and Denton went in. Several overs were passed, Wallington scoring rapidly, and Den' on played one back to Bray. C G Lawton filled the vacancy, but was soon bcwled by a yorker. Clarke was next, and made 14 out of twenty scored while he was in. England was beaten by' Johnson, Armstrong run out and Ford clean bowled, the score standing at 7 for 107. Now came a change. Hind played steadily, treating one now and again with force, and Wallington played still with free- dom. Forty-seven runs were added and Wallington I.7as bowled. He had made 72 in first-class style, at times punishing the bowling severely. His score included eleven fours, and looking at the difficult wicket and good bowling of Bray, this sem must be ranked as one of the best made for the club this Anton. NOTES BY THE WAY. The match between Cheshire and Northumberland was concluded at Stockport, on Saturday, and, though the first match at No 'rustle, in June, was wonty the Northumbrians by ten wickets, the Cheshire county concluded their second season with a victory by an innings and 60 runs to spare. Score: Cheshire, 208; -Northumberland, 54 and 94.—The game M.C.C. and Ground against Leicestershire, the last of the Lords season, finished off on Saturday with a draw slightly in favour of the home team. The North of England Eleven at Nottingham, on Wed- nesday, gained a brilliant victory over the Australians by 170 runs. Overnight the Colonists had an innings to play and 247 runs to get to win. Considering the condition of the ground the task was a very heavy one, but the Austra- lians have such a reputation for playing an up-hill game that it was thought they might pull the match out of the tire. From the first, however, it was evident that they had scarcely a chance. The first six wickets went down for 23 runs, and Midwinter and Blackham by good batting added 32 runs. At m. this no stand was made, and the match ter- minated as stated above. Score : North of England, 91 and 255 ; Australians, 100 and 76.—After playing a stub. bum defensive game for three hours and a half at Kenning- ton Oval, London, on Wednesday, Kent succeeded in draw- ing their return match with Surrey. The merit of the per- formance lay almost entirely with W H Patterson, the old Oxonian, who was in the whole time, and eventually car- ried out his bat for a wonderfully patient 73 In conjunc- tion with Mr Thornton be made the stand for the fifth wicket, which fairly saved the match. Surrey, of course, had all the best of the draw, as at the finish Kent, with only two wickets to flll, stilt wanted 107 to win. Score: Surrey, 123 and 214; Kent, 79 and 153. Cricket has found some new and distinguished votwies in Cumberland, one or two matches having been played re- , cently in which ladies of high social pesition have taken part. The ladies of Greystoke gained a victory over the ladies of Brayton three weeks ago, but when the return match was played this week the result, as will be seen from the subjoined score, was reversed: Greystokep33 and 33; Brayton, 21 and 64.

DISTURBANCE AT BUIZTONWOOD, —Before Messrs. R. Houghton and C. Pilkington, at the Newton Town Hill on Saturday. Elizabeth Costello, Thomas Costello and Patrick Pepper, were summoned for assaulting Jeremiah Chenery at Burtonwood on the 12th August. A cross-summons was issued by Thomas Costello against Catherine Chenery for assaulting him at the same time and place.--After hearing the evidence, which was of a contradictory character, the Bench ordered the two Costelios and Catherine Chenery to be bound over to keep the peace, and the summons against Pepper was dismissed.

The Rev J YONGE made the presentation to Mr Rippon. In doing so he said that the oftener he heard the Mayor speak the more ho was disposed to envy his Worship. The Mayor had a gift of fluency which he (Mr Yonge) very much coveted, and he had a very happy knack of saying just what ought to be said in the way it ought to be expres- sed. k Hear, hear.) He thought he might not be going out of his way if in introducing the few sentences he had to utter he said they. were heartily pleased to see his Worship present amongst them that night. (Applause ) It was always an appropriate thing when the gentleman who for the time being occupied the most conspicuous place in the bora,ugh took his place at a meeting of that description; and he thought that they were the more indebted to the Mayor for his presence there that evening when they re- membered that he did not belong to the particular religious denomination to which the gentleman belonged in whose honour that meeting had been conversed. (Hear, hear.) The Mayor had very properly reminded them that the character of that meeting was one of a mingled description. He was very sensible of that himself, and as he stood there to per- form the pleasant duty which had been entrusted to him he looked forward to saying farewell to his friend and brother Mr Rippon with feelings of a great deal of personal regret. It was a very pleasant thing when brother ministers could work together, and that had been the case between Mr Rip. pea and himself ever since he came into that town. (Ap- plause.) They were there that evening to give some ex- pression to the sense of gratitude which they as Warrington people felt towards Mr Rippon for the special line in which be had distinguizhed himself. They were not there to con- gratulate him-33 they might well do—for the services he had rendered to the town as a Wesleyan Metho- dist minister, but they were there to acknowledge in the frankest, fullest, and heartiest manner their sense that he had done a full share in helping on the cause of temperance in their town. (Applause.) Mr Yonge then read the address as fellows:—" To the Rev Thomas Rippon. —Dear Sir,—On behalf of many friends connected with the Warrington Temperance Union and the cause of total ab- stinence generally in this town we desire to offer to you this valedictory address. Your removal from our midst is regarded with very considerable and sincere regret, as you have during your residence here thrown in your energies and your influence as a Christian minister with the cause that we hold of such paramount importance to the well-being of the community. We believe that your labours will leave lASling results, and that temperance in Warringtmt haS been well advanced by your repeated advocacy. While thus congratulating you upon the position you have held in this town on this subject and gratefully t tking leave of you on your departure for Preston we would venture to express the hope that in that important and populous town as in all places where your lot may be cast in the future your devo- tion to this noble cause may become even more conspicuous, and your efforts yet more largely successful. We are, dear sir, on behalf of the subscribers, Robert Garnett, John Yonge, William Mules, William Roberts, and William Hall."

The Rev W MuLxs next made the presentation to Mrs Rippon. Every sentiment, he said, which had been expressed by Mr Yonge in the able speech which he had just made he (Mr Mules) cordially re-echoed. If there was one word in the vocabulary of the English language which he disliked to use it was that word which they had to use that night in reference to their friends Mr and Mrs Rippon as they left that sphere of labour in which they' had been so eminently successful during the past three years. When they were engaged in 8 lying Good-bye" to Mr Rippon they were not merely saying " Gooddt e" to a minister who was leaving the neighbourhood on the completion of his term of office, but they ' were bidding God-speed to one who in the noble cause of temperance had made himslf a universal man. (Loud applause.) There were representatives there from every existing denomination in Warrington to say " Good- bye" to their friend Mr Rippon. Mr Rippon had been a universal friend and a universal favourite througheut the whole of the time he had been in Warrington, and such a man was bound to win a universal respect. (Loud ap- plause.) The meeting was also addressed by Dr. Mackie, the Rev. J. B. Anderson, the Rev. Mr. Moore, Mr. Wm. Roberts, the Rev. J. McTurk, and Mr. J. W. Hall. Mr. RIPPON, on coming forward to acknowledge the pre- sentations, was received with loud applause. In the course of an appropriate speech which was intently listened to he said he thanked those who had given birth to those gifts, and especially the secretaries and th 3 committee who had had all the trouble. He thanked the subscribers who he was glad to know were not all Wesleyans. (Hear, hear-) He felt very grateful that the Mayor of Warrington had honoured him and honoured the temperance party by ap- pearing on the platform—(hear, hear)—and he also felt thankful that on that platform they had Dr. Mackie. And in mentioning his name he might say that the churches and temperance party in Warrington were obligated to the Press of the town for the influence which it had given to their temperance and church work. They had sometimes spoken to a hundred from that platform, but tho Press had enabled them to address a constituency of thousands. Thank God that the Press was with them in the matter. (Hear, bear.) lie thought that temperance sentiments were never stronger in Warrington than they were today. He alluded t ) the great service rendered to the cruse of temperance by the Roman Catholic League of the Cross, and said he regretted that the temperance question should be left in the main to Liberals and Dissenters. If he might give a word of advice to his Conservative friends it would be "Do not leave this matter of temperance to any one political sect." (Hear, hear.) They should sink totally their political and ecclesias- tical differences and combine altogether in fighting that drink demon. He also urged them to support the United Kingdom Alliance, and to help forward the cause of tem- perance by the use of their votes at election times. In con- clusion Mr. Rippon moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor. (Applause.) This was seconded by the Hey. J. YONGE, and carried by acclamation.

PRESENTATION AT BEWSEY-ROAD CHAPEL. On Tuesday evening further presentations were made to Mr and Mrs Rippon by the friends in connection with the Bewley-road Wesleyan Chapel. Prior to the presentation a tea which had been given by Mr W J Horton, was partaken of in the school-room by over 100 persons. The presents on this occasion consisted of a solid silver pocket communion service to Mr Rippon, and half a dozen silver table napkin

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 6, 1884. PRESENTATIONS TO MR. AND MRS. RIPPON AT WARRINGTON. On Monday evening a very largely attended meeting in connection with the Warrington Temp-trance Union was held in the Workmen's Club, Mirket-pl ice, for the purpose of taking a public leave of the Rev T Rippon, who is about to leave Warrington for Preston. At the same meeting Mr 12,ppon was presented with a beautifully illuminated ad- these, encased in book form in handsome bindings,; and Mrs Rippon was also presented with a fine silver tea ser- vice. '1 been presents have been chiefly subscribed for by Sir and Mrs Rippon's temperance fiends to show their recognition of the great services th it hid been rendered by them in the cause in which they were mutually engaged dining their three veers' residence in Warrington. At the meting the chair was occupied by the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), and there were also on the pletfortn the Revs J Tongs, W Mulee, J Merrick, J P Anderson Averpool), and e Moore; Dr Mackie, and Messrs J W Hall, W B,eberts, and Croefield (Manchester). The meeting having been opened by the singing of a hymn, The MAYOR said as he was not a teetotaller himself they would not expect from him a teetotal speech. But if he did not make a teetotal speech it would not be becaus3 he was not in the fullest sympathy with the teetotal ctuse. He knew that total ahetention was the only thing they could adopt under certain circumstances, and therefore he should he very sorry indeed if he thought be was capable of lordt- iig with an unfriendly eye upon the *e fferts that were put forth for the purpose of making people sober and better, and for doing away with an evil that had almost become na- tional. When he locked around that room he was reminded very forcibly of what an essayist once wrote for the pur- pose of proving that this world, to use his term, was a world of compensations—that there was hardly such a thing to be found as an unelloyed pleasure ; that if they had a pleasure it was alloyed, there was some drawback to it. At the same time there was always, as they were told, a silver lining to every dark cloud. He thought the meeting that night was no excep- tion to that rule. They were all met there for the purpose of performing a little duty which he might say was ex- tremely pleasant to all of them. But still there was at the Lame time a little drawback to it for they knew perfectly well that it was only the prelude to their bidding adieu La an esteemed and patriotic citizen who had earnestly cone his duty, and more than could be said to be hie duty, for the purpose of raising his fellow-men tea higher level, socially, morally, and intellec'u tl ly. (Applause ) Their friend Mr. Rippon, as was well known, hid devoted himself assiduously to the great object he had in view. When he first came to Warrington he found that the town was not by any means in the condition he would like to see it, so far as its sobriety was concerned, and he determined to devote himself in all his spare moments to the endeavour to correct that evil, and Mr. Rippon had, he was quite sure, with great d germination anti with great perseverance and sacrifice of time, devoted himself to that object. It did seem a pity that when War- rington was beginning to feel the effects of what he had done that he was about to leave them. (Hear, hear.) But he supposed there was no help for it; they had to accept the inevitable. As he had said, the fact of Mr. Rippen's leaving them was the alloy of their complete pleasure that night. (Hear, hear.) He (the Mayor) cull only repeat the wish that he had heard expressed before, that, Mr. Rip- pon might find in that town, which they had heard described as "Proud Preston," all the help and support and encourage- ment he had met with in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He was quite satisfied that Mr. Rippon would very soon make for himself a position in Preston, and he had no doubt that Preston would be as loath to part with him as they were in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that at the ex- piration of three years it was impossible for a Wesleyan minister to remain longer, however earnestly he and his flock might wish it. The law was imperative that at the expiration of three years he must leave. He (the Mayor) hoped that sometime it would b 3 found that that period of three years might be extended to at least double that length of time—(hear, bear, and applause)—for he could not help thinking that in the case of one like Mr. Rippon it must be a source of dietress to him to think that he was to leave so many friends as he had been able to make whilst amongst them. (Hear, hear.) He might say th it Preston was to be congratulated open receiving Mr. Rippon, and he hoped that his ministry there would be blessed in the same way as it had been in Warrington. (Loud applause.) A song was then excellently Bung by Miss Horton, after which

rings to Mrs Rippon. The communion service was inscribed as follows:—" Presented to the Rev Thomas Rippon by the Beweey-road Wesleyan congregation, Warrington, August, 1884." The presents were supplied by Me J Robinson, watchmaker and jeweller, Arthur•street. After tea the chair was occupied by the Rev J Ben- net-Anderson, of Liverpool, and there were also present the Mayoress (Mrs Harrison) and the Rev J McTurk, the newly. appointed superintendent of the Warrington Wesleyan circuit. The CHAIRMAN in the course of a few introductory remarks said that he felt it to be a privilege to be there to take part in a meeting connected with his friend the Rev Thomas ttip- pon. He might say while they were bidding "Good-bye " to their friend that he was not going very far—only to Preston. He would not there have the joy of seeing the living body of the venerable Joseph Livesey, who drew out the pledge of the seven men of Preston. Joseph Livesey had gone home that atternoon, but hundreds would go to Preston and see him laid in his last resting place. (Hear, hear.) The Chairmen also read A letter from the Mayor stating that he would have beentpreseut at that meeting if it had not been for an important meeting of the Town Council the same evening. He (the chairman) thought the Metho- dists must be taking posseseion of the Mayor and aldermen and councillors. for he was told that the Mayor was present on Sunday night in the chapel, he had been at the Workmen's Hall on the previous night, and he would have been there that night but for a meeting of the Council. (Hear, hear.)—" the Lost chord" was then sung in an effective manner by Miss L Horton, after which Mr W J HORTON rn Ade the preeentation to Mr Ripon. In doing so he expressed hie pleasure at seeing Bo many present that eveuing, and he mentioned that the' present had been subscribed for by the people connected with that place of worship, as a memor- ial of their appreciation of Mr Rippon's services amongst them. Their lereeent was but smell, but they were sure Mr Rippon would not regard its value but the feelings which had prompted it, and it would no doubt cause him to think about them when some of them had passed away: (Hear, hear.)—Miss H ll.ntton then sing in a very pretty manner " He wipes the tear from every eye."—Mr E S DALLOW then made the presentation to Mrs Rippon. He could not help thinking, he said, that he was in the wrong place that night. He had never had a job like that in his life before, and he had been in many a scrape, but never in such a one as that. (Laughter.) But he was sure that what he slid came from his heart. There was, as the A iyor had said the night be- fore, never a pleasure without alloy, and as they were met there that night they had to say "good bye" to their pastor and Mrs Rippon. He hoped Mr and Mrs Rippon would be spared for many years to come, and although the ministers in their Methodist connection were not allowed more than three years in one circuit, they slid that if after six years a circuit liked it could invite a minister back again, so that if Mr Rippon did not get up to one of those first Lon- don circuits from whera there was no getting them back again —(laughter) they would have him in Warrington once more. (Applause.)—Mr RIPPON, in acknowledging the present said that he felt hard we for speech that night. In the face of such kindness as he had received from his friends there, he found it a difficult task to respond, and use words that would in any way con- vey his thought or feeling. He came there three years ago succeeding a minister who was very much beloved, and also , another minister who was an indefatigable visitor; but he I felt the first time he stood in the pulpit in that chapel that there was sympathy there. That was not a feeling he had felt in every pulpit in that circuit. Ile in- vited them—if they would not all come at once---(laughter) —to visit him at his new home at Preston, and alluding to his three year, service in that town, he said he had gone on very pleasantly with those with whom he had been connec- ted. At the end of the three years they were able to report progress in that congregation to the tune of 30 per cent. They had increased in their membership quarterly since he came, and the spirit and tone of their society hid been everything that could be desired. (Applause.)—The Rev, J. MeTtertx, who also addressed the meeting, said that Mr. Rippon would go to his new sphere heat tened by the kind- ness and the earnestness of their expressions towards him that night. He further alluded to Mr. Rippon'e services in connection with the Blue Ribbon Mission in Warrington, and said that he had been in meny a workman's home where he was told that Mr. Rippen hod been the means of mem- bers of the family signing the pledge. (Applause.)—ln the course of the meeting fruit, also provided by Mr. Horton, was served round. The proceedings concluded by votes of thanks to Mr. Horton for his hospitality, and also to the Chairman. SILVER-STREET GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION.

In connection with this mission a tea meeting was held on Saturday at the Temperance Hotel, Sankey-street, there being about 20 members present. After tea the meeting was presided over by Mr 11 Richard, who stated that they were there to take leave of their esteemed minister, the Rev T Rippon. Messrs Willett, Grou4h, William Thomas, and John 8 Mercer also spoke is kindly terms of Mr Rippon, and Mr Whitehead presented Mr Rippon with a dressing case on behalf of the mission band. Mr Riopon thanked those present for their kind expressions of friendship to- wards him, and assured them that no present could give him more pleasure than the one he had received. The meeting closed with singing and prayer.

'WARRINGTON BREWSTER SESSIONS. The annual licensing sessions for the borough of Warring- ton took place on Monday at the Police Court. The magis- trates on the Bench were the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair. Aldermen Davies and Holmes, and Messrs. C. Broadbent and J. Faircloegh. A number of the clergy and ministers of the town were also present.—On the magis- trates' clerk (Mr. U. B. White) asking if there were any ob- jections to the renewals of the licenses of any of the fully licensed houses, the Rev. R. W. P. Montgo,nery said that he had been entrusted with a memorial on behalf of the clergy and ministers of all denominations of Warrington. He thought it had reference to the granting of fresh licenses, renewals, and also grocers' licenses.—The Mayor: You in- clude the whole posse comitatus as it were.—Mr. Montgom- ery : I represent all the christian communities in Warring- ton.—The Clerk: Legally these gentlemen have no status or right to address the Bench, but if the magistrates choose e to hear them, then there is nothing to prevent it.—Mr. Montgomery: I se by the papers that it is a course that has been followed throughout the country. There are other memorials, and I will simply content myself by reading this. —The text of the memorial read by Mr. Montgomery was as follows :—" That your memorialists again approach your worships with a deep sense of the arduous and painful duties which the legislature has imposed upon you for fulfilment at the Brewster Sessions. That your memorialists, in view of the inevitable results of the traffic in ictexiceting liquors in the production of drunkenness, crime, and pauperism, re- gard the responsibilities imposed open your worships as too great for any body of gentlemen to reet under without the ' aid and sympathy of their fellow-citizens ; they therefore desire to respectfully assure your wor- ships that every effort which you may make to diminish the number of licensed places of temptation will meet with the approval of the great body of inhabitants of this town, and your memorialists would express their satis- faction at the announcement made last year by the magis- tretes of their intention upon the present occasion to con- siderably reduce the number of licenses. Your memorialists desire at this time to remind your worships of the full and complete power over off-beer licenses which the Act of 1882 has placed in your hands, making them subject to the same conditions as all licenses for consumption on the premises. Doubts which some magistrates had have been removed by the decision in the C 390 The Queen v Kay, which was heard in the Queen's Bench, wherein the decision of Mr Justice Field and Mr Justice Stephen declared that all such licenses are held from year to year at the discretion of the licensing magistrates; the judgment further declared that the power of the magistrates was complete, not only in regard to the granting and renewal of licenses for the sale of beer off the premises, but also over all licenses for the Bela of and con- sumption of intoxicating liquors on the !eternises. Your memorialists therefore pray your worships to exercise in the public interest your undoubted powers, not only in refusing all new applications for licenses, but also in greatly reducing the number of present houses, inasmuch as many of those already licensed have during the past year been the princi- pal cause of the notorious drinking among young people especially girls of tender years, as well as largely produced, the misery and crime brought before you for considera- tion and punishment." The memorial was signed by the various clergymen and ministers of the town. In conclusion, Mr Montgomery said that he was almost a perfect stranger in Warrington, and he was sorry that some other minister had not been chosen to present the memorial.—The Clerk : Do you object to any specific licensed house? I cannot, because I do not know of any.—The Rev. T. Rippon said that he had a petition from the Warrington Temperance Union if the Bench would kindly hear it. It was " That your memorialists having been engaged for many years past in the work of rescuing men and women from the evils of intemperance, beg very respectfully to approach your worships in order to appeal most earnestly against the grant- ing of additional licenses in the borough, and also for a considerable reduction of the present number of off licenses. Your memorialists would also urge that licenses should be refused to those houses who have been notorious during the past year for bad conduct, and more p trticuleely fur exces- sive drinking amongst young people. Your memorialists would assure your worships that any actioreyou may take to ceery out the promise made by the Bench last year will meet with the hearty approval of a large section of this community." He should be disposed to fellow up the peti- tion with a few observations if time permitted, but he knew that the time of the Bench was limited, and therefore he at present would refrain from doing so. He had no objection to any specified house.—The Rev. J. Yonge said that he had been requested to present a memorial on behalf of the Warrington Bind of Hope Union, which was a campera- tively [IOW institution in tho town, but which represented some 4,000 children resident in the borough. The tenor of the petition was similar to those already presented to the Bench. He thought that perhaps the plea of the children was entitle] to be heard, because children suffered greatly if there was any drunkenness in the home Reference had been m ide to the promise of the magistrates a year ago, and he would personally express his strong hope that the magistrates would not forget the expressions then used. The memorial handed in by Mr Yonge, who made so specific objection, was as follows:—" That your memorial- ists, representing four thousand children inhabitants of this borough, feel great interest in the welfare of the commu- nity generally. That the drinking habits fostered by the traffic in intoxicating liquors have been a source of great injury to our town, notably amongst young people, having induced poverty, pauperism, disease' and crime, in many in- stances to the great grief of several families. Your mem- orialists therefore pray your worshipe not to grant any new licenses whatever, and also to reduce the number of licensed houses where they are in excess of the absolute requirements of the district."—The Mayor said that it was only courteous to say that the memorialists might rely upon receiving the inset respectful and earnest consideration of the Beech. It might perhaps gratify them to know that durieg the last year drunkenness had not progressed in Warrington' and there had been comparatively few persons fined for infrac- tion of their licensee. It appeared to him that there had been a great improvement, and that a steady improvement was at the preseet time going on. Whilst they were anxious to do everything they possibly could to promote the sobriety and temperance of the town, they mast not indulge in any- thing like persecution, as that would only tend to promote the evil they were so laudably endeavouring to suppress.— Mr. Broadbent thought that there was one unfavourable feiture„ and that was that the diminution of drunkenness did not apply to females. There were a large number of femeles who had been convected.—The Clerk: Ten years ago the number of convictions was 1,030; it has gradually decreased until this year to 051. Alderman Davies thought it would be satisfactory to see that the number of convictions ten years ego was 100 per cent, more than they now were. He was then speaking of men. .Taking men and women to- gether as regarded drunkenness the convictions were 40 per cent. less this year than last. A 9 regarded females it was deplorable that 124 convictions took place in 1875 and that there were now 174, being an increase of 50. He was afraid that drunkenness amongst females was largely brought about by the off-licenses, which gave an opportunity to people to take drink to their homes. He was sorry that more power was not put into the hands of the megistrates, or anyone who had the granting of licenses, to determine as to whether there should be an off-license granted or not. The people who held these licenses had acquired a kind of vested interest. The Bench had to be careful that no in- justice should be done. They wete desirous of suppressing the licenses, but had to be careful to avoid an appearance of injustice.—The Clerk: As a matter of fact, you had no power then to refuse these licenses.—Tke Mayor: The bon- st,uction put upon it by the j estices to whom allusion was made has settled the question that the magistrates bad the power.—Mr. Rippon remarked that in the district that he representerl—Bewsey-road— the off-licenses were curses, especially to children and women. He wished to mention that there was a kind of club in this district which he be- lieved was a great curse to the working-men. The Chief Constable would be able to supply information that he could Lot give, but he had heard from several of the evil caused by it. He believed that they could keep the house open all night, and that drinking went on there. He should also mention that Mr Greening, chairman of ihe Board of Guardians, and occupier' of a house in Bewsey-road, would have been pleased to have been present to support the peti- tion but for the fact that he was on the eve of leaving for America. Mr Greening was strongly in favour of decreas- ing the licenses.—The Clerk : You understand that appli- cations for new licenses will be heard on Monday next. This is simply the day for renewals.—The Mayor said that it was a matter of congratulation that there had been no conviction against licensed victuallers during the year.— Alderman Davies: The average convictions of licensed vic- tuallers during the last ten years has been four per annum, whereas this year there are none.—The licenses of the fully licensed houses were then renewed, and the beerhonse licenses were then proceeded with.—Mr Hunt said that teere had been two beerhouse keepers summoned during the year. They had received notice to be present that day. One, Kate Jenks, was summoned for harbouring a police. constable when upon duty, and was ordered to pay the costs. The other, James Kennion, was tined 5s including the costs for selling drink during the prohibited hours.— The Mayor said he remembered that the case against Mrs Jenks was a very slight one, as the offence was net com- mitted with her knowledge. The other offence was not a very flagrant one.—Mr Hunt remarked that it appeared on the defaulter sheet that a publican had been convicted. It was a person who held a license at Townsend, who was con- victed for selling drink in Battermarket-street, without having a temporary authority.—Mr Roberts said that he should like to draw attention to a house in Pitt-street, where there were frequent fights, which generally occurred in the streets outside.—Mr Hunt said that there had been previous complaints about the house in question, but he was in hopes from what be had beard during the last month that that sort of thing had died out. From the fact that a man named Albert Woods had opened a house as a club he had been led to believe that the other house had been cleared. Albert Woods sold drink without a license, and the police seemed to have no control over him. He got the house under the pretence that he was going to sell tea and coffee to the forgemen, but no excisable liquors. The police had done what they could, but it was a matter of time. There seemed to be no law to touch him. The police had kept an eye on the house mentioned by Mr Roberts. —The Mayor -(to Mr Roberts) : You make a specific complaint against the renewal of the license ? Yes. The Clerk : It will be adjourned, and you must give seven days' orifice to Mr Worrale—Mr Roberts: I am not pre- pared to do anything more than I have said in public court. —The Mayor: Then you leave us powerless.—The Cleat said that anyone could give the necessary notice.--The off licenses were next considered.—Mr Hunt said that an off license holder, George Bradburn, was summoned on the 10th and 19th June for selling beer contrary to law. In

one case he was dismissed, and in the other he was lined 103 and costs. In respect to a man named Hill, who had been convicted, Mr Hunt said that he had now left the house and the license had been transferred to another person.—The magistrates retired to consider the question of granting the oftlicenses, and on returning the Mayor said that they had come to the conclusion that they must renew the licenses in cases where convictions had not been obtained against the holders. Cases where convictions bad been obtained would be adjourned until the 29th of September for further consideration. There was a perfect concensus of opinion that off licenses were a great hindranc4 to th 3 sobriety of the town. He was not quite sure what might be tie ulti- mate fate of these licenses, but where convictions bad been obtained it weuld not be advisable to renew them.—Mr Broadbent said that he should have been in favour of ad- journing the consideration of the subject until the 29th just, as there was 'a general feeling in the town that the off licenses were injurious in their effects. There was an unusually large number of those licenses in Warrington, and he therefore thought it would have been well to have adjourned the consideration of the subject.—The licenses were then renewed with three exceptions, those held by Jas. Worrall, John Monks. and James Bradburn.—This con- cluded the business.

Appended is the report of the Chief Constable (Mr Hunt) to the Bench :—I have the honour to inform you that the annual Brewster Sessions for this Borough will ba held in the Session Room on Tuesday next, September 2nd, 1884. Underneath is table for the last ten years of the number of licensed victuallers, beerhouse keepers, and off license holders, with number of offences committed by them, and the number convicted and dismissed ; also the number b-ought up for drnokenness and the convicted and dismissed. The bottom line of the table shows the numbers for the year ended August 21st, 1884. The transfers for the year have bean—licensed victuallers 18, beerhouse keepers 6, and off license holders, elec., 15; total transfers 39.—Yours obediently, SAMUEL Hum; chief constable.

div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

HUYTON QUARRY WE3LEYAN CHAPEL:—TWO Liverpool gentlemen, Mr Ellis Davies and Mr Edward Hutchinson, have each given the sum of £250 towards this place of wor- ship, and thus have secured the building for the Wesleyan body, the place being formally handed over to the new trustees on Monday. After the building has been repaired and painted, re-epening services will be held. HUTTON TEMPERANCE ASSOOIATION.-00. Tuesday the first weekly meeting was held in the Huyton Park school- room. The Rev J W Walker, 8.A., presided. He urgod the members and temperance workers to go shoulder to shoulder, and so strengthen the cause. Messrs W D Stoba, H, It', and P Cappers gave readings, and Mr T Smith made a speech. The attendance WAS encouragingly above the average, and signatures to the pledge were taken at the close of the meeting.

FASHIONABLE WEDDING AT RUYTOM.—On Wednesday morning the Parish Church was well filled, when the nap- trials of Mr Robert Wilson Alexander and Miss Annie Bernard, second daughter of Mr John Bernard, both of kites'- toil, were celebrated. The Rev Canon Penrhyn performed the service. and Mr Hodgsm officiated at the organ, Mendelsohn's Wedding March being played, and the bells rung merrily as the newly-wedded couple left the edifice, amid the congratulations and showers of rice of their friends. The presents were of a nurrytous and costly character, con - !tieing of plate, furniture, dm. FeratOtiS Duivfica : AN EXCITING RACE AT HUTTON.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday John Dunville and William Webster, yming, men, from Sankey, near Warring- ton, were summoned for furiously driving in Liverpool-road, Huyton, on the 23rd ult —P.C. Carter said that he was on duty in plain clothes and saw the defendants each in charge of a horse and cart. They started racing along the road as bard as they could, shouting and yelling at the top of their voices. As they drew near to him witness spoke to Webster and asked him to stop, but Webster told him to "go to —,"and drove on. Witness attempted to seiz3 the reins, but the shaft of the cart struck him and knocked him on the footpath. Dunville followed behind and witness suc needed in seizing the reins and got the defendant's name and address. He then followed Webster to Prescot, and witness had to take Webster to the police station before he would give his name end address.—The Bench imposed a ffne of 103 and costs on each defendant. VIOLENT ASSAULT AT MUCH WOOLTON "A COMPLETE MANIAC "—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday Stephen Ilson, a labourer, residing at Much Woolton, was charged with assaulting P.C's. Carlton and Strong on Saturday night —P.C. Carlton visited the prisoner's house to serve a summons upon him, whereupon the prisoner struck him on the breast and otherwise assaulted him. He had to get the assistance of three other constables and they had to carry the prisoner to the police station after tying his legs.—P.C. Strong said he went to the assistance of P.C. Carlton and the prisoner severely bit him on two fingers.—Superinten- dent Barker said the prisoner was a complete maniac when in drink and as he had been previously convicted he asked the Bench to deal with him severely.—The Chairman re- marked that the prisoner seemed to have been mad and had conducted himself in a disgraceful way. It was no excuse to say he was in drink. He would be committed for six months with hard labour.

div.head: HUYTON LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: HUYTON LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday evening, when there were present, Messrs Dobell (in the chair), Dalzell, Siddeley, Cooper, Swift (clerk), Worrall (surveyor), and Dr Hall (medical officer.) The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.— OUTBREAK OF FEVER AT HUYTON QUARRY.-Dr Hall reported that during the month of August the deaths had been—lluyten two, Roby one, Huyton Quarry two, total five. He complained that the registrar (Mr Pendleton) had not given him due notioe of a death from scarlet fever at Huyton Quarry, on tho 6th August, and the news of which did not come to his ears until the 25th. He bad had the place disinfected, but a second case of scarlet fever had occurred. The surveyor was instituted to call upon the parents of the child in the cise alluded to, and ask them te keep it isola- ted as much as possible. THE SUPPLY OF WATER AT HORN'S SMITHY. - The Medical Officer said he was instructed at the last meeting to make an analysis of the water at Horn's Smithy, and he hod done so. He did not think the water was fit for domes- tic use, but if the Bolrd proposed to take any steps in.the. matter he suggested Or CampbAl Brown, of Liverpool, should analyse the water. The Clerk was ordered to take a sample of the water to Dr Brown for analysis. . .

THE SUPPLY OF GAS —The tender of 'the Iluyton and Roby Gas Company for the supply of gas for the lighting of the township from the 14th September to the end of April next for £2Ol 103; and for lighting, extinguishinet cleaning, and repairing 102 lamps for £BO was accepted Mr Mellor, of Tarbock-ro id, wrote a lengthy communication complaining of the want of gts lamps in that vicinity, and the letter was referred to the Cho Committee.

Tnz ExTmm-rioN OF FIRES.—The Chairman drew at- tention to the necessity of establishing some system by which fires in the township could be better coped with than at pre.ent. He remarked that they had no appliances at all, and he suggested that arrangements should be came to for the Telephone Company to erect a wire from the Board's offices to the West Derby Fire Brigade station. The Clerk was ultimately instructed to see the secretary of the Tele- phone Company upon the matter. This was the principal business.

EARLESTOWN.
