div.p: i' I
Asssum—&t the Newton Petty Sessions on Satur- day, William Haseldine, of Newton Common, was fined 2s 6d and costa for assaulting William Hancock, a lad, on the 16th ult.

Foormuz. —On Saturday the Earleetown club opened the season with a practice game between the let and 2nd teams on the ground at Wargrave. The first team was not fully represented, while the second were represented by about 15 members. After a fairly good game the result was a draw—four goals each. The Earlestown Wanderers club also opened their season on Saturday, when the first and second teams met on the ground near St John's Church. The game was pretty one-sided, the first team winning by no less than eight goals to none.

ODD—FELEOWS DianvEn.—The anniversary dinner in connection with the Loyal Viaduct Lodge of the Indepen- dent Order of Oddfellows, Manchester Unity, was held at the Wellington Inn, Earle-street, Earlestown, kept by Mr J W Thorpe, on Saturday evening. The dinner was of a most cacellent character, and reflected the highest credit 'upon the host. Nearly SO members sat down and thoroaghly enjoyed the feast. At the subsequent proceedings the chair was occupied by Bro. James Dolan. The usual toasts were duly honoured; the proceedings being interspersed with-- musical selections.

• DOXIMBIIO INPELICIITT. —Thomas Cartwright: a fore- man at the Viaduct Waggon Works, Earlestown„ was sum- moned at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before Mr. R. Houghton and Mr. C. Pilkington, hr assaulting his wife, Hannah Cartwright, on the 25th ult.—Mr. Browne, of War- rington, appeared for the complainant, and Mr. P. Davies, of Warriagton, represented the defendant. —The parties had been married 'about three years' and it was stated that recently the husband had several times assaulted his wife, and she was afraid of her life. On the date alluded to he struck his wife in the course of a quarrel, and it was alleged that be violently kicked her. She had a black eye and the complainant stated that it was the result of her husband's violence.— Phe_Bench imposed's fine of 5s and costs.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST TEA. PATITY. —The first of a series of social tea parties in aid of the baz tar fund was held in the Primitive Methodist schJolroorn, Legh-street, on Thursday evening. The congregation, teachers and scholars propose holding a bazaar in aid of the new schools in De- cember next, and with the object of raising a necessary amount prior to that undertaking, it has been decided to hold a few social gatherings. As stated, the first of these was held on Thursday evening, when about GO friends sat down to a most enjoyable tea. The Rev F N Shimrnin presided at the subsequent proceedings, several scholars giv- ing selections of music, recitations, &a. Mr W Austin pre- sided at the harmonium. The meeting was of a very plea- sant character.

THE ANTI-VACCINATION MOVEIIENT. —The resolu- tion passed at the recent anti-vaccination meeting held on the Market Ground, E,trlestown, has been forwarded to the members for South-West Lancashire. It was as follows : "That this ifleeting of Earlestown people considers the Vac- cination Acts immoral and unjust, and pledge themselves when they get the Franchise to vote only for those persons who will pledge themselves to vote for the repeal of the Vaccination Acts." The following are the replies which have been received :

Hale Hall, Liverpool.—Dear Eir,—l have to acknowleOg receipt of a resolution passed at Earlestown tin the Vaceinatioa Acts, which shall ree:lve my best atteatlon.—Yout4 faith- fu ly, J. IRELAND BLACKBURN,".-Mr. B. Harrison.

. . . Ei:cle Riggs, Br.,ugbt xidn-Furcet.s —.Sir Richard Cross begs leave to acknowledge receipt of c ,py resolution. THE SATURDAY NIGHT Row : POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS. The disgraceful row in Bridge-street, Earleetown, on Saturday night week, particulars of which we gave in our last issue, has since formed the subject of police court proceedings. It will be remembered that an individual whose name was described as "synonymous with 'stone ' " received a severe thrashing, and in the course of the disturbance was rendered insensible. On Saturday last, at the Newton Town Hall, Michael Rock, the person alluded to, was summoned for being drunk and disorderly on the previous Saturday. On being asked whether he was guilty or not the defendant replied, "Guilty, and well beat in the bargain,"—evidence of the latter being afforded by sticking plaster upon his head. He shortly afterwards added "Well. I suppose there's somebody in court who will have a bit of feeling for me. I got well beat in the bargain; got locked up, and what are you going to do with me now?" (Laugh- ter.)—The Chairman: You will be fined 53 and costs. CRUELTY TO HORSES AT NEWTON FAIR.—At the New- ton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Mr. H. Houghton and Mr. C. Pilkington, George Shaw was summoned for cruelly working a mare at Newton Fair on the 12th ult. ; and William Fairhurst, of Warrington, was summoned for causing the horse to be worked.—Mr. P. Davies appeared for the defendants, who pleaded guilty.—Fairhurst was fined lOs and costs, and Shaw was fined 53 and costs. --William Turner, of St. Helens, was summoned for cruelly working a horse in an unfit state at Newton on the 12th ult. It was stated that the defendant was driving a horse which had upon its shoulders two wounds, each about the size of a crown. Blood and matter were found under the collar and the horse was suffering great pain.—The Bench imposed a tine of 5s and costs.--Anthony Gilbert, of Newton Heath, was summoned for cruelly beating a pony, of which he was in charge at Newton fair on the 12th ult. The defendant vehemently denied the charge, and created some amusement by stating that he "could not hurt a flea."—lle was fined lOs and costs.

A "BEGGING LETTER" INDIVIDUAL SENT TO Pnrsox.—At the St. Helens Town Hill, on Wednesday, be- fore Dr. Gasket! and Mr. J. C. Gamble,‘ James Gibson, an aged man, was charged with begging at Parr on the pre- vious day.—P.C. Byrne deposed that about half-past twelve on the previous afternoon the prisoner was begging in Broad Oak, Parr. He saw him go to the house of the Rev. Mr. Nunn and be asked for alms; whereupon witness took him into custody. On the way to the station prisoner offered witness 61 to let him off, but the officer refused to do this. The prisoner also offered a purse to his daughter, stating that there was only lOid in it, but when the constable looked it was found to contain £1 14s. When the prisoner was searched at the office £2 5s 110 was found in his pos- session.—Superintendent Johnston informed the Bench that three copies of the following statement were found in the primer's possession Haydock, October 6th, 1880. Ladies and gentlemen,—l, James Gibson, Met with a sad ac- cident. Since that time I have not been able to follow my usual employment. Kind and benevolent friends, lam wholly dependent upon your support. Please help. Respect- fully yours, Ja.nes Gibson. He that giveth to the poor lendeth to the Lord."—The prisoner's daughter pleaded to the Bench to allow her the money found in possession of the prisoner, stating that all of it was not his.—The Chairman remarked that the prisoner would be committed for 14 days, and the money found in his possession would be devoted to- wards his maintenance during that period.

NEWTON INPROVENENT COMNISSIONERS. -- The monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Commission.. ers should have been held at Newton Town Hall on Monday afternoon, but owing to the absence of a quorum no business could be transacted. The only pra ms present were Mr W F Gooch (cbairmtn of the Board), Mr Thomas Hunt, Mr E We-sley (law clerk), and Mr It Brierley (surveyor). GOOD TF3EPLADS ENTERTArNMENT: —On Monday evening, after the weekly tneoting of tbs Hop.: of Fades- town Lodge of Good Templars, in the Lodge-room, Bridge Street, a selection of songs, recitations, and readings were excellently rendered by Brothers John Taylor, W Kenning,. J Thompson, J Barnard, and other members. The chair wee occupied by Bro. John Taylor, W.C.T. The proceedings were of an enjoyable character.

• EAnutsTolvi Berner CRAPE:L.—The school anniver- sary services in connection with the Baptist Chapel were, held on Sunday, when special sermons were preached by the Rev E Dyer, of Atherton, to large congregations. In the afternoon Mr Dyer delivered an interesting address to the parents, scholars, and teachers • and a selection of hymns wells snug by the school children. At each of the sevices a collection`was made in aid of the school expenses, and towards the cost of placing additional pews in the , chapel. The total amount realised was £l4.

dIIIIRCH AFFAIIIS'AT EARLESTOWIT.—IieIigiOUS affairs in the parish of St. John the Baptist, Earlestown, still remain in a discreditable state. The attendance at the services are still of a very meagre character; and the 'scattered flock" are now agitating for the erection of a suitable building in which to hold divine service. A meeting was held some time ago and a committee appointed to go into the matter, and, as a result of this, a decision has been arrived at to erect a commodious wooden structure. Negotiations are in progress for the acquirement of land on lease for a term of years, and it is expected that shortly a building will be erected for the accommodation of the scattered worshippers. Tau PEOPLE'S RIGHTS AT NEWTON CONNON.—It will be remembered that a week or two ago Miss Jessie Craigen, of London, delivered a series of anti-vaccination lectures on the Earlestown market-place, and at the close of the last one she alluded to the land question. In the course of her remarks she asserted that the people of Earlestown and Newton were being robbed of their Common by its enclosure, and she gave a promise to come again to Earlestown on September Ist and take the responsibility of pulling down the fences which had been erected during the past two or three years. As Monday last was September lot a large number of persons anxiously exp-cted the arrival of Miss Craigen on her mission of "public rights," and in the even- ing more than a few walked in the direction of the Common In the hope of witnessing the fence-destroying performance. But the lady failed to pat in an appearance, and thus the local supporters of the "land ,for the people" movement were disappointed. Some communications on the subject have passed between Miss Craigen and a resident of Earles- town, and Miss Craigen expressed her willingness to fulfil her promise if certain preparations and arrangements were made on her behalf. These arrangements could not be satisfactorily carried out by Monday last, and thus the ab- sence of Miss Craigen is accounted for.

FUNERAL OF AN OLD ODDFELLOW.—On Saturday the- remains of Mr. James Southward, aged 81, were interred at Newton Match. About 30 relatives and friends and up- wards of 80 Oddfellows assembled at half-past three and proceeded to the church. The funeral service was conducted by the Rev H Monk, vicar. After the funeral the relatives returned to the house in which be had lived all his life, and the Oddfellows proc eded to the Good by Lodge-room ad- joining, where dinner was partaken of: The chair was filled by P.G. John Mussel] (trustee), and the vice-chair by P.P.G.M. John B ill (secretary.) The dinner arrangements were carried out by Mr H Houghton (treasurer.)—The Vice- chairman, in proposing "To the memory of our departed Brother," alluded to the long ard useful services of P.G. Southward, who joined the blood Intent Lodge in January 1833. He bad passed through all the lodge offices, and after acting as treasurer for 15 years, became one of the trustees, a position he occupied to hia death. P.G. Southward had left behind him a noble example of duty, for during the first 50 years of his 51 years membership he had never mis- sed a single ledge attendance, His name was the first on the lodge dispensation board. His homely and comfornsble manner was always appreciated, and his memory would long live in the minds of those old and young Oddfellows who had that day paid the last mark et respect to departed worth.

NEWTON LICENbING SESSIONS. The annual brewster sessions for the Newton-le-Willows Petty Sessional division were held at the Town Hall, New- ton, on Saturday forenoon. before Mr Rqbert Houghton and Mr Charles Pilkington. The annual report of Superinten- dent Jackson (of Leigh) for the Warrington Petty Sessional division showed that the population was 21,510, the number of townships 12, licensed victuallers 47, beerhouses 15, out- door license holders 11; convictions during the year- licensed victuallere one, beerhonse ktepers and outdoor license holders none, persons summoned for drunkenness 179, last year 162, apprehended for drunkenness 42, last year 66. In the Warrington police division the number of town- ships was 21, licensed victuallers 132, beerhouse keepers 164, off license hollers 35, convictions 18, last year 15, summoned for drunkenness 790, last year 753, apprehended for drunkenness 424, last year 377. Superintendent Weir, of the Wigan division presented his annual report, which showed the number ei licensed victuallers in the division was 12, spirit grocers 2, beerhonse keepers 14, off licenses 5, Sunday drunkenness-persons apprehen led 4, convicted 2, ordered to pay costs 2, summoned 18, convicted 13, warrants unexecuted 5. drunkenness other tlatn on Sunday-persons apprehended 3, convicted 6, discharged 2, summoned 90, convicted 64, ordered to pay costs 13. dismissed 6, warrants unexecuted 7, proceedings for all kinds of offer ces-appre- heeded 25, summoned 297, total 322, last year (1883) 311, previous year (1882) 307. None of the licensed victuallers or beer sellers have been convicted during the past year of any offence against their licenses in the district. There were no new applications of any kind to lay before the licensing justices from any part of the licensing district of Newton-le-Willows.-The Chairman remarked that there did not appear to be anything calling for special notice so far as the Newton district was concerned, and as there was no objection to any of the old licenses they would be renewed. One or two cases of a temporary transfer were then disposed of, and the licensing business concluded.

PARK-LANE SICK AND ACCIDENT SOCIETY.—Th mem- bers of 013 Park-lane Sick and Accident Society held their 24th anniversary at the Golden Bill, Park-lane, on Satur- day. The members and their wives set down to an excel- ent tea. Brother David Shaw was appointed chairman, e and Brother Wiltiam Lowe, vice-chairman. Various toasts were proposed; and songs followed. The members danced at intervals during the evening. ASHTON Local, Boenn.—The monthly meeting was held on Widnesday. Mr 'Monbert presided, and the following were also Present : Messrs. Barton, Boardman, Britton, Gasket', Leith waite, C Latham, Painter, Pimblett, Roberts, Hill (clerk), and Cioldsworth (surveyor.)Mr B )atdman, captain of the volunteer fire brigade, drew attention to a paragraph in the newspapers referring to the recent tire at some cottages in Long-lane, which stated " that there was not sufficient force to raise the water to the required altitude." He wished it to go forth that there was a sufficient force of water, though, fortunately, on that occasion it was not required.— At a meeting of the Highway and Sanitary Committee a letter was read from Daniel Houghton, of Lamberhead Green, asking the Board to make him some compensation for injuries to himself, horse and cart, alleged to have been caused by the dangerous state of the road near to the Golden Ball, Park-lane. The committee directed the surveyor and clerk to make inquiries into the matter, and report to the ,neat meeting of the committee. The medical officer ra- per' ed that scarlatina was still somewhat prevalent—most particularly in Stubshaw Cross direction. The disease or its sequoia had caused nine deaths during the present month, which showed an increase in the mortality therefrom. Several cases had been treated in the hospital, but that in- stitution was now free. The usual precautions were being taken to prevent the disease spreading. Cases of diarrhoea had been and still were very frequent, consequent upon the extreme heat, and errors in eating and drinking. Two deaths were registered from this cause. Gas and Water Committee: A meeting of this committee was held on the 27th ult. The clerk stated that the station meter had been repaired, but as it bad only been working a few dans he was unable to report as to the make of gas. The committee gave instructions for the lamps to be lighted at the usual time, viz., September Ist. The surveyor reported that the depth of water in No. 1 reservoir was 24. 2in. as against 4ft. Gin, last month, and 41t. 21n. in the correspond- ing month of last year. No. 2 reservoir had a depth of 3ft.; No 3,4 ft.; and No. 4 was running over. No. 1 tank had a depth of 6! t. Din , and No. 2 4ft. 3in. The question of dis- continuing the supply of water for trade purposes was con- sidered by the committee, and the surveyor was authorised to cut off all such supplies, fin his opinion they were likely to interfere with a proper supply for domestic purposes.— The minutes were passed.

CHURCH TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. —The annual excur- sion in connection with the St. Helens Parish Church Tem- perance Society took place en aturd when, notwithstand- ing the showery staPe of the weather, a pleasant day WU spent at Southport. About 400 members and friends were conveyed thither by a train which left about seven o'clock in the morning, and arrived at its destinatioa shortly- after eight o'clock. The return journey was commenced al 7-15 p.m., and the trippers arrived back at St. Helens shortly be- fore nine o'clock.

FROM THE ALTAR TO TUE GRAVE.—A. sad occurrence in St. Helens this week has occasioned a painful impre,ssion throughout the town and nei4hbourhood. It appears that about three weeks ago a Miss Sarah Eliza Mortimer was married at Coventry to Mr. Paul Haver, excise officer, Present, and the happy pair spent the honeymoon at Ruthin, North Wales. At the beginning of last week they arrived at Prescot, and on Friday Mrs. Hayer visited a friend ha Argyle-street, St. Helens. Shortly after her arrival she was taken ill, and although every possible assistance was rendered she becaml worse and expired on Sunday morning. Tbe unlooked for death came as a great blow and surpt is a to the relatives and friends of the deceased, who was only 24 years of age. On Tuesday morning the body was conveyed to Coventry in a special van belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company. The remains were placed in a shell, incased in an oak coffin with brass mount- ings, and removed to the station by Mr. T. T. Fletcher, wh.o had charge of the arrangements. The greatest sympathy is felt for the bereaved husband and frien Is of the deceased.

TREES sea* Mama GROW.—Axle-trees. FAVOURITE GAME WITH THE OCEAN.—Pitch and toss. Insurance official: "Of what complaint did your father die?" Applicant: "The jury found him guilty." Ate' Sung Them Wes ALL. IT WAS !--e. gentleman out fishing with an Irish boatman expressed his fear of a down- pour of rain. He was reassured by the remark," Och, 'tis only a shmall dhrop of perspiration out of the clouds I" A LITTLE Boy's Tama. —A little boy who had been amongst the mountains for his holidays was told to write, as concisely as possible, a theme on the thoughts that sug- gest themselves when ascending a high mountain on a beautiful summer day. He wrote "I wish I were at the top." VICE ARTICLE TO FIT.—A young man who took his affianced to hear Nillsson warble her sweetest songs asked the young lady how she liked the singer's repertoire." "Very much indeed. I think it fits her beautifully ! " was the surprising reply. THE JEALOUS WIPE.—A gentleman who had experienced a little discomfort from the whims of a auspicious wife was asked the question: "Who do you think was the happiest man that ever lived?" "Adam," he answered promptly. "And why Adam ? " "Because he never had an oppor- tunity to make Eve jealous." A popular comedian, says the Topical Times, had in his service a short time since a domestic whose name was Mary, whom he had taken, out of charity, from the workhouse. One day Mary was very insolent to her mistress' whereupon the popular comedian expostulated with her on her conduct, and told her that, if it occurred again, he should certainly send her back to the place whence she came. "I won't go there," she replied," on any account. If the worst comes to the worst, I'll go on the stage ! " • SIMPLE METHODS ARE BESP.—An amateur of pictures has for some time past haunted the studio of a Bohemian painter, the whole of whose productions he purchases. More than that, he takes his protege about withhim, though he blushes a little at the shabby toilette of his companion, especially at a feariully and wonderfully battered hat, in which it is the painter's pleasure to distinguish himself whenever he goes abroad. You must get yourself another hat," the amateur ventured recently. " Never !" replied the Bohemian decisively. " Oh, don't misunderstand me; Ido not mean to put you to any expense! My hatter--" "Never, I tell you! I'll stick to my old hat,' because it frightens away all half-and-half friends." A gentleman was out driving with his wife, who was noted for her bad temper, and, in a narrow road, met a waggon which they had some difficulty in passing. The lady, apparently thinking that the carter was not making as much haste as he ought to do to get out of the way, be- gan to rate him pretty freely. Just however as they drew clear, the man stepped up to the carriage, and, respectfully touching his hat to the gentleman, asked whether he might speak a word. The lady, thinking that he was going to apologise for his slowness, interposed, and said very sharply, " Yes ; Bay whatever you have got to say." Whereupon the man, again touching his hat, and looking hard at the gentleman said very quietly, "Sir, I do pity 'ee from the bottom of my heart, for I've got just such another brute at home myself." Tins SMALL FRY.—" My child," said Rattler to his I youngest," I always eat the crusts of my bread." "I know it, papa," lisped the incorrigible, "I'm saving mine for you, too."—Yes, a baby is the most dependent of the animal creation. He is unable to help himself; but he soon gets over that and helps himself to everything he can lay his hand to. Sometimes he wants the earth and tries very hard to get it.—A father was telling his little son abut the won- ders of modern science. "Look at astronomy, nqw ; men have learne I the distance of the stars, and, with their spec- troscopes, what they are made of." "Yes," said the boy; " and, pa, isn't it strange how they found out all their names 7" A MERRY WAY—One day, when Wry, the French novelist, was visiting the late Jules Sandeau, an organ- grinder halted in front of the Academician's house and began to play. Sandeau, with a gesture of irritation, rose from his seat, took a half-franc piece from his pocket, and flung it to the tormentor, calling out as he did so, "Bs quiet, and go away !" "What," said Miry—" you encourage that de- testable kind of thing That man will now return every day; and not only so—he'll pass the word to all his com- rades." " What am Itodo ? " asked Sandeau. "The-street I live in," replied Miry, "is one of those most infested :by organ-grinders. I had only just moved into my apartment and opened my window for the first time, when one of them planted himself on the pavement opposite. He ground out the Miserere' from If Trovatore. I manifested a lively satisfaction. After the Miserere,' he obliged me with a raise. I took the chair and seated myself in the balcony. He then played me the air of one of the most popular songs of the day; I clapped my hands enthusiastically. Then he passed to the air of a sentimental song; I called to my servant to come and listen to it. 'Encore!' I cried. He played the tune over again, then politely took off his cap and held it towards me; whereupon I instantly banged to the window, and from the curtain witnessed a scene that would have been touching to anybody else. With an air of desperate bewilderment, the man gazed up at my window, then hitched his organ on to his back and staggered away, after having ca efully noted the number of my house. I went through the same panto- mime with five or six of the colleagues of my first musician, and then the cure was complete. From that time forth never—no never has an organ grinder stopped in front of my window. Better than that even; for yesterday morning, as 1 was quietly taking the air, I saw a man in velveteen trou- sers and with an organ on his back approaching. He raised his eyes to mine and quickened his pace, and lifting his thumb to the end of his nose, as much as to say, 'You'd like me to play you a tune or two, wouldn't you? But you've taken me in once; you'll not do it again! "

• • PROPOSED LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT RAINFORD'—A ' dernonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill, and to pro- test against the action of the House of Lords in stopping its progress, is announced to be held at Rainford Hall, the residence of Mr. Richard Pilking^on, on Saturday afternoon, the 13th inst. Arrangements for a procession from St. Helimy and train arrlngements will be -made known in a few days. The question is of special interest to the house- holders of St. Helens. In the district, with 10,437 houses, there are now only 1,945 voters. The Government bill would confer a vote on at least 6,000 persons who are at pre- sent deprived of the right to vote. DB. PRESCOT.

- - DRAG-Pox GUARDS AT PRESCOT.—On Thursday, about half-past one o'clock, a troupe of the sth Dragoon Guards, en route to Liverpool,' passed through Prescot. They started from Warrington in the forenoon, and journeyed through Rainhill, Prescot, &c, to their destination. In all there were 64 men, whose glittering helmets and swords and general smart appearance attracted considerable notice. ACCIDENT.—On Saturday morning a sad accident occurred at the Wigan and Whiston Colliery, Prescot, when John Thomas, son of Thomas Thomas, of Whiston, had one of his arms severed from his body. He along with another child was playing under some coal waggons which were standing in a slip-siding, and when the engine proceeded to take them away the child was knocked across the metals and run over. The arm was dressed be Dr Brindle, and the child is now progressing favourably. PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD—Tuesday was the day for the holding of the monthly meeting of the Prescot Highway Board, but no quorum eels present, and the meeting bad to be postponed. There were present: Mr. W. L. Evans, Mr. Leatberbarrow, Mr. Goldsworth (surveyor), and Mr. H. Cross (clerk.)—The surveyor (Mr. Goldsworth) submitted ethefollowing statement of expenditure for the four weeks ending August 28th: Bold £l3 161, Knowsley £6 17a 4d, R einiaill £6 12s, Whiston £l4 17s 2d, team labour £45 Is Id, new materials £32 4s 71d, incidentals'Si 'ls 10d, total £l2O 1.6 s OD. NEGLIGENT HUSBANDS AND FATHERS.—At the Porescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr E Gibbon and Mr. W L Evans, John Gerrard, a painter, formerly of Widnes, was charged under a warrant with deserting his wife and two children, whereby they became chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr S H Hartley (clerk to the Board of Guardians) prosecuted, and stated that the prisoner had left his family entirely unprovided for. The relieving officer found them in a state of abject poverty, without home and food, and with only very little clothing. The prisoner had been in full work, and there was no reason why be should have left his work or his family. The Guardians thought it a Very bad case —The prisoner was committed for a month with hard labour.--Wm. Lievesley, of St Helens, was charged with neglecting his wife and family.—lt was stated that the case bad been adjourned to give the prisoner an oppor- tunity of paying the 'costs incurred by the Guardians, but as he had failed to do this, he was committed for one month with hard labour. THE MAINTENANCE OF AGED PARENTS.—Before Messrs. E. Gibbon and W. L. Evans, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, George Dunne, Thomas Dunne, and William Dunne, all of Widnes, were • summoned to show cause why they should not contribute to the support of their father, who was at present chargeable to the Prescot Union. Mr. S. IL Hartley (clerk to the Prescot Board of (luardians) stated the father of the defendants was an inmate of the Workhouse, being stricken with paralysis, Ha was 60 years of age, and quite unable to work. The Guardians thought the sons, who were in receipt of good wages, were well able to contribute towards the support of their father. The defendants George and Thomas received over £2 per week each, and William had a standing Wage of 303 per week.—Tbe Bench made orders for the defendants to con- tribute the following weekly amounts: Thomas 3s 6d, George 21. and William is 6d.--John Smith and Thomas Smith, of Widnes, were summoned to show cause why they should not contribute towards the support of their aged mother, at present an inmate of the l'rescot Workhouse; and the Bench made an order for Thomas to pay 3s per week and John Is 61 per week. SERIOUS RESULT OF THROWING A TEA Cup.,--At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr E Gibbon and Mr W L Evans, Richard Smith, a middle-aged man, em- ployed as a labourer, was charged with unlawfully wound- ing a young woman, named Sophia Renshall, on the previous day.—Superintendent Barker briefly described the assault, after which the following evidence was given :—Prosecutrix stated that she was a single woman, but cohabited with a man named John Winstanley, and lived in Pottery-place. About five o'clock on the previous afternoon she went to prisoner's house, which was close to her house, and she saw the prisoner there. She asked him what was the matter with him, but he made no reply. He took up a tea cop from the table to throw at her, and she tried to make her way out of his road. The prisoner threw the cup, however, and it struck her behind the head, which caused a severe wound from which blood flowed very profusely, saturating her apron and jacket. When the cup struck her she was in her own house, and she afterwards became unconscious: The prisoner subsequently visited her house again, and with a stone in his hand said he would give her more than what he had done. He had previously threatened her.—A lice Smith, 10 years of age, daughter of the prisoner, said she saw her father throw the cup, which struck Sophia Renshall on the head, and she fell down.—Dr U S Hall deposed that on the previous evening the prosecutrix came to his surgery, and he found her suffering from a lacerated and contused wound on the hick of her head.—P.C. Middlebrook said he appre- hended the prisoner, and was present when he was charged with unlawfully wounding Sophia Renshall. The prisoner replied, "She unlawfully cut and wounded me; she threw a stone at me.' The prisoner admitted having thrown a tea cup at her, adding that if she had kept away from him he would not have touched her.—Superintendent J Barker remarked that the ptisoner had been a great many times be- fore the Bench previously for various offences; and the Bench said the prisoner had no justincatiem for the assault. He would be fined 40s and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment. PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD*—The monthly meeting of the Prescot Local Board was held on Wednesday evening, when there were present—Messrs H nage (in the chair), W Hatton, H Beesley, G S Preston, H Whitfield, II Cross (clerk), W Goldsworth (surveyor), and Dickenson (nuisance inspector).—Births and Deaths: The registrar's report for the menthe August showed the following deaths: Prescot 3. corresponding month last year 7; Eccloaton 0, last year 3; total 3, heat year 10. The death rate was 5i6 per 1,000 of the population estimated at 6,418, and last year 1868. The births were: PreecoLl6, corresponding month last-year 11; Eccleston 5, last year 3; total 21, last year 14.—The Ob- struction by a S7topkeeper: In reply to the chairman, the Clerk stated that the obstruction caused near the premises of Mr Morton in Eccleston-street had since been remedied. Mr Hatton observed that there was not the same obstruction as formerly, as the practice of showing goods on the footpath had been abated. Audit of Accounts: The Clerk intimated that he had re- ceived notice that the accounts of the Board would be audited by the Local Government Board's auditor on the 16th inst.—Nuisances: The Sanitary lospector drew atten- tion to a nuisance in East-street; and Mr Whitfield remarked that all bad smells should be kept down as far as possible, as they would create fever or any other disease if they were ' allowed to exist. He afterwards asked what was the system adopted in other towns—The Surveyor replied that it was just the same.—Mr Whitfield said he never noticed the abominable smells in Liverpool and other places.—Mr Pres- ton: Oh, yeas—The Surveyor stated that similar complaints were made at Liverpool and almost every town.—Mr Whit- field expressed the opinion that the best plan would be to disconnect all middens with the main sewer.—The Chair- man remarked that that was a question affecting the whole township. What they bad to deal with at present was the particular nuisance in Eaststreet.—Mr Preston moved, Mr Beesley seconded, and it was resolved that a n tice be served upon the owner of the property requesting him to abate the nuisance within 14 days.—The Registrar's Report: Mr Whitfield asked if the monthly reports of the registrar were paid for.—The Clerk: Yes.—Mr Whitfield: Then less reports we have, and the less money it costs ?—The Clerk: Yes.—Mr Whitfield: Then I shall move that we have only one report every quarter.—The Clerk: We pay only two guineas per year.—Mr Whitfield: It is enough, too; twe guineas per year is, for a small thing like that.—The Chair- man: If there was a serious epidemic in the town we should be glad to get the monthly report.—Mr Whitfield : That does not make it any better.—The matter then dropped.—This was the principal business.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The .fortnightly meeting of the Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse at Whiston on Thursday; present— Mr W A Meadows (in the chair), Revs T Chambers and J Barnacle, Messrs Joseph Griffiths, W Newscme, J Jackson, J Fidler, J Matthews, W Birchall, W Gerrard. E Johnson, T Dobell, J Lowe, J Fisher, J Leatherbarrow, and S 11 ikartley (clerk). WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT.--Th) Clerk said the Master reported there were 406 inmates in the house this week, against 422 last week ; and 417 in the correspond- ing week of last year. There were 161 boys and girls chargeable to the Union; there had been 56 vagrants re- lieved during the week, and precisely a similar number in the corresponding week of last year. THE CIIARGES AGAINST UNION OFFICIALS.—The Local Government Board wrote stating that they had received the application for them to institute an official inquiry into the charges preferred by Mr W Law against Dr. Hall, medical officer of health for the Prescot Uninn, and added that after Dr. Hall had furnished them with explanations, they would further communicate with the Guardians on the sub- ject. A letter from the Local Government Board dated 26th ult was read, in which they stated that as Mr Law also made certain allegations against the clerk (Mr Hartley), they were desirous of being furnished with any observations or explanations be might desire to offer in regard to them.— The Clerk added that in reply to the latter communication ..he had stated that he preferred to reserve any observations or explanations until a public inquiry was held, fie asked the Guardians to say whetner or not he should engage lezal assistance in defence of the Guardians and their officials. He did not think the officials Ought to be called upon to per- sonally pay for defending the good name of the Prescot Union, for the charges against the Guardians were much more serieus than against either himself or Dr Hall.--The Rev T Chambers moved that the clerk be ordered to obtain legal assistance ha the matter if necessary.—Mr Fidler seconded the motion, and remarked that they ought to try to get to the man Law, and prosecute him criminally for making his allegations—Mr E Johnson expressed the opinion that before they instructed the •clerk to obtain legal assistance the Guardians should know definitely that a pub- lic inquiry was being held.—The Clerk said be might re• ceive notice of the public inquiry before the next meeting, and be wanted permission to engage legal assistance at once n that case.—The Rev T Chambers said they ought to be prepared for such an emergency as that.—The Clerk added he would not incur any expense unless he was certain a public Inquiry was being held..--The motion was ultimately carried nnanimeusly. THE WIDNES RELIEVING OFEICER.—Mr John Scannel,

.. -- relieving officer, Widnes, having applied for a vacant post in the Burnley Union, asked the clerk to procure a testi- monial on We behalf from the Guardians.—The Clerk said he had replied to Mr Scannell's letter to the effect that during the three years Mr Scannell had been in their employ

be had faithful' and efficiently performed his duties ; and , his character and conduct bad during that period been satisfactory.—The Guardians approved the clerk's action. CHEAP Itlern.—Mr W J Donaldson, of Grimsby, wrote offering to supply the inmates of the Prescot Union with cod, haddock, ling, plaice, etc., at 2id per poun4, carriage paid; or 2d per pound, carriage not paid. He could war- rant the fish to be of good quality, regularly supplied, and ' cleaned out ready for cooking.—The letter was referred to the Visiting Committee. Poem Lew CONFERENCE.—Mr W A Meadows and the Rev Father Finegan, with the Clek (Mr Hartley), were ap- pointed Union representatives at the Poor Law Conference at Manchester' RI October next. EXPENSIVE FIINEHALS.—Mr Fidler drew attention to a case which had been before the Relief Committee that morn- ing, in which it appeared that the wife of a deceased man had received £l2 from a club.; and out of this she had to pay £3 153 for a hearse and two coaches, and £2 lie 101 for a coffin, shroud, and two wreaths. He expressed the opinion that such charges were excessive, owinu to the poor circumstances of the woman; and said ho thought that the £l2 ought to have lasted her a longer period than it bad done. The Board ought not to entertain applications for ielief by poor people when so much money was unnecess- arily spent.—Ths Rev T Chambers said it would not be so bad if the £l2 had been paid to a doctor; but he thought • they should set their faces against such practices as the one in question.—Alderman Johnson suggested that the Board' should instruct someone to apply to the undertaker for a portion of the money to be refunded; and in the event of the money not being refunded that he should be exposed on account of his high charges. He (Mr Tobsson) promised to see the undertaker himself, and said he would bring the matter forwardlat tha next meeting of the guardians. THE ACCOMMODATION FOR THE Thutss. The Rev T Chambers brought before the Board the uncomfortable posi- tion of the reporters with regard to their seats, and moved that the necessary provision be afforded the re-, presentatives of the Press.—Mr Dobell seconded the motion which was carried. This was the principal business.

THE WATER RITE. Sir,—lo your issue of Saturday last appears a letter from lffr John Platt under the above heading. de not propose ta occupy my time and your columna by a detailed reply to the various allegations which the writer makes against the company and myself personally, although quite prepared with an answer to them when required. 1 mustcoafine my- self to giving an unqualified denial to the writer's assertion that the company are "making every effort just or uojust to increase the revenue," in order to "wring from the rate- payers" an increased purchase money for their undertaking. No such attempt is being made on my part—and my direc- tors, as representing the company, have no desire to press the purchase upon the Corporation, either now or at any future time. They are well content to hold their property and to receive from it such a dividend as any commercial eaterprise is reasonably entitled to expeet in return for the gods it supplies and the risks it undertake-c. At present that dividend is £5 per cut. Nevertheless the directors, knowing that the position of a Waterworks Company pre- sente points of dissimilarity. with most other commercial undertakings—it being possessed of statutory privileges which place it on a footing of independence—are willing to depart from the ordinary rule, which entitles a seller to fix his own prices, and to obtain as much as he can get from a purchaser who requires his wares, to this extent, that they are willing to abide by the rd clsion of the Local Govern- ment Board equally in Mr Ratt's case as in Mes.rs Rylands'. Only they naturally stipulate that if the question is referred to the Local Government Board, the decision ef the latter will be accepted and acted upon by Mr Platt as well as by the company. If Mr Platt declines thie proposition, as Messrs Rylands have done, the people of W arrington must draw their own inference with whom the fault really rests, and whether the secret really is that the company deni Inds excessive charges or whether it is that consumers want to get their water for less than it is reasonably wortll.—l remain, sir, your obedient servant, J'3l,lN ROSS, secretary. Warrington, September s:b, 1884.

- DRINKING WATER. F•Ja WORKPEOPLE. Mr,---Vir. Ross, Senretiry of the ;Varringtou Waterworks C onpany, thinks himself called up )n " in fairness," as he says, to put before the public in your issue of August 30M copv of a letter to us on the above subj Yet. There %souk"' have been more of "fairness " if he had, along with the ,py of the Cumpiny's letter to us, published cur reply to their c ,tumunicition, whin was as folio 019

We are favoured wlth 3r3tir 'Ater of yesterday, and regret that you decline to let us have drinking water at 81 per he id per annum, unless we cirlti pay you in addition the sum of £5 for "water closets and washing offices." We dtstinctly told Mr. floss that we u“2,1 c iniensed water for closats all wash- ing, aud that we would not t ave our closets, or offi.ce, con- n'tcl.ed with your pipe. This being the case, we do nit see why you should Insist on £5 per annum for what we shall not take from you, and we are obliged to decline to pay it. From this it will be seen that we were quite willing to pay the Waterworks Company's charge of 61. per head per annum, which is very heavy az compared with water by meter measurement ; but we were not willing, to pay £5 per annum for water for officr purposes, as we are already con- nected with our own tanks coutakiing condensed water from out steam engines, which is heter for office use. Indeed, if the Company would let rai hive water for office use for nothing, we would not COI:ISUMR it. Ours is a similar Cl5O to that which Mr Platt describes in your issue of last Saturday. We formerly got water for the whole of our workpeople at a charge of £2 a year, but tbe company declined to let us have it at that fignre any longer. Recently we aporoached the Waterworks Company, and wanted to take it for drinking by measurement, but they declined. Then we offaed to pay 61 per head per annum, and this they declined also, unless we would pay the £5 per annum already alluded to for water for office purposes which we should not take.

This puts the case fairly and correctly, and we leave your readers to form their own opinion on the matter.—We are, sir, yours faithfully, rOR RYLANDS BROTHERS, LIMITED. Warrington, September 4, 1894. Sarol. Barlow, sec. PERMITTED TO DRINK, BUT NOT TO PRAY!

Sir,—May I ask your permi.ssion to review as briefly as possible the words and deeds of certain of our borough au- thorities daring the pt'esent week ? It is by no means a pleasurable nodertaking to criticise men whom you would like to be able to cnnmend, but there are times in which can- did and fearless criticism becomes positivcly necessary in tbe interests of truth and righteousness. I believe that two of

our local bodies of officials have this week committed grave errors in judgment. and since their ernrs, as I deem them, affect matters of social order and religious freedom, I claim the right, ass religious teacher and as a Nonconformist, to call attention to th:m. First of all, I wish to protest in the strongest possible . . . . . _ . . . .

manner against the decision of the Licensing Committee at Brewster Sessions. last Tuesday, in respect of the renewal of the " off" licens7s. Your readers are aware that several memorials were p;esented to the magistrates from important public bodies in the town, respectfully urging that every possible rest lotion should be put upon the ex- tension of the liquor traffic. and especially that the Bench should use its undoubted prerogative of curtailing, if not wholly refusing the renewal of "off" licenses. The memorialists were greatly encouraged to present these memorials, which represent a very strong feeling prevalent in the borough, by the words spoken from the Bench a year ago by Mr. Alderman Davies. When, through 801113 mis- adventure, the memorial of the clergy and ministers was
then presented a wn.,lx too late, Mr. Alderman Divies ( - - - - ---- •
quote from the Guardian report of September 5, 1883), ob- served "that it SIM a very mfortunate thing that the peti- tion was not presented last Tuesday. because it would have . . . . .

armed the Bench with mor d 4uppor't in what was the intention of the magistrates, the general restriction of the of licenses." A little later, on the same occasion, the Alderman proceeded t) add, "I think a word from the magistrates as to the general character of your memorial should be said. It was a great misfortune you did not present it last week. That would have been the proper time. I believe it would have

been of great use, b c'ause there is a feeling amongst the magistrates that the granting of these off-licenses has been a great curse to the town. I might say in addition that they would have been glad to hava had the moral support which the petition was intended to give because it is well to pre- pare the public mind that when the renewal of these licenses is applied for the B nch will take seriously into considera- tion the curtailinr; of their number by some means or other consistent with justice. I have said that with the approval of my brother magistrates." Surely this was language suf- ficiently plain not to be misleading. It seems, however, that what was said was not intended to be construed earnestly. Indeed, hat Tuesday the same magistrate made very simillr comments respecting the "off " licenses,. the rest of the Beach appearing to acquiesce in his stringent criticisms. Mr Davies said that "he had come to the conclusion that

the drunkenness among females WM brought about by the off-licenses and grocers' licenses, by. means of which women could get drink under cover, as it were, of a fraud, and with- out the knowlege of their husbands." And yet, after all this brave and trite speech about the off-licenses being a "curse 0 the town," and women being enabled to "get drink under Cover of a fraud and without the knowledge of their hue- binds;" and notwithstanding the Mayor's remark that in Warrington there is an unusually large number of these licenses, after all this the Bench agreed to renew the "curse," and to continue opportunities for the widespread female drunkenness "under eoycr of a fraud" for another year! I submit that this decision is not only disappointing; it is reprehensible. It is a serious failure in a public duty, and for all the social die- order, and misery, and personal degradation which may accrue from the "off ' licenses during the next twelve months, our local magistracy will be largely responsible. It is no extenuation to say that "the first licenses being granted, a sort of quasi interest arose in those licenses." It is well known that it has been established by legal decisions over and over aglin that there is no such thing as a vested interest in a liquor lice,:se. This has been settled in the Court of Appeal before the Lords Justices Dec. 12, 1882, it being then made clear that the Act of 1882 put beer " off " licenses in the same p,sitien as " full " licenses which had no renewal as of rigbt. It would be very easy to add krona things, and they I would not be unmerited. I have, however, no wish to ani- madvert needlessly upon the action of the Bench in this matter; but they seem to lack the courage of their convic- Cone, or else to suppose that the friends of the social wel- fare of this town are to be put off by eloquent assurances and stem denunciations which, alas, mean nothing. It is because I think we have a right to expect our magistrates to act up to their own words, as well as because these officials are bound to consider first the welfare of the com- munity, and not that of any individuals, that I venture to publicly criticise their action of Tuesday last. The other matter, sir, upon which I beg leave to say a very few words, is the decision of the Town Council on Tuesday last in the matter of the room in John-street. Your readers are aware that by a previous decision of the Council a room in the Club Building in John-street had been let to two young Nonconformist Welshmen for the purpose of holding religions services in their own language. This previous decision of the Council was reversed, on the motion of :Kr Councillor Burgess, on Tuesday last. It was reversed noon the principle that corporate property should not be u5...1 for religious or political purposes. Now I am not surpris- th it Mr Councillor Burgess ehould hays ‘-en the pcsi,ion he has done in this matter. He is consis- -ith the ecclesiastical and political creed which he so ;resents. He seeks to put down that with which he ~ot agree, and does so by a resort to spc:cial pleading. as quite fair, however, he should also object to any of rooms in the Town Hall being used, as I understand they have been, for meetings of Clergy of the Church of England. In my opinion, the use of such rooms by the clergy with the consent of the authorities is quite proper. Only, it ie equally proper that the clergy of any church should enjoy similar use of the Town Hall if necessary. Corporate property belongs to the town, and is for the use of the town, without respect of party, and without restric- lion (save that of morality) of purpose. Do our councillors and aldermen know that every other town in the kingdom nearly allows what in their superior wisdom they assume the right to pro.dbit ? Is it not the flat th tt it Birmw,l.-an Mr 11-ight can address his consti- tuents in the Town Hill one evening, and the Conservative candidate another? Is it not the fact that the Manchester Town Hall has been I.9ed for religious and political gather- ings Also that the Mansion House and Guildhall, London, are used for such purposes ? And yet, forteDth, a little Cbri

score place in John-street, Warrington, which ia lying empty and unused, may not be put to a usefel purpose. because Oat purpose is religious! I can understand, I repeat, that this should appear right to Councillor largess and kis [Herds. But that Radicals, and Nonconformists, and mem- bers of the Society of Friends, should sufport such a propo- sition, is one more illustration of how good men. suffer un- consciously from the evil atmospheres they sometimes are compelled to breathe. It is an unfortunate thing that even Liberals on the Council do not vet understand the funda- mental principles of religious and political equality, or they would se that these ardent young Welshmen have a right to use this room on proper terms, and that, when vacant, any other people of any other religious or political party hove similar right upon similar terms. In my belief, the Council have neither legal nor moral right to refuse the buildings which are corporate property for any proper and moral purpose whatever for the benefit of the people. In closing may I point out the singular position our local functionaries, in some instances the same individuals, have this week assuined ? They will not hinler the " curse "of ' drin'aing, but they will hinder the blessing of prayer! Men and women may drink "under cover of a fraud" if they like ; but at any rate upon "Corporate property" they must not, by prayer and praise, seek after rigkteousness!— ! Apologising for es long a letter, yours faithfully, JOHN YONGE. ; 13, Wilson Patten-street, September 4. 1834.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held in the. Workhouse on Friday. There were present—llesers Darby- sh re (chairmen), W Long, Z Armitage, Cooper, Forster, ',Vr Houghton, J Houghton, Broadbent, Gibson, J C Sutton (clerk), William Owen (valuer and surveyor), and George Bawling (inspector). PENKETH DRAINAGE.—The CLERK reed the following letter which had been sent to the Local Government Board with regard to this subject, viz.:—My Lerds and Gentle- men,—l am directed by the Rural Sanitary Authority to in- form your honourable Board that the Peneeth Parochial Committee, after holding several meetings on the subject of the drainage of Penketh, have concluded to provide a system of settling tanks for the reception of the sewage of inhabited houses. It is proposed to fix four of these tanks (a plafi of elle of which is hereto appended) at convenient places upon the edge of the Penketla brook, the sewage bin g conducted into the tanks by means 0 pipes, and there thoroughly deodorised and treated with lime before being turned into the brook. The Authority unanimouely approve of this scheme, which it is thought will effect all that is needed; and Dr Sephton, the medical otlic?r of health, has also pro- posed his approval thereof after the ex erninetian of the plans and inspection of the ne'ghbourhood. The brook is being thoroughly cleaned out by direction of the committee, sanctioned by this Authority, and I am di-ected to ask for an early reply hereto, eta log whether the course suggested meets with the approval of your hon- ourable Board. I am at the same time to ask that your honourable Board will be pleased to issue an order de- claring the expenses incurred in carrying out the work to the " special expenses," as the Authority consider the charges will not Cllll3 un ler the definition of " special ex- penses "in sec. 22D of the Public Health Act, 1875. In reply to this communication the Local Government Board wrote that they were advised that if the effluent from the proposed tanks were discharged directly into the brook a nuisance would be mesa], and that sewage after treatment by the process referred to must be filtered through land before any approach to its full clarific Ltion could be made. It was also stated that the Local Government Board , would be willing to consider the application to declare as "special expenses" any cost incurred for the proper dispo- sal of the sewage—This reply, the clerk stated, was at pre- cent under the con3ideration of the Parochial Committee.

-- Tau SANKEY CANAL Nuisance —The Clerk stated that he had also sent the following letter to the Local Govern- ment Board, vie. :—My Lords and Gentlemen,—l am direc ted to acknowledge the receipt of your letter enclosing cor- respondence with Messrs Bolton and Johnson, inhabitants of Penketh. The Authority do not is the least question the annoyance, and in Mr Johnson's case the commercial disadvantage and loss complained of. The canal certainly emits offensive odours, ant the Authority feel grieved that they are powerless to relieve the persons who are so loca- ted as to have no choice but to endure the impurities. It is simply the old story of the Sankey brook with which Dr. Ballard is well acquainted and upon which appals and re- ports have often been made to your honourable Board; no doubt aggravated by omissions to remove accumulations of filth. Thu Authority direct me to complain in the strongest terms of the statutory difficulties by which Sanitary Author- ities are beset when attempting to preserve their bro )ks and witers from pollution, and to point out the anomaly that however oppressed with taxes and otherwise burdened a dis- trict may O', costly systems of drainage and other sanitary works may be enforced, regardless of the hardships to be borne, vet when (as in the case of the Sankey brook), a naturally pare streem of greet value if it retained its purity, is treated outside the district of the Authority as a receptacle of impure matter, poisoning its whole leneth and creating each wrongs as those complained of by Messrs Bolton and Johnson, no practicable remedy appears to be available. The canal above its junction with the brook is in a satisfactory condi- tion; it is only after receiving the contents of the brook that it becomes se foul. The Authority will rejoice to find steps taken in the direction of removing the anomaly they complained of. Meanwhile all they can apparently do is to require such rem )v al of accumulated filth as adds to the nuisance. To this end they had already be nin cerrespen deuce with the London and North-Western Railway Go, whe own and occupy the canal and extracts therefrom are herewith sent. It will be seen that the company complain of the St Helens '.Urban - Sanitary Authority, and I am directed to ask that your honourable lineard will be pleased to consider this portion of the Railway Com- pany's explanation. Beyond the correspondence with the company notices had been served upon them requiring re- moval of the accumulated matter. The Rural Sanitary Authority are quite prepared to give effect to any recom- mendation that may be made to them by your honourable Board in connection with the purification of the brook and canal.—He (the clerk) likewise read some further corres- pondence which had taken place between himself and the London and North-Western Railway Company. from whom, owing to the absence of the official in charge of the matter, he was now awaiting an answer.—Mr Cooper said he had heard that the Railway Company were taking s'ep3 to pre- vent the brook from going into the canal, and he ask.d the inspector if he knew that to be the case.—Mr Bawling said he had heard that this was being done, but he had not himself seen whether it was so or not.—The Clerk said that if the Company were dint that it was all they could do.—Mr Long: Can the Railway Company supply the canal with water without using the brook ?---Mr Cooper said they had a large supply of water at Cermill Detn.—Mr Long expressed his satisfaction with the letter which the clerk had sent to the Local Govern- ment Board, and said he was of opinion that they could not go further with the matter until they received the answer to the communications.—The further consideration of the matter was then left over till the next meeting THE Esamweern.—The Clerk said the estim ate for the half-year ending Lady Day, 1835, amounted to £lO9 4s 7d, which represented a rate of fi in thee. Tern S WAGE Vases—Some conversation took place with regard to the mariner in which the contractor performed his duty in removing the sewage in the Authority's Latchford district, in the course of which Mr Cooper referred to the Vans used by the Warrington Corporation for sewage re- moval. There was, be said, sometimes a continual stream of these vans passing along, and the gases that were given off was something abominable. He thought these vane' ought to be worked in the night-time in the same way as they were used in Manchester and other large towns.—Mr Armitage agreed with Mr Cooper that the vans were a great nuisance.—Mr Rylands : DJ they work in the night-time as well P—Mr Cooper: No.—The subject then dropped. SURTEYOR'S REPORT.—The Surveyor (Mr Owen)reported that during the month inspections had been made of Mr J Swales's five houses off Lovely-lane, which might be certi- fied for valuation, as they were completed. Mr William Bennett, of Padgate, thinking the water certificate was suf- ficient, had tenanted his cottages near Padgate station be- fore the drains had been put in. He (the surveyor) had written that the drains must be put in at once. Mr Thorn- ton submitted plans for a house at Fearnhead Cross, which might be approved. Mr Thomas Jolley submitted plans for extension of back yard to house occupied by Captain Litton, in Grappenhall, which might be approved. COLLINS GREEN WATER STIPELY.—The Chairman said there had been several complaints about the deficiency in the supply of water at Collins Green owing to the Collins Green Colliery Company pumping the water and then selling it to the St. Helens Corporation —The Clerk said that if private owners of property were affected by the company action they could take proceedings against them.—Mr Broadbent thought the scarcity of water would affect the sanitary condition of the district.—Mr Derbyshire said the colliery company had the right to the coal, but he did not think they had any right to take the water.—Mr Rylands : The property owners can apply for RR injunction.—The Clerk said there was no law in the woeld to prevent people from clearing water off their property, and then disposing of it in a legal manner. If water was wanted from the company it would have to be purchased.—The matter then dropped and the business concluded.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES. :was what they asked him to remain ter after the reporters RUNCORN BWIRD OF ,COMMISSIONEES. retired, because it was a question he might have refused to The monthly meeting was held at the Town Halle Water- discuss with them in the presence of the reporters. Mr R Shaw presided glad to say the law clerk did consent to reduce his bill by £6O and there were present Messrs Meadowcroft, Priechard, was why they dealt with this matter when the reporters throu the way in which they approached him. That • gh White, Taylor, Fisher, Fairhurst, Lightburn, Dobson, Wil- had retired.—Mr Lake' Hams, lithe, Brookes (secretary), and Barker (eurveyor,). 1 . s motion was not oecondade and the meetin terminated. TWENTY DEATHS FRO) DIARHCE A.—The Medical Clficer g of Health reported that the number of deaths registered in I Runcorn for the past month amount to 50. Of these deaths I 20 were due to diarhcei, 7 to abdominal diseases. 6 to scar- latina, 5 to cardiac diseases, 3 to cerebral diseases. L to childbirth, representing a death rate of 40 per 1000 per annum. Two incpeets were held. Total deaths 52. Twelve deaths occurred amongst children three years and undertand were under one year. The death rate was considerably in- creased owing to the epidemic of diarrhoea consequent on the intensely hot weather which prevailed during the month, —The Surveyor said during the corresponding month last year there were 27 deaths. There had not been so great a mortality for several years as deflate the present month. WHO SHALL RULE P CONISS.7.7SH OR B ann. —On the minutes of the last meeting being read, Mr Lake said there was no report from the Election Committee, who were in- ' structed to supply a register of voters. He understood that no such register had been provided by the committee, who had of their Own sweet will disregarded the wishes of the Board. They had set their own opinion in oppoeition to ! the will of the Board. It was now too late to obtain one, and the result would be thatthe election could not be car- ried on with that convenience and expedition and comfort to • all parties that might have been had the register been pro- 1. sided. The Board should make it clearly understood that e when a committee was instructed it should take the requi- site steps or the Board should be called together before it I was too late.—The Chairman remarked that the chairman of the committee was not present.—Mr Fisher said that all he -could say in the absence of the chairman was that the committee after going into the matter thoroughly considered , that it was establishing a thing that had never been done before, and they really could not see any necessity for it. They farther thought it would be a useless expenditure of , about £8 or £lO, which it would cost to provide the register, ' as the assistant overseer would be present at the election , with his rate back, and he had always been able to far to settle vicious points satisfactorily.— nee Chairman thought I tho register of voters would have been of great advantage. because while the rate bock gave the occupiers th it were mi- -1 titled to vote, it did not give the owners. Therefore there might be some difficulty in reference to the matter. Some years ago a register of voters was prepered, and he thought that to provide one occasionally it would be an ; advantage, and would enable the returning officer to • comply with the Act of Parliament in a better way than he could now.—Mr Fisher said the register would simply have been a copy of the rate book, but the names might perhaps , be placed in alphabetical order, and that was the only ad- vantage that would be gained.—Mr Lightburn remarked that perhaps the committee came to a wise conclusion, bat • lithe Board deputed certain work to a committee it was pot • for that committee to say whether that work ehould or • should not be don,.—The Chairman concluded the discus- sion by the remark that as a rills committees ought to carry i out the instructions of the Board. Taw Fistwomena' Rineris.—Tita PROVISIae Ow Daum- 'Na Pornenutes.—The minutes of the Highwey and Sani- tary Committee contained the following letter, dated August .25e from Mr John Williams, of Percival-line Bir.—l had occasion a few weeks since to call your attention to the absence of the water cart in this locality. If you give It a pulsing notice, or even call the attentlon of the officials ts ' It, the effect is n Alceable only by withholding it altogether, for I can safely say the cart has not been seen ID Percival-lane three times since; but I suppose we are punished for telling tales. Bo long as we here contribute to the comfort of others , In that respect, I think It ought to be reciprocated; if net , please inform one the way to enforce it. In this part of Run- co-a, I may add for your info"mation, there has been no rain , for four or five weeks, except this morning, when lam writ- log. Yesterday was enjey ible dust and wind combined. ' A memorial, signed by 25 residents in Percival-lane, com- plaining of a nuisance from the slaughte-houses was pro. • tented. Resolved that a reply be sent stating that the matter was under consideration, and that the surveyor be ! instructed to consider and report upon the boat means of deal- jog with the nuisance. The committee farther recommended " That a Parliamentary and Legal Committee consider the • question of the right of the friarquis of Cholmondeley to • lease the quarrying in Runcorn Hill, and as to whether such right is not vested in the Dacher of Lancaster, and further, that if the Committtee are of opinion that the right is in the Duchy, to communicate with the Chancellor of the Duchy on the matter. And that the Parliamentary and Legal Committee take into consideration the question of ac- quiring the rights of the freeholders in the Runcorn Corn- ' mon, and that they be empowered to take such proceedings as they may be advised to acquire such rights." Letter was read from Major Orred's agent, asking what the Cream's- sioners intended to do with reference to repairing the fence in Clifton-road. Resolution that a reply be sent stating that tee fence had been approved and adopted by the agent when it was first erected.—Messrs Norman, Dobsoo, and White were appointed a sub-committee to consider the ad- visability of providing drialring fountains.— the Chairman moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr Pritchard seconded the motion. Referring to the question of drinking lean- t time, he said in was very probable that the sprinch spring would not be fit for drinking purposes ageio, bat as they all knew the pipes of the Water Company passed by the foun- tain in Bridge-greet, and he thought a reasonable arrange- ment might be made with the company to supply water to that fountain for drinking purposes only. It was a reflec- tion upon the Board that during the intense heat of the last summer the fountain should stand there, a sham fountain to deceive every thirsty being that might approach for a cool- ing draft.—Mr Lightburn said he should like to know what the Parliamentary and Legal Committee had done with res- pect to the stopping of the road on Runcorn HIII.—The Chairman replied that the committee were asking for powers to investigate that matter and take what steps the Law Clerk might consider alvisable.—Mr Liglifeurn took it that action should have been taken with respect to ' the road a week ago, in justice to the people ' and Mr Guest, because Runcorn Hill was really ' the people's park, of which they ought not to be deprived. If Mr Guest had no right to destroy the road the sooner he was informed of the fact the better, be- cause the longer it was delayed the greater would be the cost of putting it right. As agent to Mr Johnson he wrote to Mr Guest on Friday the 23th August requesting him to make good the road he had destroyed and make good the obstruction in the field. Mr Guest gave private reasons for his proceedings. One was that he had had permission to do what he had from a person who had no tight to give him permission, and secondly that he would have the road made good by Christmes.—The Chairman suggested that an addition should be merle to the minute on the subject to the effect, that the Paeliamentary and Legal Committee take steps to prevent the roads on the Hill being obstructed or destroyed. —Mr Lightburn proposed, and Mr Lake seconded the amendment as suggested.—Mr sleadowcroft wished for some informetion on the subject. The minutes supposed that the Marquis of Cholmondeley had no rights in Runcorn Hill. They must remem- ber that the Marquis had been exercising those rights for a considerable period, and he was not aware that they had bean questioned before.—The Chairman did not think it would be wise, supposing they had more in- formation than they had to at present discuss the rights of the Marquis of Chohnondeley with reference to Runcorn Hill. No legal proceedings could be taken without the sub- ject being brought before the Board again.—The minutes were Caen passed as amended THI INFEC TIMIS BOSPITAL.—ANOTTIER WARD TO EH BUILT.—The Garret Boats and Hospital Committee recom• mended that the female ward at the Infectious Hospital (as shown on the approved plans) be erected and furnished; that tenders be obtained, and the cost defrayed out of loan repayable in SO years. Mrs Sophia Bowles was appointed nurse.—The Chairman moved, and Mr Fisher seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr Pritchard asked for an ex- planation with regard to the erection of a female ward.—Mr Lightburn said that if they were to take their place upon the ordinary platform of civilisation they should at least have an hospital where they could separate one sex from the other.—The Chairman explained that there were only four beds la the hoepltal now. If they divided the room with two beds in each compartment, and there were four patients— three men and a woman—they would be in the same diffi- culty as now. It was found by experienced men that it would costae much to put up a temporary as a permanent erection.—Mr Dobson considered that it was not necessary to spend £3OO on the hospital at the present time.—Mr Fisher said the Local Government Board passed the plans as a whole, and they were not aware but that the female ward was erected.—The minutes were passed. FtelaNcs —The Finance Committee's minutes contained the usual summary of receipts for the past month. It was resolved that notice be published to require perm mt of the General District Rate. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr Fisher. TNE BEASLEY LITIGATION' AN APPLICATION AND AN Exemeerareom—A. letter was read from Mr 0 Leak reques- ting that on behalf of the Ratepayers Association he should be allowed to inspect the pleadings and other documents in the action Beasley v Commissioners.—Mr Lake understood that for a fortnight before the auditor came all these docu- ments would be open for inspection as a matter of course, and by granting permission for them to be examined now, they were only allowing them to ascertain what was done a little earlier. The Board had nothing to hide and if it would not inconvenience the officials of the Board, he moved that the request be granted.—Mr Lightburn agreed that they should act fearlessly in the matter. A question arose whether the pleadings were in the possession of the Board, and would be submitted to the auditor, but it could not be definitely answered.—The Chairman said there was a matter he wished to call the attention of the members to a para- graph in the Examiner of Saturday last. It was stated that the Ratepayers Association had a meeting, and one of the subjects discussed was the legal expenses incurred in the Beasley litigation, and the action of the Commissioners in passing the bill after the reporters had retired from the Boardroom Was commented upon in strong terms. It was not always wise, continued the Chairman, to refer to these matters, still when it was supposed that they were doing something when the reporters were away that ought to be done when they are there, perhaps it was only fair that they should understand exactly the position. There was no discussion on this bill at all after the reporters left. „ Every ratepayer ought to know that when the Board had entered intoobligations there was no discussion required, or necessary, about paying the bill. The law fixed what was to be done, and when they received the law clerk's bill they could have it taxed. Now the committee thought it would be wise if they could get the law clerk to make some considerable concession before the taxation of his bill. That

was completely blocked up, and, as the sewer was conveyed under gardens enclosed with thick stone walls, he recom- mended that the clearing out operations be abandoned and a new sewer constructed.—The Authority decided to con- struct a new sewer, and advertise for tenders for the woik. The meeting then concluded.
