div.p: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMIrTEE.

Tho monthly meeting of this Committee .was also held in the Workhouse, there being present Messrs Bylands (chair- man), W Long, Z ArLanage A McCorquodale, Derbyshire, Bromtbent, Appleton, J 0 Sutton (clerk), and W Owen (valuer).

• VALtER'S REPORT.—The Valuer (Mr Owen) reported that he had valued the following works and had entered the valuations in the Union books :—Messrs Slee and Co, machine works, Earlestown, gross £lO6, rateable £B5; Messrs Borron and Co , class bottle works, Newton-le-Wil- lows, works, gross £3BO, rateable £303 ; house, gross £3O, rateable £25 lOs ; house, gross £l5, rateable £l2 103 : 16 cottages, gross, £132, rateable £lOB. Since the last meeting he had made the alterations ordered by the Committee in assessment of the L. & N.-'W low level railway, in the town- ship of Warrington and Latchford, and they had been ac- cepted by Mr Edmonds on behalf of the company. He had not yet had an interview wan Mr Edmonds with respect to the high level railway.—The report was adopted. THE VALUATION OF PUILIC-HOUSES.— Ile landlord of the Bull's Head, Bridge-street, Warrington, attended and asked that the assessment of his house might be reduced because of its being above the rental. The house, he said, belonged to Sir Gilbert Greenall.— The Cu/unmet; explained that although the assessment might be in excess of the rental, that did not sht,w that it was more than tha value of the property, as public-houses were often rented at less than their market value.—Mr APPLETON contended that they ought not to assess public-house property at more than its proper value simply bec WS! a brewer might have paid a large sum for it. He thought there was not a more ill-used class than publrcans, to whom a great deal of injustice was done. The trade might be objectionable to some people, but still it was patronised, and he did not think they ought to b 3 so hard upon it.—The CHAIRMAN said they knew of many cases in which the rent of public-hous:s was not mare than half the real letting value of the houses.—Mr APPLETON did not think they dealt reasonably with publi- cans.—The CHAIRMAN : We are very anxious to do so.— Mr APPLETON: I know we do not do it..—The valuer was instructed to report as to this case.—This was all the busi- ness of public interest.

THE MANCHESTER, LIVERPOOL, AND NORTH LANCASHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. ANNUAL SHOW AT STOCKPORT. More favourab!o weather than that of Thursday could not have teen desired for the annual show of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society at Stockport. The dark clouds of the early toot log threatened a wet day, but they were dispelled, and towards soon brilliant sunshine prevailed, and there was consequently a considerable influx of visitors into Stockport from Manches'er and the surrounding district. It must, however, be acknowledged that the lumbers of visitors to the show did not equal the anticipations of the executive of the society. Special trains were run from almost all parts ' of Lancashire and Cheshire, and every inducement was offered to bring about a successful financial result. The day's takings only reached £3OO, but this was irrespective of the amount that had been paid for tickets by the 3,000 and old pasteboard-holders who pissed through the gates. It is expected that on Saturday the working-classes from Manchester will assemble on the show-ground in large num- bers. The sum offered for competition in the various classes exceeds £2OOO. The show-ground is situated a little over half a mile from the London and North-Western Railway Station, and it has been exceedingly well laid out for the purposes of the society ; and although it does not cover a large area, there is grouped upon it a collection of exhibits that must setisfy, in point of (panty, the most fastidious agriculturist, The entries in the aggregate are considerably less than the total of the show last year at Liverpool, the total being 2,690, as compared with 4.,147 at Liverpool. In all classes there has been a decrease. The entries of live stock number 470; of roots, cheese, grain, and butter there are 92 entries; implements and miscellaneous articles num- ber 1,469; and the poultry and dogs total up 659. The implements, machinery, ate., were on the ground on Wednes- day, and the quality of these exhibits was on that day ad- judicated upon. Seldom has there been seen ouch an immense gathering of appliances adapted to the purposes of agricul- ture. Taere are steam traction engines in great variety, and innumerable implements of various kinds. Messrs Richmond and Chandler, of Manchester, received the society' gold medal for an implement which has been devised to cut grass and other material and throw it into silos. The same firm were awarded a prize for a collection of machinery for chaff-cutting, slicing and pulping roots, grinding corn, and proViding food for cattle. Messrs W N Nicholson and Son, Newark, in this competition were highly commended, as also were Messrs Picksley, Sims, and Co., Leigh. The first prize was given to Mr Thomas Hunter, of Maybele, for a collection of implements for the cultivation of land. In this section Mr D Harkes, Knut,ford. received the commendation of the judges. Mr H Bracewell, Barniev, for a collection of lorries, waggons, and carts for general work, took first honours. Messrs J A Lavrton and Co, of Hardman-street, Liverpool, were awarded the first prize in the carriage competition. They exhibited a very handsome and choice collection of conveyances of various descriptions, including a C-spring victoria, which obtained a special medel, and brougheme, landaus and vic- tories of splendid style and fi fish. They were also the recipients of a special medal for a metal and wooden dog- cart, the workmanship of which was of a very superier character. In this class Mr C S Windover, of London and Manchester, was highly commended. For the beat collec- tion of hurdles, field, and garden gates, ant other farm fix- tures, Messrs Francis Morton and Co, Liverpool, obtained the first prize. Messrs T Bradford and Co, Manchester and Loncloo, were fi st for a collection of chums and other requisites for the manufacture of butter. Mr T Corbett, Shrewsbury, was awarded a special prize for a new chaff cutter to be worked by horse or steam power. Althoneti, comparatively speaking, There(' ay's- show of cattle was not numerous, the aniin ale displayed points of general excellence which fitted them for c iraparison with any of their predecessors in the society's competitions. The shorthorns were unexceptionally fine, and included some of the best animals in the country. For the best bull above two years bat under four, first homours fell to Mr William C comer, Nantivich, who showed hi 3 celebrated " Sir Staf ford." Mr George Cook, of Chester, took the first prize for the best bull above one but under two years old. There were but six entries in the class for the best cow above three years old, in milk or calf. "Roes," belonging to Mr James Dickinson. of Upholland, Wigan, won the first prize. In the class for a family of shorthorns, consisting of one bull, one cow, and two of her offspring, there were only two entries. Mr James Dickinson was again sucessful in carrying off the premier award. The prize of the society's gold medal or £lO for the best bull of any age or breed was awarded to Mr John Rowley, of Doncaster who exhibited his famous "Self Esteem." Mr T H Hut- chioson, of Catterick, was deemed by the judges to be the possessor of the best cow of any age or breed. 'The Channel Islands cattle were but a smell display. Welsh cattle were not numerous. Major Platt, Bangor, an enthusiastic agri- culturist, and well-known exhibitor of this class of stock, was first with his "Black Prince," in the competition for the best bull above one year old. He also took the first prizes for the best cow above three years and for the best heifer calved in 1882. The dairy cattle were of very high quality, and the classes were well filled, the awards meeting with the approbation of the visitors. In one or two in- stances, however, the judges had some difficulty in coming to a decision. There was a magnificient show of draught horses. Hunter stallions, roadster stallions, hunters and ' roadsters, cobs, and ponies in harness were all good, and some of the draught horses and mares were grand specimens. The cart horses and leapers were also worthy of the commen- dation bestowed upon them by the judges and the visitors. Sheep were a level lot, and of better than the average character, but there were few of them. The earns observa- tion will apply to the pigs. The Earl ef Ellesmere, in this department, was the largest and most successful exhibitor. Cheese, butter, and cured meats and farm and garden pro- duce formed agreeable features of the show. Dog ftficiers had the opportunity of enjoying to the full the spectacle of the assemblage of some of the finest members of the canine tribe in the country. Especially deserving of mention were the mastiffs, collies, fox terriers, and several of the St Bernards'. The class for bulldogs contained two or three exceptionally admirable dogs. Of poultry there was an immense variety, some of the best known exhi- bitors being represented. The leaping contest attracted a good deal of atteation, and passed off satisfactorily on the whole. One rider was thrown at the water jump, but he fortunately escaped unhurt beyond a severe shaking. The arrangements of the show were most ad- mirably conducted under the superitendence of Mr Rigby,' the secretary,

THE LICENSING Quagriorr. The temperance party in Warrington have determined upon making a stand in de- fence of their prin.dples at the Barough Court on Monday next, the day fix,.tl for hearing new applications for licen- ses. They have secured the services of a distinguished Manchester barrister, and we understand that the licensed victuallers will also be represented by counsel. Derroauous ECONOIAY.—Mr Rowland Taylor, borough coroner, held an inquest at Bolton, on Monday, on the body of Henry Isherwood, a ballast maa employed by the Lanca- shire and Yorkshire Railway Company. Deceased left his home at Darcy Lever for Brindle Heath en the 20th ult, and at night was seen in Hall-lane, Farnworth, on his way home. It was about ten o'clock, and although the night was dark, the lamps were not lighted. A carter in the em- ployment of a firm of chemical manufacturers was returning with two horses and a lorry, the wheels of which passed over decnased, who died from his injuries at the Bolton In- firmary. It Wad stated that the lamps had been lit since the accident, and the coroner remarked that Farnworth had an economical Local Board. There was no economy in keeping the lamps unlit, and the accident was purely attri- butable to a want of light. The best thing to bring Local Board officials to their senses would be to commit some of them for manslaughter. A verdict cf "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: BLOCKING BTRLI.EI,-, WIDNEE BY MANUFACTUREAS.
div.p: BLOCKING BTRLI.EI,-, WIDNEE BY MANUFACTUREAS.

A special meeting of the NVidnes Lecal Board took .place on Thuis lay. Mr F H Gossage presided, and there were also present—Messrs Pankhere, Midwood, Wright.. Forster, Dalton, G skell, Martley, Sadler, Houghton, Dr O'keeffe, T Allen (clerk), Higginson (surveyor).—The subject under consideration was an alleged stoppage of two public thoroughfares by Messrs T Bolton and Sons, copper manu- facturers. Mr Midwood,as chairman of the Highway Com- mittee, was asked to intrec.'.uce the question by the chairman. Lls !said his attention had been c died to the proceedings of the firm by the chairman of the Health Committee. He I found that they were puttigg up a building, for which no IVeins had been deposited with the committee. He called a , meeting of the Highway Committee, who wrote the firm, stating that they must submit a plan, as the building was within 30 feet of a dwelling-ho,use. A plau was afterwards sent, and Mr Bolton saw the committee and regretted that the regulation of the Board lead not been complied with. After submitting the plan, Mr Belton requested to be allowed to block up the street, but he was told that he could not be allosed to do anything of the kind, as the owners , I would sh:ject. The firm next purchased from Mr I I Kershaw twelve houses which were in the way. On inspecting the place a few days ago, the street was found ,to be blocked up with slag and cinders. In fact, both West- ' bank and Feel-streets were blocked ira this manner. The • manager of the works bad been told that the obstructions must be removed. In addition to this, a wall had been built Iright across West-bank-street, enclosing a portion of land o r both sides and the public sewer. A letter hal also been received from the Rev, Fattier Clarke, complaining that the obstructions seriously interfered with the 700 children who attended St. Patrick's School, and expressing a hope that the Board would not tolerate the high handed proceedings , of the tircn.—Messrs Lightburn and Fisher, of the Runcorn I Building Society, attended the meeting as a deputation, and, after a brief interview, were informed by the chairman that they might rest assured the Board would do their duty, and take all necessary steps for the protection of tile public against these very improper proceedings. Mr Oppenheirn, solicitor, was then called into the room, and expressed the opinion that as the public had had the nnobstrucled use of the road for over twenty years, Messrs Bolton had no legal right to interfere with the West Bank-street. —Mr Midwood : I main- tain that any ratepayer in the town could go and knock the whole thing down, and that Messrs Bolton would have no legal remedy.—Mr Allen (clerk) said the board had had to forcibly take down two erections in the past—one at SiMM3 Cross, and the other in a case where the Cbeshire Lines Railway Company attempted to lay some rails across the main road.—Mr Oppeuheim said the legal decisions were clear as to the board having power as surveyors of the high- ways to remove such elestruction.—After some further dis- cussion, it was unanimously resolved, on the motion of Mr Midwood, secosded by Mr Sadler, that the board should give Messrs Bolton and Sons 24 hours' notice to remove the walls and rubbish which had been placed by them in West Bank and Peel streets, and restore the thoroughfares to their ori- ginal condition; and the, failing this, Mr fligginson, sur- veyor, be instructed to remove the walls and rubbish with- out further notice. It was also mentioned that, if necessary, the aid of Inspector Wood, of the Widnes police force, should be called in.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr J W Ashton presided, and there were pre- sent—The Revs Canon B relay, J W N Tanner, John Lock- wood ; Messrs R Ashton, Aaron, Weir, Hamilton, Rigby, J Midwood, Jackson, Campkin, Andrews, Neild, Mclntyre, Linaker (clerk), and W H Linaker (deputy clerk). FINANCL—Au estimate of the general expenses of the Authority for the half-year ending Lady Day, 1835. It shswed that the bance in favour of the Authority at Lady Day, 1884, was £114; and the cells, Michaelmas half-year, amounted to £253; total, £367. The expenditure during the half-year was £373, showing a balance against the Au- thority of £6. The estimated expenditure for the next half-year was £143, after deducting a Parliamentary grant of £l3O towards the salaries of the tnedicil officar and the inspector of nuisances. The rateable value of the Au- thority's district was £160,917, and a rate of lin the £ would realise £163.

THE FEVER OUTBREAK AT SUTTON.—Dr Tovey, assis- tant to Dr Adams, medical officer of health, reported that I he had visited a hones at Wilderspeel, Appleton, where a young man was suffering from typhoid fever. The house was situated near the river side, from which during the late hot weather very font smells had arisen. Dr Tovey also reported that ten deaths had occurred from typhoid fever at Suttoe, and one at Dutton, which had been visited and reported upon by Dr Adam°. A death from scarlatina had occurred at Weston.—The Clerk said he should like the chairman to ask the Inspector of Nuisances whether the first case of fever at Sutton was not an imported case. If so, whether it was even reported to the Board as such, and also whether there was any report from the 21st April to the o,h July, when the first death took place ; whether during that time the public pump belonging to the Board, and from which the majority of the inhabitants drank water, was not out of order and entirely neglected.—The Rev J Lock- wood: Whose fault was that.—The Clerk : It was the fault of the Authority.—The Rev J Lockwood pointed out that a special committee had been ap- pointed to inquire into the fever at Sutton.— The Clerk remarked that the case at Dutton was imported from Sutton, and the first case at Sutton was imported from elsewhere.—Tee Rev J Lockwood What was the duty of the inspector with regard to this case 2—The Cie It ought to have been reported to the Authority as art im- ported ease. lam not quite satisfied whether I shall not ask for an inspector from the Local Government Beard to come down —Mr- Mclntyre then moved that James Far- rington be re-appointed inspector of nuisances for one year from the 29th September, 1884, at a salary of £l4O per annum, and also as inspector of canal boats for the same period at a salary of £lO per annum. Mr Mclntyre said there was us doubt that Mr Farrington WAS a very efficient officer.—Mr Aaron seconded the motion, and spoke in terms of praise of the way in which Mr Farrington did his labours. —The Rev Canon Barclay (who entered the room afrer the proceedings had commenced) said he had heard great Com- plaints of Mr Farrington neglecting his duty. He did not say that he had seen it himself, but he thought it would be as well that the Authority should say that th.er were not satisaed with the way in which he discharged his duty, and general conduct, and appoint him for three month on Probi- tion —Mr Aaron said he should not like to heau that the Inspector had everybody's good name. He should be afraid he was doing work that owners of property ought to do.—Mr Campkin stated that there were four cases of typ- hoid fever at Dutton, and note death had occurred there. There were lodgers in the house where the first case took place, and he thought Mr Farrington was to blame in not sending the patient into the hospital at once.—At the sug- gestion of the Rev J Lockwood Mr Farrington was celled into the room.—The Chairman asked him if he could tell the Board whether the first case of typhoid fever at Sutton was imported or how it arose.—Mr Farrington said he could not. He did not hear of the case until the man was con- valescent. In answer to further questions, Mr Farrington said the pump Was out of order when the first case occur- red, and for two or three weeks afterwards. He might men- tion that these people did uot drink water from the public pump at all, so that it really mode no difference to them. He described that the well from which they ob- tained water while the public pump was out of order was about 30 yards from a closet, and he thought slops had con- taminated the water. At the time of the outbreak at Sutton a man named Barnes lived at Leach's farm there. The family began to be ill one after the other, and Barnes also was taken ill and he west away. He made numerous in- quiries in order to ascertain where Brown was, and he was twice told that he had gone to Cattenhall to a distant rela- tion.—Mr Campkin thonght it was the duty of the inspector when he knew there was a case of fever at Dutton to ascer- tain how many persons were in the house, and whether it was a suitable place.—Mr Farrington: Dr Adams went there. We had no power to remove him. He is not a pauper.— Reference was made to the fever at Sutton, and Mr Farrington said it was a great mistake they did not know of the first case, but they would never receive proper infor- mation of those cases until there was compulsory notifica- cation,—Mr Farrington then retired.—Mr Campkin seconded the amendment. He considered Mr Farrington bad neg- lected his duty.—Mr Rigby suggested that they should try the inspector at the rate of £lOO a year. They paid him vastly too much money.--Five members voted for the amendment and seven for the original motion. The motion was therefore carried.—Mr Farrington was celled into the room and informed of his appointment by the Chairman, , who said he felt it his duty to tell him that there bad been several complaints about the way his work had been carted out, and that he had not consequently been appointed unanimonsly.—Mr Farrington said he did not know that he had been remiss in any way, but if he had he should be glad to make amendment for it. His district was a very large one, and if some little matters had not been attended to at the moment the delay had not occurred intentionally, Mr Weir moved, and Mr Aaron seconded that Mr Farring- ton be empowered to destroy clothing that had been used about the person of a patient when he thought it neces- -BTV.

THE INSPECTOR AND THE DARESBURY MAGISTRATES Mr Farrington reported the result of the case against Messrs Perks and Son at the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on the pre- vious Tuesday, and added that the chairman of the magis- trates, in dismissing the case, administered a rebuke to him. He must say that the statement that he got up his evidence in an indifferent, clumsy way was incorrect. On the present occasion he was represented by Mr Browne, of Warrington. —The Chairman : Have you had any cases dismissed before ?—Mr Farrington : Yes.—The Chairman : I cannot see how the chairman could say you were to blame if you were legally represented.

TnE-Oci) 41:TAY Chaist.—Mr Farrington presented an elaborate report of an examination of the Old Quay Canal. It was referred to the solicitor of the Authority (Mr W H Linaker), to consider and advise the Board.—On the motion of Mr Mclntyre, seconded by Mr Ashton, £2 was voted to the inspector to cover his disbursements in connection with the inspection. SMALLPDX AT CREWE. —The outbreak of smallpox at Crewe is assuming a serious aspect. Daring the week seven fresh cases have been reported including one of the nurses at the hospital, three members of a family living next door to the hospital, and a carter who is believed to have caught the infection while delivering provisions for the patients. One death has occurred.

G"'S HOSPITAL—The Medical Session commences on WEDNESDAY, October Ist The Hospital contsins, besides the beds for Medical and Sur- gical cases, wards for Obstetric, Opthalm'c, and other special departments. Special classes are held in the Hospital for students preparing for the Examinations of the University of Lendon and of other examining boards. APPOINTMENTS.—The House-Burgeons and House-Physicians, the Obstetric Residents, Clinical Assistants, and Dressers are selected from the students according to merit and without pay- ment. There are also a large number of Junior Appointmects, every part of the Hospital Practice being systematically em- ployed for instruction. LATEST NEWS. Charles Foster, stockbroker, was committed for trial on Friday, at Leeds, charged with forging bills of exchange. CRICKET.—Tbe Australian innings closed yesterday for 233 ; Zingari had lost three wickets for 45 when the stumps were drawn. Mr Piet Joubert has accepted the presidency of the new Boer Republic in Zululand. By the will of the late Duke of Wellington, states Vanity Fair, the Duchess gets a sum of £1 500 ready money, £lO,OOO to buy a house, and a jointure of £4,000 a year. An express train from. Liverpool-street, London, to Brighton, ran into a gang of platelayers between Sydenbam I and Forest Hill Station en Friday morning, and killed two of them. At Sheffield, on Friday, a fish dealer named Isaac Stave- ley was fined £25 for exposing for sale kippered herrings, which were putrid. Eighty boxes of herrings were seized on defendant's premises. Mr Joseph Arch, in the coure of a series of addresses he has been delivering this week to the labourers of South Norfolk, has intimated that it is not improbable he will con- test that division at the next dissolution. • DREADFUL FATALITY Ili CRESHIRE.—On Friday morn- ing Mr. Churton, coroner, Chester, held an inquest at Acton on the body of Richard Leech, a canal boatman. The de- ceased was assisting to open Dutton Locks, when the great windlass at which he was assisting slipped from his grasp in consequence of a portion of the machinery giving way ; and, hitting him on the head, clove his skull open. He was killed instantaneously. A verdict of "Accidental death " was returned. FATAL AND DESTRUCTIVE THUNDERSTORM IN SCOT- LAND.—During a severe thunderstorm on Thursday, Fern- bank House, Scone, Perthshire was set on fire by lightning, and the furniture was totally destroyed. A house was struck and greatly damaged at Blairgowrie. A young man was killed by lightning at Stromness, and at Dalguisse, on the Highland Railway, the station agent was struck and ren- dered insensible. Last night seven degrees of frost were registered at Kin,guisse, Inverness-shire. THE NILE EXPEDITION. The Government have taken up another small transport. Her n aise is the Neptuno, and he belongs to Tatham and Co., Liverpool. She is of about five hundred tons register. She will be ready to load with stores and provisions for Egypt on Monday. COLLIERS' STRIKE. At the meeting of colliers on strike held on Friday after- noon, at Netherton, Dudley, it was stated that at a meeting of masters and men it had been decided to refer the dispute to five arbitrators unconnected with the coal trade. This decision was accepted, and it is probable work will be re- sumed in the meantime. THE DUKE OF EDINBURGH AT CORK. The Cork Harbour Commissioners on Friday presented an address to the Duke of Edinburgh, on board the Minotaur, flagship of the Channel Squ sdrou at Queenstown. The Mayor of Cork was present. His Royal Highness subse- quently launched with Cork Yacht Club, and then returned to the flagship. A large crowd had assembled on the quay, and the band of the King's Liverpool Regiment performed the National Anthem, and the Minotaur, with the other vessels of the Channel fleet, left Queenstown at four p.m. WRECK OF A NEW ZEALAND BOUND SHIP. WELLINGTON, FRIDAY.—The ship Lastinghatn, bound from London to Wellington, has been lost in Cork Strait. All on board perished, except fourteen of the crew. REPULSE OF REBEL ATTACK ON KASSALA. SOUAKIM, FRIDAY.—News has just been received here that Kassala has been attamted in great force by the rebels, who were detested with heavy loss. All was well at Mas- sawah and Senkit. THE CZAR'S VISIT TO POLAND. BERLIN, FRIDAY.—It now appears certain that the Em- peror of RUSSiI will travel to Warsaw by rail, as a special inspection of the line is being made, and military patrols are posted at frequent intervals along the entire route. Tao Emperor will review the troops at Moscow on his arrival there on the Bth inst. The provisions her the Imperial table, during his Majesty's stay, will be supplied direct from St Petersburg. THE CHOLERA ROME, FRIDAY EVENING.—The cholera epidemic at Naples continues. Signor Maneini, foreign minister, has been visiting the hospitals. A general order of the Local Government Board, dated Friday, appears in the Lonion Gazette prohibiting the land- ing of rags from Italy at any port in England or Wales ex- cept for the purpose of export, or unless they shall be proved to the satisfaction of the local sanitary authority not to have come from any place where cholera has occurred ' during the present year.

CADISIIEAD. SUDDEN Darns—There was rather a sudden death of a child about nine years of age, David Arstall, on Tuesday. It was in the school in the morning, but was taken with sud- den illness. The master sent it home, and in a few bourS the child died. The cause of death, it is understood, was exhaustion through diarrhoea. COTTAGE GARDENER'S ,SOCIETY.—Tbe fourth annual show of the above society wee held in a field near the Rail- way Hotel, on Saturday. Though friend "Sol," who this year has " ruled the roast," did not favour it with hia presence, but sent " Jupiter Pluvius " instead ; yet the show proved a great success. There were 42 classes, neatly 200 entries, and 50 competitors. About £l5 was awarded in prizes. The exhibits were arranged in a tent 25 yards by 12. The window plants were especially beautiful. In vegetables, potatoes, onions, and cibbages were very good. A plate of six potatoes, grown by Mr Wm Barber, ireglied 7lbs 13oz. A model garden, cmtaining 30 beds, a conser- vatory, and a hall with grounds (the work of Mrs Har- greaves and Miss Ingham), was kindly lent by E Har- greaves, ER] , Mill Bank Hall, Partington. Another attrac- tion was a model corn stack get up by Mr George Whitfield, of the Railway Inn. The judges were Mr T Plant, of Sale, and Mr Auater, of Mill Bank Hall. About 700 visitors paid for admission, thus testifying to the increasing popularity of the show. The Cadishead brass band was in attendance, and contributed greatly to the enjoyment of everyone. The Midland Railway Company's waggon works at Sheffield were destroyed by fire on Wednesday night. The damage is estimated at £5OOO. PROPOSED RAILWAY TO AIIBLESIDE.—A committee of the Clverston Local Beard reported on Tuesday that they bad met a similar committee from Am bleside and considered The plans and sections prepared by Mr Donaldson, and, subject to any deviation or alteration which might thereafter be thought desirable, have approved the same. Directions were given to ascertain whether the landowners through whose land the line would pass were favourable. Very satisfactory replies were received, and it wan reported that the engineer- ing difficulties were slight, and the line could be made from the Farness Railway to Hawkshead and Ambleside for from £7,000 to £lO,OOO per mile.
